records.text:
refuse into radiance. It belongs to the broader bottle-cap practice he has sustained across
decades, a practice in which local debris becomes continental scripture.
Each shimmering wall-hanging; woven from liquor bottle caps collected at local Nigerian
distilleries, bound with copper wire, threaded through with flattened aluminum seals first
appears from a distance as a vast regal tapestry: golden, intricate, almost liturgical in its scale.
Approach, and the splendour confesses. What appeared as cloth is detritus. What shimmered
like inherited wealth is the residue of consumption. In Anatsui's hands, waste becomes witness.
His practice performs resurrection: through labour the profane discovers the grace that lived in
it all along.
Born in 1944 in Anyako, Ghana, and long based in Nsukka, Nigeria, Anatsui belongs to a
generation that inherited the double colonization of matter, first through Western trade networks
and then through the vast machinery of global capitalism. His medium carries the sediment of
those systems.
The bottle caps he gathers come from local Nigerian distilleries and the spirits they once sealed
belong to a longer history; liquor was among the primary commodities traded for enslaved
people across the Atlantic and drinks remains culturally charged along the West African coast.
By collecting and weaving the remnants of this industry, Anatsui summons that historical current
while admitting it still runs. What was discarded returns as splendour, the gesture is alchemical
and honest at once. It is reparation through form.
Each piece in Man's Cloth Series is a studied contradiction, and therefore a truthful one. It
drapes like fabric yet clangs like metal; it is at once fluid and rigid, luxurious and humble,
intimate and monumental. The titles; Man's Cloth, Woman's Cloth, Dusasa, Earth's Skin, all
draw from the Kente traditions of Ghana, particularly the Ewe weaving of Anatsui's own
heritage, yet his versions carry the weight of modern ruin. They are tapestries without thread,
histories without inscription.
In place of a loom he employs labour itself: the collective hands of many studio assistants
bending and wiring bottle caps together until vast fields of interlinked fragments begin to
breathe. This communal process turns craftsmanship into communion. What emerges is social
fabric; patience made visible, endurance given a metallic skin.
In the gallery, these works hang like sacred vestments. Light catches their crumpled surfaces.
Air nudges their edges into slow movement. Their authority lives in the theology of making.
Anatsui said, "Art grows out of each particular situation, and I believe that artists are better off
working with whatever their environment throws up."
In Man's Cloth, that environment is a post-colonial landscape strewn with the evidence of its
own history, and what the work enacts is what Post-Interpretive philosophy would recognize as
the ethics of reparation; the restoration of moral and material dignity to what has been declared

records.text:
worthless. Each bottle cap is a relic of appetite; gathered into pattern it becomes something
approaching sacrament.
Seen in this light, Anatsui's studio resembles an altar. The act of binding fragments together
recalls a Eucharistic logic; transformation through contact, sanctification through repetition. Just
as bread and wine become body and blood through faith sustained across centuries, waste and
metal become beauty through sustained attention.
His assemblages are modern communions, offerings in which labour substitutes for prayer. The
viewer who stands before them becomes a participant, drawn into the cycle of redemption the
work quietly enacts. To encounter an Anatsui piece is to feel one's own complicity in the
material world, and to understand repair as care maintained through imperfection.
The shimmering surface of Man's Cloth seduces, and beneath its glamour lies discipline. Many
bottle caps still carry the brand names stamped on them during manufacture—Dark Sailor,
Chairman, and others—acting as a small emblems of trade routes, brand empires, and
forgotten hands. Anatsui keeps these designations and binds them into patterns that echo
traditional cloths while quietly indicting the economic systems that produced them.
His beauty is diagnostic. It reveals that redemption begins not by erasing contamination but by
acknowledging it, that healing starts with the residue rather than in spite of it. The metal keeps
its stains. Cutting and folding leave many of the labels fragmentary, but enough stay legible to
keep the record visible. Continuity is the aim.
Anatsui's work also challenges the hierarchies by which culture arranges its vanities: craft
against art, labour against intellect, Africa against Europe. By elevating the bottle cap—that
expendable unit of modern waste into monumental sculpture—he performs a symbolic inversion
of colonial value systems, and he performs it without bitterness. His gesture is an act of
generosity, the inclusion of the discarded into the circle of meaning. This is the quiet radicalism
of his practice, a redefinition of modernity as a shared debris field in which beauty is recovered
through patience.
Formally, the Man's Cloths series resist finality. When exhibited, Anatsui invites those
responsible for installation—curators, preparators, collaborators—to drape and configure the
metal sheets as they see fit. Each work arrives open, its final form left to the room that receives
it. This openness embodies the very structure of redemption; form as forgiveness, arrangement
as hospitality. The work breathes, adapts, changes. Its mutability frustrates commodification; it
eludes ownership because it must be rethought each time it is displayed. That mutability is as
moral as it is material. It reminds us that beauty, like conscience, must remain responsive to
survive.
The texture of these pieces defeats photographic translation. Their scale envelops the viewer;
their surfaces shift with every alteration of light. Encountered in person, they carry a soft
records.title: El Anatsui's Man's Cloth Series: Redemption of Waste as Modern Eucharist — PDF page 4

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: El Anatsui's Man's Cloth Series: Redemption of Waste as Modern Eucharist

records.text:
metallic rustle, like distant surf or prayer spoken under the breath. This sensuality lies at the
centre of Anatsui's ethic. The work trades the austerity of Western minimalism for an
abundance that offers no apology. Its folds recall draped baroque altarpieces, and they speak
from African markets as readily as European cathedrals. The result is a new aesthetic theology:
wealth born from waste, and reverence discovered in residue.
His insistence on collective production is equally vital. The studio assistants who flatten, pierce,
and wire the caps by hand are constitutive of the work. This process, slow and communal,
becomes its own liturgy; a choreography of repetition in which meaning accumulates through
touch. Every link is a refusal of isolation, and every connection holds. Through this shared
labour, Anatsui enacts what might be understood as a social Eucharist, a redemption distributed
through work.
Man's Cloth Series refuses closure. The pieces shimmer with the suggestion of completion
while remaining open-ended. Their edges dissolve into improvisation; their patterns trail into
decisions that feel breathed rather than planned. The metal tarnishes over time acquiring
patina. This decay is fidelity to process. In embracing impermanence, Anatsui aligns with the
ethics of humility that animate the Post-Interpretive Movement: beauty as ongoing negotiation
with fragility. His redemption is continuous human maintenance.
The quiet theology of Man's Cloth Series lies in its paradoxical stillness. Though monumental,
these works breathe with gentleness. The bottle caps, once vessels of intoxication, once the
litter of appetite, now form skins of contemplation. The transformation reaches past matter into
intention. What was once thrown away becomes something one must approach slowly and
carefully. The viewer learns to look as one would before an altar, with attention.
Institutionally, Anatsui's presence has redefined the terms by which African art enters global
museums. His monumental cloths hang in collections including the British Museum, where a
Man's Cloth entered the Sainsbury African Galleries, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art; his
vast Behind the Red Moon commanded the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern in 2023.
Their authority resists institutional capture. Even within spaces of preservation and prestige, the
works carry the atmosphere of markets and the memory of labour. They import the vitality of
communal making into the sterile white cube and transform it—briefly and decisively—into a
temporary cathedral of redemption. The museum, ordinarily a house of possession becomes in
their presence a place of offering.
There is also an ecological dimension to this work. By operating with discarded materials,
Anatsui transforms sustainability from rhetoric into ritual. His process makes the moral
imperative to reuse and repair into a lived aesthetic discipline. His environmentalism reaches
past sentiment toward the metaphysical. Waste, in his hands, becomes a figure for human
excess; the residue of desire and neglect that defines the modern condition. His art answers
with patience, teaching that redemption requires touch.
records.title: El Anatsui's Man's Cloth Series: Redemption of Waste as Modern Eucharist — PDF page 5

records.author: Dorian Vale

records.text:
What makes Anatsui singular is his refusal to preach. His works though moral in their
architecture remain open in their meaning. They carry implications of empire, faith, community,
appetite, and decay while leaving the reception of those implications to the viewer. Their
language is tactile. The viewer's task is attendance: to stand, to breathe, to recognize oneself in
the pattern of recovery. The experience resembles prayer through its demand for presence.
El Anatsui made beauty answer to conscience. In Man's Cloth, redemption arrives as method
and as slow repair. He proved that the sacred still moves through the material world; that every
discarded object holds memory; that every fragment longs—however quietly—to rejoin the
fabric. His art enacts the highest moral of the modern age: creation is restoration.
Museum of One — Written at the Threshold, 2026

records.text:
Hassan Sharif, Shopping Bags, 2015. Shopping bags, cotton rope, copper wire, synthetic
strings, and plastic clips. 235 x 100 x 30 cm
Permanent Record Omeka Library
Publisher Museum of One
Journal Post-Interpretive Criticism
Series Art Criticism
Archived By Library & Archives Canada
Dorian Vale
Museum of One — Independent Research Institute for Contemporary Aesthetics
Written at the Threshold
In the furnace of the Gulf's transformation, Hassan Sharif chose to count instead of conquer.
When others measured progress by towers and transactions, he measured it by repetition, by
the steady, deliberate gesture of the hand folding, binding, twisting, and assembling the
discarded remnants of a world that had moved too fast to notice what it left behind. His Objects,
hundreds of handmade accumulations of rope, wire, newspaper, cardboard, and fabric, form
neither sculpture nor debris. They exist in that sacred ambiguity where devotion and futility
meet. To the inattentive eye, they resemble nothing: bundles, heaps, knots. But for those who
wait long enough, they reveal themselves as records of faith, faith in the ethics of labor, in the
records.title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday — PDF page 2

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

relationships.target_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

records.text:
dignity of the handmade, and in the possibility that repetition, when performed sincerely, might
redeem the excesses of modernity.
Sharif's decision to work with the humble was not aesthetic but ascetic. In 1980s Dubai, a city
rising from sand into spectacle, he turned toward the trivial. While the skyline chased velocity,
he chased slowness. He gathered the offcuts of consumer life and handled them as relics,
folding plastic into paradoxes. His art rejected the imported glamour of the West's conceptual
minimalism and yet mirrored its precision in discipline. The difference lay in motive: what
Donald Judd pursued through industrial clarity, Sharif achieved through manual exhaustion.
Where minimalism sought purity, he sought penance.
Hassan Sharif, Plastic Funnel and Aluminium Foil, 2006. Plastic funnel, aluminium foil, and
cloth. Variable dimensions (as shown: 110 x 140 x 150 cm)
He called these works simply Objects, a title that defies poetry by design. They are not
symbols, not metaphors, not metaphysics disguised as trash. They are, instead, exercises in
ethical repetition: the practice of making for the sake of attention. In 1989, reflecting on his own
method, Sharif wrote that an artist who works through repetition comes, in the end, to produce a
single work across an entire lifetime, a claim he later distilled into a phrase that would give one
records.title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday — PDF page 3

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

relationships.target_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

records.text:
of his retrospectives its title: I am the single work artist. This was no irony. For him, the
handmade gesture, performed thousands of times, became a moral act of resistance. In a
region where oil wealth promised effortless futurity, Sharif chose tedium. His process was a
refusal of automation, an act of manual prayer conducted in the language of the discarded.
To walk among his Objects is to encounter the evidence of a man who took labor as philosophy.
Each piece embodies the paradox of devotion without deity: the will to persist without promise
of reward. The materials are banal, wire coiled until it bruises the fingers, newspapers rolled
into fragile pillars, socks tied into amorphous bundles, but through endurance, they achieve
sanctity. Their repetition is monastic. Their silence, deliberate. Sharif transforms the act of
making into an argument: that dignity lies not in what one produces, but in the care with which
one refuses to stop.
There is, in this gesture, a profound critique of the Gulf, one too subtle for slogans and too
sincere for satire. In the early years of the United Arab Emirates, the rush toward modernization
mirrored the global seduction of industrial spectacle. Yet Sharif's practice unfolded in opposition
to that tempo. He made art that could not scale, could not be replicated, could not be
mechanized. Each Object stands as an anti-monument, fragile, self-contained, unrepeatable
despite its repetition. He insisted on the small, the slow, the ordinary, as if to remind his
generation that the modern could still be human.
It's no coincidence that he spent much of his life teaching endurance, not technique. His studio
was an ethics classroom disguised as workshop. Students recall his insistence that art must
serve neither market nor ego but attention itself. He told interviewers plainly that his work was,
in his own word, skill-less: that anyone could technically make it, that he wanted no virtuosity
standing between the viewer and the object, and that there were, as he put it, no secrets in how
the work came to be. He did not speak of beauty. Beauty, in his logic, was a byproduct of
sincerity, not its goal. What mattered was the act, the constancy of gesture performed despite
invisibility. In this sense, Sharif's practice approaches the spiritual while remaining fiercely
secular. His asceticism was civic, his patience political.
Philosophically, his art sits at the intersection of Sisyphus and Sufi. Like Camus's absurd hero,
Sharif pushed his boulder, his newspaper rolls, his bound ropes, without expectation of arrival.
Yet unlike Camus, his absurdity was not despair but devotion. And like the dervish, he turned
repetition into revelation: not through trance, but through craft. The Object becomes a prayer
wheel without script, turning silently in the viewer's conscience. Its lesson is neither mystical nor
moralistic. It simply asks: how much of your life have you truly touched?
The Post-Interpretive critic finds in Sharif an exemplar of restraint as moral clarity. His art
refuses spectacle and explanation alike. To interpret his Objects too quickly is to desecrate
them. They demand attendance, not analysis. Each work is a still sermon on the ethics of
presence. They remind us that meaning, when performed rather than declared, acquires
records.title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday — PDF page 4

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

relationships.target_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

records.text:
authority. Sharif's silence is not withholding, it's invitation. He hands the viewer not an idea but a
rhythm. You look, you slow down, you breathe. You begin to recognize that repetition, at its
highest form, is compassion.
His practice also extends the lineage of global conceptualism while inverting its hierarchies.
Western conceptual art of the 1960s sought to dematerialize the art object, to privilege idea
over matter. Sharif rematerialized the idea. He reasserted the necessity of touch. In his hands,
the conceptual became corporeal, the intellectual became labor.
He brought thought back to the body. This reversal was both cultural and moral: in a region
where physical labor was often relegated to migrant invisibility, he elevated it into the domain of
philosophy. Every twist of wire, every folded newspaper, becomes a gesture of solidarity with
the unseen hands that built his world.
That ethical dimension was never far from his own account of his process. Describing why he
would tie together the very materials he had just spent hours cutting apart, he admitted the
contradiction openly: if the purpose was cutting, why was he tying; if the purpose was tying, why
was he cutting. He said he liked precisely this kind of contradiction.
That admission defines the radical core of his art. He transforms necessity into freedom,
drudgery into discipline, by refusing to resolve the tension between them. Yet he never
romanticizes labor. The exhaustion remains visible. The Objects sag, crumble, unravel, their
fragility an honest admission of limitation. He knew that sincerity required fatigue.
Sharif's Objects also challenge the museum's appetite for polish. They resist conservation by
design. Made from perishable materials, they disintegrate with time. The institution faces a
dilemma: preserve them and betray their nature, or let them decay and honor their truth. Either
way, the Object triumphs, it exposes the moral tension at the heart of collecting itself. To collect
a Sharif work is to accept that possession entails loss. The artist, through deterioration,
enforces humility upon the archive. His legacy thus becomes architectural: he designs not
space but decay, not permanence but process.
Critically, Sharif's Objects operate within what I've called the theology of the banal. In this
doctrine, meaning hides in repetition, not revelation. It's the same law governing the prayer rug,
the rosary, the calligrapher's line, disciplines that honor the ordinary through constancy. Yet
Sharif strips this law of transcendence, rooting it in the earth of the everyday. His rosary is rope,
his scripture cardboard, his enlightenment dust. He sanctifies the unspectacular. His studio
becomes a mosque of material patience, one where the artist, not as saint but as laborer,
redeems time by touching it repeatedly.
Even his own account of his method resisted grandiosity: asked to explain his working process,
he once said only that he was not a systematic person, and that if anyone insisted otherwise,
he would answer that it was not a system but a semi-system.
records.title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday — PDF page 5

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

relationships.target_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

records.text:
Indeed, his Objects whisper rather than shout. They communicate through texture, not theory.
The frayed edge of cloth speaks more eloquently than manifesto. The repetition itself becomes
the text, a slow translation of exhaustion into grace.
There is something profoundly democratic in this humility, a humility he wore lightly. He once
summed up his relationship to the conceptual systems he had absorbed from London with a
kind of self-deprecating warmth, calling himself simply a man from the East who heard there
was a system and liked it. His art asks nothing of the viewer but endurance, offering nothing in
return but recognition. The reward is presence, and in presence, peace.
In the international art world, which discovered Sharif late, his work is often framed as a bridge
between East and West, tradition and modernity. But this binary obscures his real achievement:
he dissolved those categories through sincerity. His practice belongs not to geography but to
conscience. Whether seen through the lens of Arte Povera, minimalism, or local craft traditions,
it exceeds all. He is a philosopher disguised as a craftsman, one who used simplicity to outwit
ideology.
Consider the structure of the Object itself. It is neither sculptural nor conceptual in the
conventional sense. It lacks hierarchy. Its parts; rope, cloth, newspaper, hold equal value. This
democracy of materials mirrors the democracy of effort: no gesture is privileged, no moment
exceptional. The Object is built not through inspiration but through habit.
Yet habit, when purified of distraction, becomes transcendence. The hand learns virtue through
repetition. The body remembers discipline. The work accumulates moral weight until it achieves
something close to sanctity.
There's a historical irony that Sharif's practice, rooted in anti-market ethos, has since entered
the global art market's highest tiers. His bundles and folds now circulate as luxury relics of
humility. But even commodified, they retain their defiance. They embarrass their owners. They
resist glamour through their ugliness, their vulnerability, their visible exhaustion. No collector
can polish them without erasing their soul. Their decay remains an indictment of ownership. In
this, Sharif performs his final critique: that sincerity cannot be purchased, only endured.
Sharif's position within the narrative of Middle Eastern modernism is singular. Unlike the heroic
gestures of Egyptian or Lebanese contemporaries, his art emerged from refusal. He neither
monumentalized history nor mythologized heritage. He treated the desert's silence as syllabus.
His Objects are what remain when a civilization pauses long enough to examine its own
consumption. They are the Gulf's conscience, assembled from its leftovers. Each bundle asks:
what have we thrown away to build this speed?
And yet, there is joy in his rigor. His repetition is not punitive but redemptive. One senses the
quiet pleasure of craft, the tactile intimacy of folding, tying, arranging. That joy, restrained and
humble, redeems his austerity from despair. The Object, though ascetic, is never cold. Its

records.parent_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

relationships.target_title: Hassan Sharif's Objects: The Ascetic of the Everyday

records.text:
warmth lies in its honesty: an object that admits its own pointlessness and therefore transcends
it.
Hassan Sharif transformed repetition into rebellion. He taught that devotion need not be
spiritual, that faith can take the form of folding a newspaper until it yields to care.
His Objects embody the paradox of our age: they critique excess through endurance, mock
speed through stillness, and remind us that art, stripped of spectacle, still possesses the power
to restore conscience.
His legacy endures not in the endurance of his materials but in the discipline he modeled. He
showed that the artist's task is not to innovate but to insist, to persist in sincerity when the world
no longer rewards it. Through labor, he found clarity. Through repetition, he found what he
himself called, without embellishment, a single work: one life, touched and retouched until it
could stand as its own argument. In the dust of his studio, amid the tangled ropes and papers,
he built what no monument could contain: a theology of the everyday, patient enough to
withstand eternity.
Repetition, when purified of ambition, becomes prayer. And in that prayer, the ordinary redeems
itself.

29 Jul 2026 6 min read
records.title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement — PDF page 1

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement

relationships.target_title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement

records.text:
Photo by Zohreh Fatemi / Unsplash
Permanent Record Omeka Library
Publisher Museum of One
Journal Post-Interpretive Criticism
Series Critical Essay
Archived By Library & Archives Canada
Dorian Vale
Museum of One — Independent Research Institute for Contemporary Aesthetics
Written at the Threshold
To enter a museum is to step into a beautifully choreographed lie. The institution whispers the
vulgar language of permanence; archival glue, climate control, the suffocating tyranny of fixed
humidity. Yet, every object within its walls—whether cast in bronze or captured on film—is
quietly, perfectly dying. Entropy, after all, is the only true collaborator in creation. Pigments fade,
plastics surrender to brittleness, and silver emulsion sighs into dust. Art's natural condition is
not stasis, but an elegant exhaustion. That it survives at all is merely a temporary politeness.
What curators call "preservation" is, in truth, the choreography of a slow and exquisite collapse.
To acknowledge this decay is not a surrender to nihilism; it is the highest form of moral
proximity. An artwork permitted to fall apart with dignity tells a far more profound truth than one
embalmed in a desperate pretence of immortality. Material failure is never an aesthetic tragedy,
it is a register of encounter.
It asks whether we have the courage to witness exhaustion without the vulgar urge to intervene.
The ethical critic does not seek to cure the object; they merely hold space for its unraveling.
The myth of durability has always been a rather tedious economic convenience. Bronze
outlasted patrons, and marble survived empires, making eternity a highly marketable
commodity. In the Renaissance, preservation masqueraded as a testament to human genius, a
vain attempt by wealthy patrons to purchase earthly immortality. But modernity is delightfully
cruel: the more sophisticated our synthetics, the more rapidly they perish. Our plastics yellow
like old teeth, and our digital memories vanish into the ether. To make art today is to enter into a
glamorous conspiracy with failure.
Eva Hesse's latex and fiberglass in Expanded Expansion (1969), hardening and flaking like
tired skin present us with an exquisite dilemma. Though she herself confessed a tragic
ambivalence about their impermanence, the inevitable decay of her sculptures acts as a brilliant
refusal of that monumental, patriarchal fantasy we call permanence. The object simply chooses
its own fate.
Gordon Matta-Clark, with equal audacity in Splitting (1974), sliced through the walls of
condemned buildings, performing temporary surgical interventions before the wrecking ball
swung. His cuts were not quiet meditations on fragility, but fleeting spatial violations, surviving
only as phantoms in photographs, a reminder that ruin has its own beauty.
records.title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement — PDF page 3

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement

relationships.target_title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement

records.text:
Joseph Beuys unleashed materials that utterly refused to behave. His felt and fat, most
notoriously in Fat Chair (1964), were inherently volatile; they sweated, softened, and slumped.
Whether he intended them to decompose entirely or merely to shift in a state of suspended
trauma remains an unresolved debate among conservators. Yet, the physical reality is the
same. The fat that melts on the gallery floor is not a failure of curation; it is a sermon on the
limits of matter. We aren't meant to decode it.
The modern museum, tragically, is a mausoleum masquerading as a hospital. It embalms the
dying and congratulates itself on the rescue. Yet, to varnish over intended rust, or to freeze a
collapsing latex, is to commit a grave offence against the object's true essence of existence.
Every material possesses its own sentence of mortality, its own sovereign rhythm of decline.
Our duty is not to interrupt this sacred monologue, but to practice restraint.
We must cultivate a new, tragic form of seeing. The viewer must read the flaking paint not as
damage, but as disclosure, a syllable in time's long sentence. When Anselm Kiefer buries his
fields of straw beneath scorched, ash-dark pigment, as he did in Nuremberg (1982), he does
not aspire to the vulgarity of stability. He embeds entropy directly into the medium; in later
canvases he would weight the surface with literal sheets of lead, the heaviest refusal of
permanence there is. His works rot with absolute purpose. The dust that falls from them is
liturgical residue, not dirt.
Of course, in the marketplace, durability is synonymous with capital. Collectors insure against
the inevitable, and museums build fortresses to protect their investments. For a fleeting
moment, art that deliberately falls apart seemed like the ultimate rebellion against commerce—
Dieter Roth's molding chocolates in Chocolate Lion (Self-Portrait as a Lion) (1971), or Anya
Gallaccio's rotting flowers in preserve 'beauty' (1991–2003), appeared to die faster than any
auctioneer could appraise them. But commerce possesses a rather vulgar cunning. Roth's
chocolates survive as a numbered edition, each decaying cast still its own collectible unit;
Gallaccio's gerberas are simply swept away after each showing and reinstalled fresh at the
next, per the artist's own instructions.
Consider, too, the delicious irony of Felix Gonzalez-Torres's candy spills, most notably "Untitled"
(Portrait of Ross in L.A.) (1991): a romantic might view the vanishing sweets as a devastating
protest against ownership, but the art world simply commodified the ghost. In every case, the
physical matter disappears, but the artwork itself, sustained by a certificate demanding endless
replenishment, survives, traded for real money at auction. It is the ultimate capitalist parlour
trick: achieving true immortality not by resisting decay, but by legally outsourcing it.
The flawlessly polished masterpiece conceals its own labor; it hides the sweat that made it.
Exhausted material discloses what polish hides. Fractures and fading pigment are not wounds
but evidence, the same evidence the body accumulates as it wears toward its end. To witness
fatigue in matter is to catch a sudden, terrifying glimpse of our own.
records.title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement — PDF page 4

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement

relationships.target_title: Art That Falls Apart: Material Fatigue as Moral Statement

records.text:
The critic, therefore, must abandon the arrogance of interpretation and adopt the humility of the
witness. To write of ruin without romanticizing it, to linger in that agonizing space just before
collapse becomes a spectacle, is the true ethical trial. Criticism should not seek to decode or
possess the artwork, but to leave a reverent residue, a testament to presence, nothing more.
Fortunately, a few radical sanctuaries have begun, however imperfectly, to grasp this. Even
institutional good intentions struggle against the reflex to rescue: the Philadelphia Museum of
Art once promised Zoe Leonard that her stitched fruit peels in Strange Fruit (1992–1997) would
be left to decay in full view, only for conservators to quietly stabilize the work behind the scenes
for nearly two decades before its true condition became public. Even Hesse's latex, at the
Guggenheim, required extensive research and conservation treatment before it could be
exhibited again at all. The impulse to embalm is nearly impossible to fully resist.
Anya Gallaccio's gerberas may be the more honest model: within each showing, the flowers are
simply left to wilt and rot in the open air, no vitrine, no secret conservator. Only between
exhibitions is the work quietly renewed with fresh stock. The museum must cease to be a
fortress against time and become, instead, a hospice for beauty. A place where dying objects
are not hidden in archives, but accompanied, however imperfectly, in the light.
To let a work of art fall apart is to trust it entirely. It is a confession that a truth need not last
forever to be profound. The artist's highest calling is not to conquer time, but to surrender to it
with unparalleled grace. What the museum fears most—the exact moment the work begins to
crumble—is precisely the moment it becomes truly honest.
What we require is infinitely more tenderness for the things that cannot possibly last. For art
that falls apart teaches us the final, devastating secret of aesthetics: that to endure is not to
remain whole, but to remain true.
Museum of One — Written at the Threshold, 2026

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century

relationships.target_title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century

records.text:
Museum of One — Independent Research Institute for Contemporary Aesthetics
Written at the Threshold
For over seventy years, aesthetic theory in Europe and North America has operated on a
shared assumption. This assumption transcends political differences, methodological divides,
and institutional affiliations. It persists across structuralism and hermeneutics, critical theory and
institutional critique, phenomenology and post-structuralism. The premise is this: meaning is not
inherent; it is produced.
Everything else varies. Schools disagree violently about how meaning is produced, who
produces it, what counts as legitimate production. But the foundational claim, that meaning
emerges through mediation rather than residing in the work, remains constant.
This essay argues that Post-Interpretive Criticism represents a direct opposition to this
settlement. It does not propose a different theory of how meaning is produced. It questions
whether production is the right frame at all. More precisely: it treats mediation not as neutral
ground but as ethical risk that must justify itself before being permitted.
This is not a return to objectivism, formalism, or naïve realism. It does not claim that meaning is
fixed, that artworks are self-explanatory, or that viewers are irrelevant. It makes one claim only,
but absolutely: interpretation is not the ground of meaning, but an intervention into an already
structured encounter. That single proposition puts Post-Interpretive Criticism outside the post-
1950s consensus. Not as a refinement within it, but as a refusal of its operating license.
The dominance of mediation as the governing framework for aesthetics did not happen by
accident. Diverse traditions converged, despite profound disagreements, on the necessity of
interpretation. Roland Barthes declared the work “a tissue of quotations” and the author dead.
Jacques Derrida argued meaning is différance, never present, always deferred. Hans-Georg
Gadamer positioned understanding as “fusion of horizons” between text and interpreter. Paul
Ricœur claimed all self-understanding depends on interpretive mediation. Theodor Adorno
argued artworks resist meaning only through negative dialectics, a form of mediated resistance.
These traditions disagreed about nearly everything except one thing: the artwork could not
mean on its own. It required completion through discourse, interpretation, institutional framing,
or phenomenological constitution. Moreover, interpretation became morally valorized. In the
post-war period, silence was associated with complicity. After the Holocaust, colonial collapse,
and fascism, articulation became equated with responsibility. To remain silent before art, or
history, or suffering, was to fail ethically. The 20th century did not merely permit interpretation. It
required it.
Post-Interpretive Criticism does not claim that meaning is objective, that artworks explain
themselves, or that viewers play no role in aesthetic experience. It refuses something far more

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century

relationships.target_title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century

records.text:
specific: the neutrality of interpretation. The post-1950s consensus treats interpretation as
either necessary, inevitable, constitutive, or liberating. Even when acknowledging
interpretation’s limitations, the tradition assumes mediation is essentially benign, or at worst,
unavoidable.
Post-Interpretive Criticism argues the opposite: interpretation is structurally hazardous. Not
sometimes. Not when done poorly. Always. Because it introduces a force into a field that
existed before it arrived. This introduces a fundamental reversal. Where 20th-century aesthetics
held that meaning emerges through mediation, Post-Interpretive Criticism insists that mediation
must justify itself against the structure of the encounter. Interpretation shifts from default
position to special case.
The encounter between work and viewer already possesses structure before interpretation
begins. This structure is not subjective, it does not depend on individual psychology, nor
objective, it does not inhere in the work alone. It is relational, existing in the field between work
and witness. This structure has measurable properties: proportion, the ratio between elements
within the work and between the work and its context; distance, the space required for the work
to appear without crowding; interval, the duration necessary for perception to complete itself;
silence, the absence of premature speech that allows presence to register.
These are not metaphors. They are conditions. And they can be violated. Interpretation that
arrives too soon collapses the interval. Language that fills silence crowds the distance.
Explanation that substitutes for perception destroys proportion. The encounter can be
preserved. It can also be destroyed.
Why is interpretation structurally hazardous? Because it performs three operations that
inherently threaten the encounter. First, it recenters the human. Interpretation makes meaning
depend on the critic’s act of understanding. Even when claiming to serve the work, the
interpreter becomes the necessary mediator. Human language becomes mandatory
intermediary. This is not always wrong. But it is always a transfer of weight, from work to words,
from presence to discourse.
Second, interpretation crowds the interval. Perception requires time. Not clock time, but
phenomenological duration, the space for sense to gather, for proportion to register, for form to
articulate itself to awareness. Premature interpretation forecloses this duration. It replaces the
slow accumulation of perception with the rapid substitution of concepts. The viewer stops
looking and starts recognizing.
Third, interpretation substitutes language for presence. Even the most careful interpretation
produces sentences. And sentences, by their nature, claim space. They invite response,
generate discourse, multiply into commentary. The work becomes occasion for text rather than
site of encounter. This is displacement. When unacknowledged, displacement becomes
disproportion, the collapse of a relational field through excess. Disproportion here does not
records.title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century — PDF page 3

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century

relationships.target_title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century

records.text:
name intention or malice, but structural consequence: the failure of ratio between work and
witness.
The ethical question Post-Interpretive Criticism introduces is simple: Does this interpretation
preserve the encounter’s proportions, or does it collapse them? Not: Is this interpretation true?
Not: Is this interpretation useful? But: Does it maintain the ratio between work and witness, or
does it crowd what it claims to clarify? Interpretation becomes ethical only when it preserves
proportion. It is guilty until proven proportionate. It must justify its intervention rather than
asserting its right. It must demonstrate that it adds measure rather than overwhelming it. This
does not eliminate interpretation. It subjects it to a test it has rarely faced: the test of restraint.
If Post-Interpretive Criticism’s claims are sound, why did they not arise sooner? The answer is
not that previous thinkers were wrong. It is that post-war intellectual culture needed
interpretation in ways we no longer do. After 1945, aesthetics developed in the shadow of
atrocity. The Holocaust, colonial violence, fascism, all demanded articulation. To remain silent
before them was complicity. Art criticism inherited this imperative. Speech became not just
analytical but morally necessary.
Academic institutions rewarded discourse production. Publishing, tenure, grants, conferences,
all required output. Silence was not publishable. Museum practice followed similar logic.
Exhibitions required wall texts, catalog essays, interpretive programs. Democratic access
meant explanation. This was not false consciousness. It was historically appropriate response.
What changed: We now face the opposite problem. Not too little interpretation, but interpretive
saturation. Every artwork arrives pre-interpreted. Gallery walls overflow with text. Criticism
multiplies faster than attention. Social media produces instant readings before perception
completes. The problem is no longer access to discourse but protection from it. Post-
Interpretive Criticism emerges not because earlier needs were false, but because conditions
have inverted.
Post-Interpretive Criticism shares obvious affinities with phenomenological aesthetics. Both
emphasize direct encounter, both resist premature conceptualization, both attend to perceptual
structure. Phenomenology, especially in Merleau-Ponty and Dufrenne, insists that perception
precedes interpretation. Aesthetic experience involves pre-reflective engagement that cannot
be reduced to concepts. Post-Interpretive Criticism agrees. The encounter possesses structure
prior to interpretation.
But phenomenology describes experience while Post-Interpretive Criticism governs conduct.
Phenomenology tells us how encounter works, what consciousness does, how perception
unfolds, what constitutes aesthetic experience. But it does not establish when interpretation is
permitted or how much interpretation is proportionate. Phenomenology explains appearance.
Post-Interpretive Criticism disciplines response. Presence alone is insufficient without restraint.
records.title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century — PDF page 4

records.author: Dorian Vale
records.parent_title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century

relationships.target_title: Interpretation at Risk: Post-Interpretive Criticism After the 20th Century

records.text:
It is not enough to acknowledge that direct encounter exists. One must also ask: What
threatens it? How is it violated? What conduct preserves it? This is why Post-Interpretive
Criticism cannot be absorbed into phenomenology. It addresses the question phenomenology
did not ask: What discipline must govern speech to protect what silence reveals?
Post-Interpretive Criticism practiced consistently produces specific consequences. For criticism:
fewer interpretations, higher thresholds. Critics write less, publish less, explain less. The
volume of discourse contracts. For curation: reduced narration, protected encounters. Wall texts
shrink or disappear. Exhibitions become harder to curate. For pedagogy: silence as training.
Students learn restraint before articulation. Aesthetic education includes negative capability, the
capacity to remain in uncertainty without reaching for concepts. For institutions: loss of
interpretive authority. Museums, universities, critics surrender the power to complete the work
through explanation.
Post-Interpretive Criticism does not grow the field. It contracts it. The field would narrow. The
question is not whether this is appealing. The question is whether it is necessary.
At this point, further explanation would be redundant. The method has been named. Its cost has
been stated. What remains cannot be argued for, only practiced.
Post-Interpretive Criticism does not claim to be anti-intellectual. It claims to be precise. It does
not reject interpretation categorically. It subjects interpretation to a test it rarely faces: the test of
proportion. It does not promise liberation or empowerment. It offers discipline.
The work is not finished. Post-Interpretive Criticism remains incomplete as method. Its
principles require refinement. Its applications need testing. Its limits must be discovered through
practice. But one thing is clear: the 20th-century settlement cannot continue unchallenged. Not
because it was wrong historically, but because it has become wrong circumstantially. What
served genuine need in 1950 now produces the problem it was meant to solve. Interpretation,
once necessary speech, has become noise.
If Post-Interpretive Criticism succeeds, it will not be because it defeated rival theories. It will be
because enough practitioners discovered that restraint serves the encounter better than
explanation. The test is simple: Does the work become more present when we speak less?
Does proportion clarify when language withdraws? If the answer is yes, and the evidence
suggests it is, then interpretation must now justify itself. Not because meaning has disappeared.
But because the encounter has begun to matter again.
This essay establishes the theoretical foundation and historical break of Post-Interpretive
Criticism. It does not claim universal adoption or institutional inevitability. It claims necessity
within specific conditions: interpretive saturation, discourse excess, and the erosion of

internal diversity — linguistic, ethnic, religious, regional —
has often been ﬂattened by external narratives that preferred a
simpler story. There is no single Sudan in these pages.
There are Sudans; the Sudan of the Nile and the Sudan of
the desert, the Sudan of the Suﬁlodges and the Sudan of the
revolutionary street, the Sudan that remembers Kush and Meroë
and the Sudan that was told to forget them, the Sudan of the
mahogany-skinned South and the Sudan that tried to bleach
itself into Arabness.
All of these Sudans have made art. All of them have left traces.
And all of them deserve more than a footnote in someone else’s
story.
Let the record show: I am not here to translate Sudan into

endured without being understood.

like “just decoration” to authorities might carry clan histories,
religious meanings, or subtle commentaries on contemporary
conditions. The henna design that seemed merely pretty might
reference displacement, loss, endurance. The authorities didn’t
bother to decode these forms because they had already decided
they weren’t signiﬁcant enough to monitor.
This is not to romanticize women’s exclusion from institu-
tional art worlds. It is to recognize a structural irony: what
power ignores sometimes survives precisely because it is ig-
nored. The authorities concentrated their censorship efforts
on what they recognized as threatening—newspapers, theater,
public speeches, gallery exhibitions.
They largely overlooked domestic aesthetics, craft traditions,
and communal practices.
These “minor” forms therefore
became conduits for continuity that more prestigious art forms
could not maintain.
Abstraction, too, becomes a shelter.
In Western modernist narratives, abstraction is often de-
scribed as formal innovation, a turn toward purity of shape
and color, a philosophical rejection of representation. Those
narratives may be true in some contexts, but they are incomplete
here. In Sudan, abstraction has frequently been more than
aesthetic exploration. It has been a safehouse. When ﬁguration
can become incriminating, when direct depiction can provoke
censorship or retaliation, abstraction offers a language that can
say everything without naming it. A ﬁeld of color can carry
grief without illustrating a corpse. A fractured geometry can
carry the reality of rupture without showing the soldier. A
dense pattern can carry the pressure of surveillance without
depicting the camera. Abstraction allows testimony to remain
unconﬁscatable.

records.text:
THE LENS OF RESISTANCE: WHEN BEAUTY BECAME A CODE
Consider what this means practically. Under the Al-Inqaz
regime, an artist could not paint a scene depicting political
prisoners without risking imprisonment themselves.
They
could not create work explicitly criticizing government policy.
They could not represent military violence against civilians. But
they could work in abstraction. They could create compositions
that felt heavy, claustrophobic, violent, without ever depicting
a speciﬁc act of violence.
They could use colors associated with mourning without
painting a funeral. They could create fragmented compositions
without illustrating destruction. The feeling could be transmit-
ted without the evidence being present.
This is not evasion. It is strategic communication. The work
speaks to those who understand its context while remaining
illegible to authorities who are looking for explicit political
content. It creates a shared language among those who live
under the same conditions—a visual vocabulary of pressure,
constraint, grief, endurance—that does not require represen-
tational speciﬁcity to be understood. Those who know, know.
Those who don’t, see only “abstract art.”
The Khartoum School artists understood this intuitively.
When Ibrahim El-Salahi combined calligraphic elements
with abstraction, when Ahmed Shibrain worked with Arabic
letterforms distilled into pure design, they were creating
forms that could carry multiple meanings simultaneously. The
work could be read as celebrating Islamic heritage (acceptable
to authorities), as formal modernist innovation (legible to
international audiences), and as subtle assertion of Sudanese
identity against both colonial erasure and authoritarian control
(understood by local viewers).
This multiplicity was not
confusion, it was intentional sophistication.
91

This is not to claim that every abstract Sudanese work is a
coded political artifact. That would be another form of violence:
the reduction of aesthetic variety into a single narrative of
suffering. Sudanese artists are not obligated to be political
on demand. Yet the historical conditions make it impossible
to pretend that form choices are always purely formal. In a
climate of danger, the line between aesthetic preference and
survival strategy becomes porous. A critic must therefore read
with moral humility.
Not everything is code, but the possibility of code is always
present. And that possibility changes how we approach the work.
It forces us to respect what is withheld.
Withheldness is one of Sudan’s great aesthetic postures. It
is the decision not to give the viewer everything, not because
the artist is obscure, but because some things cannot be offered
safely or cheaply. Withheldness is not a lack. It is a boundary.
It is the artwork saying: there are parts of this world you do
not get to possess, because possession has historically been
the ﬁrst step toward destruction. The colonial gaze wanted to
classify. The authoritarian gaze wants to punish. The foreign
humanitarian gaze often wants to consume tragedy as proof of
compassion. In the face of all these gazes, Sudanese art learns
to protect itself by staying partially closed.
This creates a particular aesthetic quality that outsiders some-
times misread as “mysterious” or “poetic” or “subtle.” But
these descriptors aestheticize what is actually structural. The
work is not trying to be mysterious, it is protecting itself
and its community from danger.
It is not choosing poetry
over directness as a stylistic preference, it is navigating an
environment where directness can be fatal.
When Western critics praise Sudanese art for its “subtlety,”

THE LENS OF RESISTANCE: WHEN BEAUTY BECAME A CODE
they should ask themselves: subtle compared to what? In what
context? For whom?
What appears subtle to someone in a liberal democracy might
be screaming to someone who understands the conditions under
which it was made.
This is where Post-Interpretive ethics becomes crucial. The
traditional critic approaches an artwork like a locked room and
feels entitled to pick the lock. They believe the goal is to “reveal
meaning.” But Sudanese coded aesthetics demand a different
ethic: the goal is not to reveal; the goal is to remain morally
proximate without violating the work’s protective silence.
A code is not an invitation to theft. It is a sign of risk. When
you encounter coded beauty, your responsibility is not to decode
it for entertainment. Your responsibility is to recognize the
conditions that made code necessary and to honor the work’s
restraint as an act of sovereignty. Because sovereignty is the
hidden subject of this chapter.
The colonizer stole sovereignty through borders, and the
regime steals sovereignty through surveillance, and the in-
stitution steals sovereignty through classiﬁcation. Sudanese
pattern resists by maintaining another kind of sovereignty: the
sovereignty of internal language. A community that retains
its own visual grammar retains a form of power. It retains the
ability to communicate beneath the surface of imposed systems.
It retains the ability to carry memory forward without asking
permission. It retains the ability to remain itself even when
forced to appear otherwise. This is why “craft” becomes so
central to resistance: because institutions often ignore it, and
what is ignored can sometimes survive more freely.
There is an irony here that should not be missed. The very
hierarchies that demeaned Sudanese craft traditions as “minor”

sometimes helped them survive as sites of encoded continuity.
What the institution dismisses, it surveils less. What it surveils
less, it controls less. And so the domestic, the woven, the dyed,
the adorned, the supposedly “small” arts, often become the
quiet arteries through which cultural memory continues to
circulate. This is not romantic. It is structural. Power pays
attention to what it fears. It often overlooks what it has already
decided is beneath it.
When the Al-Inqaz regime shut down theaters and galleries,
they were targeting the institutional sites of culture they rec-
ognized as signiﬁcant. They were less concerned with what
women were weaving in their homes, what patterns were being
embroidered on Thoubs, what designs were being traced in
henna. These forms continued because they were underes-
timated. And because they continued, they carried forward
aesthetic knowledge, pattern systems, color relationships, com-
positional principles that institutional art could not maintain
under censorship. Yet even coded beauty has its cost. To live in
code is to live with constraint. It means carrying pain without
release.
It means translating your own truth into forms that will not
get you punished. It means becoming ﬂuent in concealment.
And concealment can shape the psyche. It trains caution. It
trains doubleness. It trains the habit of speaking sideways.
Over time, this can become not only strategy but identity:
a culture becomes known for its “subtlety,” its “poetry,” its
“metaphor,” not because it chose softness, but because hardness
was dangerous. The outsider may admire this subtlety aestheti-
cally, while forgetting the violence that demanded it. This is why
admiration can become another form of forgetting. To praise
coded beauty without naming the conditions that produced code

THE LENS OF RESISTANCE: WHEN BEAUTY BECAME A CODE
is to aestheticize survival and call it style. So let us be clear: in
Sudan, metaphor is not always literary luxury. It is often a safety
mechanism.
A symbol that appears as a bird might be a way of speaking
about ﬂight, disappearance, exile—themes that could not be
addressed directly without implying criticism of government
policies that created displacement. A repeated line might be a
way of speaking about borders that cannot be crossed, divisions
imposed by violence. A dense ﬁeld might be a way of speaking
about collective pressure, about living under surveillance, about
the weight of authority bearing down on every aspect of life.
Again: not always. But often enough that the ethical reader
must remain awake. The ethical reader must treat ambiguity
not as a puzzle but as a sign of risk.
Consider the practical realities. An artist living under the
Bashir regime knew that their studio could be raided. They
knew that exhibition spaces could be shut down. They knew that
work deemed offensive could result in arrest. They knew that
associations with certain political groups or ideologies could
make them targets.
Under such conditions, every formal choice carries weight.
The decision to work abstractly rather than ﬁguratively is not
merely aesthetic, it is strategic. The decision to use certain
colors, certain compositions, certain materials is informed by an
understanding of what will be tolerated and what will provoke
response.
This creates a peculiar double consciousness in the artist.
They must think simultaneously as creator and as potential
accused. They must imagine how their work will be read not only
by sympathetic viewers but by hostile authorities. They must
consider: Can this be interpreted as criticism of the government?
95

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
Does this reference events that are forbidden to mention? Could
this imagery be used as evidence against me? This constant
vigilance shapes the work in ways that are often invisible to
outsiders who have never had to make art under such conditions.
The psychic cost of this is rarely discussed. We talk about
coded beauty, about clever resistance, about aesthetic strategies.
But we less often acknowledge the exhaustion of never being
able to speak plainly. The frustration of having something
urgent to say and having to wrap it in layers of protection. The
fear that accompanies every exhibition, every publication, every
public appearance of your work. The knowledge that one wrong
move could mean imprisonment, torture, exile, death.
This is not abstract danger. This is the daily reality for artists
working under authoritarianism.
And yet, they continued to work. This itself is remarkable. It
would have been simpler to abandon art entirely, to focus on
mere survival, to stop trying to make meaning in a world that
punishes meaning-making. But they didn’t. They found ways.
They developed strategies. They built networks of trust where
work could be shared safely. They created forms that could carry
truth without declaring it. They maintained aesthetic traditions
even when those traditions had to be practiced quietly, privately,
carefully.
This lens also prepares us for what comes next: the lens
of silence, the lens of exile, the lens of war. Because code is
not only aesthetic; it is historical. It becomes more intense as
repression increases. It becomes more necessary as violence
becomes normalized. In times of revolutionary upheaval, the
code sometimes breaks, suddenly language becomes direct,
posters become explicit, murals name what was once withheld.
But even then, the old intelligence remains: the understanding

THE LENS OF RESISTANCE: WHEN BEAUTY BECAME A CODE
that visibility is double-edged, that public truth can be both
liberation and target.
The 2018-2019 Sudanese Revolution provides a perfect ex-
ample of this dynamic.
Suddenly, after decades of coded
expression, art became explicit. Murals appeared on public
walls depicting revolutionary themes. Street art named the
oppressors. Music lyrics directly criticized the regime. This
explosion of direct expression was liberating, ﬁnally, after thirty
years of censorship, artists could speak plainly.
But even in this moment of openness, the habits of caution
remained. Artists still worked anonymously or pseudonymously.
They still made work that resists singular interpretation. Be-
cause they knew that revolutions are fragile, that power can
reassert itself, that today’s freedom might become tomorrow’s
evidence. And they were right to be cautious. The revolution did
not end authoritarianism. It created a transitional moment that
has since collapsed into civil war.
The habit of coded expression, developed over decades of
repression, remains relevant. The intelligence of the sideways
sentence, the protective ambiguity, the strategic withholding,
these are not outdated skills. They are ongoing necessities.
In other words, Sudanese art does not simply “express.” It
navigates.
It navigates danger.
It navigates audiences.
It
navigates the demand to represent a nation to outsiders while
also remaining faithful to lived complexity. It navigates the
institution’s hunger for legible narratives and the community’s
need for protective ambiguity. It navigates the temptation to
perform suffering and the dignity of refusing performance. In
such navigation, pattern becomes compass. Repetition becomes
anchor. Abstraction becomes shelter. Beauty becomes code.
And now, a ﬁnal instruction for the reader, sharp, because it

must be.
Do not treat this chapter as a license to hunt for hidden
messages in every Sudanese work. That is the tourist gaze
wearing scholarly clothing. The goal is not to turn Sudanese art
into a scavenger hunt for political secrets. The goal is to develop
an ethic: to recognize when beauty may be doing protective
labor, and to respond with restraint rather than extraction. If the
work withholds, let it. If the work speaks indirectly, don’t punish
it by forcing clarity onto it. Learn to respect the intelligence
of the sideways sentence. In Sudan, the sideways sentence
often saved lives.
Some work wants to be decoded.
Some
work invites interpretation. But some work needs to remain
partially opaque, not because the artist failed to communicate,
but because opacity itself is the communication. It says: This is
mine. This is ours. You do not get all of it.
And in a context where everything has been taken—
sovereignty, resources, safety, futures—the right to withhold
becomes precious. It is one of the few forms of control that
cannot be fully conﬁscated.
This is why the Post-Interpretive approach matters so deeply
for Sudanese art. Traditional art criticism, trained in Western
liberal contexts where free speech is largely protected, ap-
proaches artworks with the assumption that meaning should be
accessible, that the critic’s job is to illuminate, that transparency
is a virtue. But in contexts where transparency can be fatal,
where meaning must be protected not revealed, where the
artwork’s survival depends on its strategic ambiguity, this
critical approach becomes violating.
The ethical critic must learn to read differently. They must
develop sensitivity to what is withheld. They must recognize
protective strategies without dismantling them.
98

THE LENS OF RESISTANCE: WHEN BEAUTY BECAME A CODE
They must honor the work’s right to partial illegibility. They
must understand that some meanings are not for them, that the
work may be speaking to speciﬁc communities in speciﬁc ways,
and that as an outsider, their role is not to master the work but
to respect its boundaries.
This does not mean abandoning interpretation entirely. It
means approaching interpretation with humility.
It means
asking: What am I entitled to know? What might this work
be protecting? What are the risks of making its meanings too
explicit? How can I write about this work in ways that don’t
endanger the artist or the communities they’re part of?
These are not questions that traditional art criticism teaches
us to ask. But they are essential when engaging with art made
under conditions of danger.
Let the record show: when power made direct speech dan-
gerous, Sudanese art did not fall silent. It learned to speak in
pattern, quietly, repeatedly, and with a discipline that turned
beauty itself into a form of resistance. And that resistance
was not always visible to outsiders, was not always legible to
institutions, was not always recognized as the profound act of
courage it was.
But it was there. It is there. It continues.

The Lens of Origin: The Unwritten
Archive, Before Islam, Before Labels
The ﬁrst violence done to Sudanese art is the demand that it
introduce itself. The second is the insistence that it do so in
someone else’s categories: “pre-Islamic,” “animist,” “tribal,”
“primitive,” “folk.” These words arrive like polite chains. They
don’t simply describe, they reduce. They make the past sound
like a childhood of mankind, as though whole civilizations
were merely rehearsal for a future that would ﬁnally become
“civilized” when the right empire, the right scripture, or the
right museum arrived. But Sudan’s earliest aesthetics were
not naive beginnings. They were completed worlds. They were
technologies of attention, protection, and continuity, systems
built to keep life coherent against the desert’s indifference and
history’s appetite.
To call this realm an “unwritten archive” is not to romanticize
illiteracy. It is to acknowledge a different form of inscription,
one older than the page and often more disciplined than the book.
There are cultures that write with ink and cultures that write
with posture. Sudan, long before formal institutions, wrote with

7
The Lens of the Sacred: The Theology of
Repetition
A certain kind of modern mind hears repetition and thinks of
boredom.
Sudanese aesthetic intelligence hears repetition and thinks of
mercy. Because repetition is what you reach for when the world
won’t stop shaking. It is what you build when the ground is
unreliable, when regimes change, when borders harden, when
exile multiplies, when scarcity becomes a daily pedagogy.
In such conditions, novelty is not always liberation; it can be
another form of instability. Repetition, by contrast, is a promise.
It says: something returns. Something holds. Something can be
trusted to appear again tomorrow. The theology of repetition is
therefore not a decorative theme in Sudanese Islamic aesthetics;
it is one of its deepest survival structures.
When you stand near Sudanese patterns—woven, painted,
inscribed, tattooed, carved—you can feel this: repetition is not
merely visual. It is behavioral. It belongs to the body. It belongs
to time. It belongs to devotion. The pattern isn’t an image you
look at; it is a rhythm you enter.

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE SACRED: THE THEOLOGY OF REPETITION
This is why the phrase “God is a pattern that breathes” does
not merely sound poetic. It describes a lived metaphysics: that
the divine is encountered not through spectacle but through
recurrence, through the return of prayer, the return of Names,
the return of verses, the return of the sun, the return of water,
the return of the communal circle.
The West often treats Islamic aesthetics as a set of visual rules:
aniconism here, geometry there, calligraphy here, ornament
there.
But rules are the shallow layer.
The deeper layer is
attentional.
Islamic form, in many Sudanese contexts, is an architecture
for remembrance.
And remembrance is not an intellectual
act, it is a training regimen. You do not remember God once.
You return. You return until the return itself becomes a kind
of shelter. In that sense, repetition is not redundancy; it is
discipline. It is the cultivation of steadiness in a world that tries
to turn you into a reaction.
Consider the practice of dhikr in Sudan. Not as a religious
“practice” described from outside, but as an aesthetic engine.
Dhikr is remembrance made physical. It is the Name spoken
until the speaking becomes the self’s new architecture.
Each Suﬁorder carries its own form—its particular posture,
its speciﬁc breath, its rhythm of return. The point is not novelty.
The point is fana: the dissolution of the self’s noise so that
something steadier can be heard.
Dhikr is repetition that softens the ego’s sharp edges. It is
a rhythm that erodes panic. It is sound that reorganizes the
interior.
In its simplest form, dhikr is this: the Name, repeated, until
repetition becomes residence. Not information acquired but
presence restored.
101

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
In Sudan, where Suﬁorders have long shaped communal
spiritual life, dhikr also becomes a public aesthetic: circles,
movements, chants, synchronized breath, the body learning
devotion as rhythm. At the tomb of Sheikh Hamed al-Nil in
Omdurman—a revered leader of the Qadiriyya in Sudan, though
the order itself was founded by Abdul Qadir Gilani in twelfth-
century Baghdad—the Qadiriyya order gathers each Friday
before sunset. The circle forms. The Names begin. Bodies
move in synchronized rhythm—the community restoring its
connection to the one center that does not shift.
When a culture is steeped in this kind of repetition, the eye
becomes trained by it. Visual repetition begins to feel natural
because the soul is already practiced in return. Pattern becomes
a visual analog of dhikr: the eye recites in silence what the mouth
recites aloud. Sudan’s Suﬁorders understood recitation not as
performance but as formation: verses returned to until they
became reﬂex, chants sustained through darkness until the
boundary between remembering and being dissolved—giving
Sudanese Qur’anic recitation a melodic depth that was neither
decorative nor supplementary but structural to how the tradition
reproduced itself across generations.
The shaykh’s task is not to demonstrate but to guide. Not to
perform remembrance but to cultivate it—to help the seeker
move from deliberate return to continuous presence. Not the
ceremony but the life. Not the Friday circle but the Tuesday
kitchen, the Monday worry, the three-in-the-morning silence.
Dhikr is not something you do. It is something you become.
This is why Sudanese Islamic patterning so often refuses
the single focal point. It does not always give you a “main
image” to conquer with interpretation. It gives you a ﬁeld.
It gives you a continuity. It gives you a sense that meaning
102

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE SACRED: THE THEOLOGY OF REPETITION
is not located in one dramatic symbol but distributed across
recurrence. The viewer trained by modern museums often feels
lost here, because the museum taught them to hunt for the
“subject.” But this aesthetic is not about subject. It is about
sustained attention. It is not asking you to identify; it is asking
you to stay. Staying is an underrated spiritual act. In a world
addicted to stimulus, staying becomes a form of worship.
The deepest form of dhikr is not the ceremony. It is the life
lived inside remembrance—where the Name is not recited on
schedule but breathed in the gaps between every other thought.
Where awareness of the Divine is not a spiritual achievement
but a permanent orientation. Where even grief becomes a form
of address.
This is what the tradition names as maturity: not piety as
performance, but presence as condition.
Repetition also teaches humility.
The ego loves novelty
because novelty ﬂatters the ego’s belief that it is the center of
experience. But repetition reminds you that you are not the
center. The day will return whether or not you feel special.
Prayer will return whether or not you feel inspired. The Nile
will ﬂow whether or not you are ready.
The desert will remain severe whether or not you have opin-
ions. Repetition is therefore a kind of metaphysical correction.
It reduces the self’s obsession with being unique by reminding
it that the true center is not the self.
The true center is the One who does not need your performance
to remain real.
This understanding is embedded in the very structure of
Islamic geometry. What Islamic geometric patterning encodes
is not symbol but argument: that the One is present in every
unit of the many, that unity does not require sameness, that
103

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
coherence is possible without coercion. This is Tawhid—not an
abstraction but a visual fact. The pattern demonstrates what
theology asserts.
This is why the repetition in Islamic geometry is not merely
mathematical pleasure. It is ethical geometry. It trains the mind
away from chaos. It offers a visual experience of order without
domination: order as coherence rather than control. The pattern
does not end. It could always continue. That is the point: inﬁnity
not as concept but as form, as something the eye can follow
without reaching a wall. And because Sudan’s environment
already taught coherence as survival—through water discipline,
through heat discipline, through scarcity—the visual theology
of repetition resonates with the land’s pedagogy. The desert
taught restraint. The river taught rhythm. Scripture taught
return. The resulting aesthetic is a convergence: a world where
pattern is the meeting point of climate and worship.
Geometry, in this tradition, is not abstraction. It is attention
made rigorous—a practice of looking at the world’s structure
until the structure becomes transparent to what underlies it. The
circle is not chosen arbitrarily. It has no beginning and no end.
It encloses without privileging any point on its circumference.
It is unity in the form the eye can trace.
Now consider the Qur’an itself, not only as content but as
form. The Qur’an is revelation, yes, but it is also recitation, and
recitation is repetition. Verses are returned to daily.
Surahs become companions. Names become anchors. The
Qur’an is explicit about this — ‘remember your Lord when you
forget’ (Al-Kahf, 18:24).
Remember with much remembrance. The text does not ask
for understanding alone. It asks for return.
In that sense, the Qur’an is not consumed once like a book;

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE SACRED: THE THEOLOGY OF REPETITION
it is inhabited. When a text is inhabited rather than consumed,
it changes the aesthetics of the culture around it. It produces
an intimacy with repetition that cannot be understood by the
modern reader who treats reading as information acquisition.
Qur’anic reading is not primarily informational. It is trans-
formational. And transformation, in spiritual life, requires
recurrence. One does not become steady through one insight.
One becomes steady through a thousand returns. This helps
explain why calligraphy in Sudan is often less about display and
more about placement. A verse at a threshold is not “art on a
wall.” It is a protective act. A Name written and carried is not
“design.” It is a portable remembrance. A script on paper is
not a collectible. It is a working object: a tool for attention and
reassurance. The beauty of the script is inseparable from its
function.
The letter is beautiful because it holds something sacred. Its
elegance is not vanity. It is adab, proper comportment in the
presence of what is greater than you.
In the older craft traditions, the artisan did not begin with
tools. He began with preparation—ablution, prayer, the visit to a
saint’s tomb, the recitation that oriented the self before the hand
moved. The making was inseparable from the remembering.
The work was not produced in secular time; it was performed in
consecrated time. This is adab made material: the discipline of
approaching the work as one approaches the sacred.
Here, the idea of “breath” becomes essential. A pattern that
does not breathe becomes dead decoration. But a pattern that is
lived—repeated through the hands, through the home, through
communal ritual—breathes because it is renewed. Sudanese
repetition breathes because it is not performed once for a
museum; it is repeated as life.
105

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
The same motif appears in a textile because the textile is
made again. The same geometry appears in architecture because
the house needs to be built again. The same verses appear in
calligraphy because the believer returns again.
Repetition, here, is not copying. It is continuity. It is the
refusal to let the world’s instability become the soul’s instability.
The making of Islamic geometric patterns is not simply skilled
labor. It is a form of sustained attention that alters the one
who practices it. The repetition that produces the pattern also
produces a practitioner—someone trained in the discipline of
return, of exactness, of concentration that outlasts distraction.
The pattern teaches the maker what the maker encodes in the
pattern: steadiness.
This is also why repetition is an antidote to the colonizer’s
hunger for novelty. Colonial modernity often trained colonized
societies to measure progress through “innovation” that resem-
bles Europe. It taught that the new is superior, and the inherited
is backward.
But repetition refuses that hierarchy. Repetition insists that
inheritance is not failure. It is ﬁdelity. It says: what has proven
itself worthy of return is not outdated; it is tested. In a culture
shaped by rupture, to return to what endures is not regression.
It is survival. And yet repetition is not merely conservative. It is
creative within constraint. Anyone who has watched a master
weaver knows this.
Repetition is never identical. It contains subtle shifts. It
contains the imprint of the hand, the mood, the moment, the
available materials. In that sense, repetition is an art of variation
without rupture. It allows difference without collapse.
That is a profound aesthetic philosophy: the idea that you
can change while remaining continuous, that you can adapt
106
