records.text:
THE LENS OF THE SACRED: THE THEOLOGY OF REPETITION
without severing your lineage. Sudanese art embodies this con-
stantly, particularly in craft lineages where motifs travel across
generations, altered slightly by each hand but recognizable as
belonging. The pattern breathes because each repetition is alive.
The tradition is not static. Simple forms give way to more
intricate ones—simple stars becoming complex polygons, sin-
gle units generating tessellations that could tile a wall, a ﬂoor,
a dome, a world.
What changes is not the commitment to
repetition but the sophistication within it. The constraint is
the engine, not the limit. You cannot see this if you approach
the work looking for novelty. You can only see it if you stay long
enough to watch variation emerge from ﬁdelity.
This brings us to the ethical implication for the reader. If
you approach Sudanese repetition with a modernist appetite
for novelty, you will miss its intelligence.
You will call it
“decorative” because you cannot see that it is doing spiritual
labor. You will call it “traditional” as a polite dismissal. You
will treat it as background. But repetition is not background in
Sudan. Repetition is how a people holds itself together. It is how
devotion becomes embodied. It is how memory refuses erasure.
It is how the self learns that it is not sovereign.
When the circle appears in this tradition, it is not chosen
for beauty. It is chosen for argument. It argues that unity is
possible. That something can be whole without a single point
of dominance. When the star appears, it is not decoration. It
is evidence—that complexity can emerge from coherence, that
the many and the one are not enemies.
The pattern is theology made visible, made touchable, made
livable.
So when you encounter Sudanese Islamic aesthetics, ge-
ometries, scripts, rhythms, do not ask ﬁrst, What does this
107

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
represent? Ask instead, What does this return accomplish? What
does it stabilize? What does it protect? What does it hold? What
does it train the eye to prefer? What does it teach the body to
trust? Because in Sudan, the theology of repetition is not an
abstraction. It is a lived method for remaining human under
pressure. It is the refusal to let chaos become your interior
language.
It is the practice of return as dignity. It is the discovery that the
One reveals itself most honestly not in a single dramatic symbol
but in the inﬁnite patience of return—that unity does not require
uniformity, that the divine is more legible in repetition than
in spectacle. It is the proof that a tradition of constraint and
pattern, properly inhabited, does not limit the spirit but expands
it: the art that insists beauty is not vanity, but the shape devotion
takes when it refuses to be invisible.
Let the record show: in Sudanese Islamic aesthetics, repeti-
tion is not redundancy, it is mercy made visible, a pattern that
breathes so the people can breathe with it. It is the aesthetic
embodiment of a theological truth: that God’s mercy returns,
that the faithful return to God, that the pattern holds when
everything else fractures, and that in a world of relentless
rupture, the ability to return, to prayer, to community, to the
Name, to the pattern, is not stagnation but salvation.
108

8
The Lens of Sand & Scripture: Aesthetic
Islam in Sudan
Sudan did not “become Islamic” the way a textbook becomes
a chapter. It absorbed Islam the way earth absorbs rain: un-
evenly, tenderly, with regions of deep saturation and regions
of stubborn dryness, until the result was not simply religion
but climate, a way of moving through the world where devotion
becomes pattern, where the unseen becomes neighborly, and
where beauty is not a performance but an ethic.
The great mistake, when speaking of Sudanese Islamic aes-
thetics, is to approach them as derivatives: either “Arab,” or
“African,” or a mere provincial echo of grander centers. Sudan
is not an echo. Sudan is a third thing, an aesthetic thirdness
forged at the seam between desert minimalism and river mem-
ory, between oral inheritance and written revelation, between
ancestral protective technologies and Qur’anic discipline. It is
not a compromise. It is an invention. And it is an invention born
not from leisure, but from survival.
Islam spread to Sudan from the north, after the Islamic
conquest of Egypt. But this was not a sudden transformation.
109

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
rhythm, with scar, with pattern, with the careful placement of
symbols on bodies and objects, signs meant not for museums
but for weather, ancestors, illness, envy, and fate. An archive,
in this sense, is not a room of documents. It is a set of behaviors
that preserves meaning without needing to announce it. If
you stand beside these works and ask ﬁrst, “What does this
mean?” you have already missed the ethical priority. The ﬁrst
question is: “What did this do?” Because in Sudan, long before
the Western invention of “art” as a separate kingdom, form
was often inseparable from function, and beauty was not an
accessory, it was a method of survival.
There is a particular arrogance in how modern eyes approach
the ancient and the ritual. We assume that what is beautiful
must be symbolic, and what is symbolic must be optional.
But protection is not optional, memory is not optional. The
continuity of a people, especially a people living on thresholds
of heat, scarcity, migration, and political violence, has never
been a leisurely project. It requires tools, and among the oldest
tools Sudan reﬁned was the tool of form: the ability to embed
instruction into pattern, to embed boundaries into adornment,
to embed cosmology into the simplest repeated mark. A line is
never merely a line when the world is unstable. A repeated shape
is never merely decoration when repetition is the only reliable
law the earth still obeys.
So the aim of this chapter is not to “trace inﬂuences” as
though Sudan’s early forms existed to anticipate later religions
or later nations. It is to restore dignity to what was already
digniﬁed: Nubian legacies, Kushite architectures of power and
afterlife, Nilotic cosmologies of river and cattle and sky, and
a wide constellation of ritual practices—some named, some
unnamed—that treated the unseen not as superstition but as

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
Nubia had already been Christianized, largely through Egyptian
Coptic inﬂuence, though the Nubian kingdoms varied in their
Christian affiliations.
The Nubian Christian kingdoms—Nobatia, Makuria, Alo-
dia—each had their own arc, their own century of negotiation,
their own slow yielding to Islamic inﬂuence.
This long
timespan—over eight centuries from ﬁrst contact to ﬁnal
conversion—reveals something crucial: Islam in Sudan was not
imposed overnight. It was negotiated, absorbed, translated into
local idioms over generations.
The Funj, who established their sultanate in 1504, were orig-
inally non-Muslims, but the aristocracy soon adopted Islam.
Yet even as they became nominal Muslims, they retained many
traditional African customs. This pattern, official conversion
accompanied by persistence of local practices, characterizes
much of Sudanese Islamization. The conversion was largely the
work of a handful of Islamic missionaries who came to Sudan
from the larger Muslim world, but their great success was not in
replacing what existed; it was in ﬁnding ways to speak through
it.
In the 16th and 17th centuries, numerous schools of religious
learning were founded along the White Nile, and the Shāyqiyyah
confederacy was converted. Many of the more famous Sudanese
missionaries were not orthodox jurists but Suﬁholy men,
members of inﬂuential religious brotherhoods who sought the
way to God through mystical contemplation. This is crucial.
What made Suﬁsm take root here was not doctrine alone.
When Sheikh Taj Eldin El-Bahari arrived in the 16th century,
carrying the Qadiriyya tradition from Baghdad, he did not
confront the land’s existing spiritualities—he spoke through
them. The Suﬁway of attracting followers was not compulsion.
110

records.text:
THE LENS OF SAND & SCRIPTURE: AESTHETIC ISLAM IN SUDAN
It was demonstration: patience, simplicity, a form of presence
that the people recognized as coherent.
This method of Islamization matters aesthetically.
Suﬁ
orders did not arrive demanding the immediate erasure of local
practices. They arrived with patience, with ﬂexibility, with an
understanding that conversion is a process, not an event. They
allowed singing where orthodox jurists might forbid it. They
accommodated drumming where legalists might condemn it.
They found ways to channel existing devotional energies into
Islamic forms rather than simply prohibiting them. This created
a distinctly Sudanese Islam, one that drew on Suﬁorders like
the Khatmiyya, as well as the Mahdist Ansar movement—which,
though distinct from the Suﬁbrotherhoods and in many ways
critical of them, equally shaped Sudanese Islamic identity—
to spread Islam and shape Sudanese Islamic culture through
rituals, festivals, and spiritual practices that deeply inﬂuenced
Sudanese identity.
Islamic aesthetics in Sudan are often misunderstood because
outsiders confuse ornament with decoration. They see callig-
raphy and treat it as style. They see geometry and treat it as
pattern-play. They see talismanic papers and dismiss them as
superstition. They see Suﬁspaces and reduce them to “folk
Islam,” as though devotion that breathes in local lungs is less
legitimate than devotion spoken in institutional accents. This
book refuses those reductions.
In Sudan, Islamic aesthetics are not simply the adornment of
belief. They are one of belief’s most practical instruments: tools
for remembrance, protection, coherence, and mercy in a world
that has rarely offered stability.
Start with the obvious, because the obvious is often where
misunderstanding begins: the Qur’an arrives as a text, but its
111

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
presence is not only textual. It is sonic. It is spatial. It is rhyth-
mic. It reorganizes time through prayer, reorganizes speech
through recitation, reorganizes the home through thresholds
of purity, reorganizes the body through posture. And when
a religion reorganizes the body, it inevitably reorganizes the
visual. The movements of prayer teach a certain geometry of
humility. The repetition of dhikr teaches a certain rhythm of
return. The discipline of daily devotion trains the eye to prefer
order over chaos, not order as authoritarian control, but order
as refuge: the quiet reassurance that something in the universe
remains aligned even when politics fractures.
This is why Sudan’s Islamic visuality is rarely obsessed with
spectacle. It does not need to scream. It does not need to prove
itself. It tends toward what I would call reverent containment:
a beauty that holds itself back, because held-backness is one
of devotion’s oldest manners. When you stand near certain
Sudanese Islamic forms, calligraphic panels, talismanic pages,
geometric arrangements, textile repetitions, you can feel this
containment. The beauty is not trying to seduce you. It is trying
to keep you intact. It behaves like a shelter, not a stage.
And yet Sudan’s Islam is not a sterile minimalism. It is not an
imported austerity. It is not a monochrome theology. It is full
of local breath. Sudan has always had an intimate relationship
with pattern before Islam, with protective marks before Islam,
with the unseen before Islam. So when Qur’anic language enters
the aesthetic climate, it does not erase that earlier intelligence;
it inherits it, reﬁnes it, and—at times—reorients it.
The result is not a replacement but a layering.
Sudan’s
Islamic aesthetics often feel like scripture learning to speak
through sand: the clarity of revelation carried by the humility
of landscape.
112

records.text:
THE LENS OF SAND & SCRIPTURE: AESTHETIC ISLAM IN SUDAN
This is where Suﬁsm becomes central, not as exotic mysticism,
but as a social and aesthetic infrastructure. The Suﬁbrother-
hoods played a vital role in linking Sudan to the larger world of
Islam beyond the Nile valley. But they also played a crucial role
in making Islam locally intelligible, locally livable. In Sudan,
Suﬁorders and their associated spaces have long functioned as
communal engines: places of teaching, remembrance, healing,
gathering, and moral formation.
Suﬁvisual culture is often deeply practical. It understands
that spiritual life is not maintained by abstract belief alone; it
is maintained by repeated gestures, shared rituals, embodied
sound, and objects that anchor attention. A calligraphic inscrip-
tion is not simply “beautiful writing.” It is an attentional device.
It holds the mind to the Name. It brings the unseen into the
room without theatrics. It turns a wall into a reminder. It turns
the home into a small sanctuary.
The qubba, the domed tomb structures that mark the graves
of Suﬁsaints throughout Sudan, exempliﬁes this practical
aesthetic theology. These structures are not merely memorials.
They are active sites. People visit them seeking baraka (blessing),
seeking intercession, seeking healing, seeking comfort. The
architecture itself communicates: the dome suggests heaven,
the circular form suggests perfection, the elevation suggests
aspiration. But the forms remain humble enough to be approach-
able.
They do not intimidate. They invite.
Inside these spaces, aesthetic choices serve devotional func-
tion.
The whitewashed walls create calm.
The geometric
patterns in woodwork or textiles create rhythm. The calligraphic
panels create focus.
Everything works together to produce
an environment conducive to remembrance. This is aesthetic
113

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
intelligence: the understanding that physical space shapes con-
sciousness, that beauty can assist the soul toward its purposes.
Calligraphy, then, is not an “art form” ﬁrst. It is a posture.
The Western gaze often fetishizes Arabic calligraphy as an
aesthetic object detached from its devotional function. It frames
it as elegant design, collectible décor, cultural motif.
But
Sudanese calligraphy—especially in its Suﬁand talismanic
contexts—often operates closer to medicine than to decoration.
It is used to stabilize. It is used to heal. It is used to protect. It is
used to align. The letter becomes a vessel. The verse becomes a
shield.
The Name becomes a kind of architectural beam holding
the interior life upright. When you understand this, you stop
describing the work with the thin language of “visual appeal.”
You begin describing it with the thicker language of care.
The faqīhs, Islamic jurists and teachers who were often also
Suﬁpractitioners, understood this intuitively. They did not sep-
arate religious knowledge from aesthetic practice. When they
taught students to write Qur’anic verses, they were teaching
theology, yes, but also teaching rhythm, proportion, spatial
awareness, patience.
The physical act of forming letters with care was itself a
devotional practice. The student learned that beauty requires
discipline, that sacred language requires sacred handling, that
the hand can be an instrument of worship.
And now we must speak of talismanic papers, because they are
frequently mishandled by both secular critics and pious mod-
ernists. The secular critic dismisses them as superstition and
reduces them to anthropological curiosity. The pious modernist
sometimes dismisses them as illegitimate folk practice. Both
stances can be forms of violence when they refuse to see why

records.text:
THE LENS OF SAND & SCRIPTURE: AESTHETIC ISLAM IN SUDAN
such objects exist.
These objects do not announce themselves as art. A verse,
folded into leather, worn at the chest.
A prayer, sealed in
a pouch, hung above a doorway. A name written small and
tucked near the heart, carried into spaces where danger is
possible.
What they hold—Qur’anic verses, divine names,
prayers for protection against illness, against the evil eye,
against misfortune of various kinds—is the same protection
that orthodox theology also claims to offer. Orthodox Islam
sometimes objects: protection comes from God alone, not from
objects.
The tension is real and ongoing. And yet—when the world is
large and hostile and the body needs somewhere to locate its
hope, the tangible is not nothing. The object does not replace
trust; it materializes it. It gives the fear somewhere to land.
Even if one rejects certain practices doctrinally, the ethical task
remains: don’t mock the human longing underneath them.
Don’t treat people’s survival strategies as embarrassing. The
modern world has its own talismans, insurance policies, secu-
rity cameras, biometric locks, antidepressants, brand rituals,
algorithmic reassurance.
We call ours “rational” because we like ourselves. Sudan’s
objects simply wear their hope more openly.
The aesthetic intelligence of talismanic objects should not be
dismissed. The calligraphy on these papers is often exquisite,
miniature, precise, carefully proportioned. The folding and
enclosing in leather requires skill. The wearing or placement
requires understanding of where protection is needed most:
over the heart, at thresholds, near children. This is material
culture that encodes care. Whether or not the objects “work” in
a metaphysical sense, they work psychologically and socially.

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
They say: you are not alone in your vulnerability.
This
vulnerability has been named, addressed, ritually managed. You
have done what you can.
Now consider geometry, nomadic geometry, desert geometry,
the quiet mathematics of patterning that appears in textiles,
architecture, and ornament. Geometry in Sudan is not merely
imported Islamic design; it is a meeting between Qur’anic
discipline and environmental pedagogy. The desert already
taught restraint.
Scarcity already taught minimalism. The Nile already taught
rhythm. So Islamic geometry does not land in Sudan as foreign
abstraction. It resonates with what the land already trained the
eye to honor: repetition without waste, order without spectacle,
structure that can hold a community’s breath.
The geometric patterns in Sudanese textiles, architectural
decoration, and craft work often combine what might be called
“Islamic” motifs—star patterns, interlacing designs, arabesque
forms—with patterns that seem to reference older, pre-Islamic
traditions. A woven basket might incorporate both. A textile
might layer both. Rather than seeing this as syncretism or
confusion, it should be recognized as sophistication: the ability
to hold multiple aesthetic lineages simultaneously, to honor
both scripture and soil.
This is why I call Sudan’s Islamic aesthetics a “visual the-
ology,” but not the kind that argues. The kind that organizes.
Theology, here, is not merely doctrinal statement. It is spa-
tial behavior.
It is the organization of attention.
It is the
refusal of chaos as an internal condition.
It is the crafting
of environments—homes, zawiyas, mosques, objects—where
remembrance can happen naturally.
In this sense, beauty
becomes ethical because it assists the soul. It makes certain

virtues easier: patience, modesty, recollection, gratitude.
Aesthetic life becomes spiritual ergonomics.
Think about what this means practically.
In a Sudanese
home where Islamic aesthetics are taken seriously, every visual
element potentially serves devotional function. The calligraphic
panel on the wall is not décor, it is a daily reminder of God’s
presence.
The geometric pattern on the prayer rug is not decoration, it
creates a visual ﬁeld that helps focus attention during prayer.
The arrangement of objects creates order, which creates calm,
which creates space for remembrance. This is environmental
design in service of spiritual life.
And here a crucial line must be drawn: Sudanese Islamic
aesthetics are not “ornamental.” Ornamental is what the bored
call what they do not need.
In Sudan, Islamic form has often been needed.
Needed
because it turned homes into reminders when formal institu-
tions were unreliable. Needed because it offered communal
rhythm when politics produced fracture. Needed because it
offered a vocabulary of dignity when colonial hierarchies trained
shame. Needed because it offered a language of return when
exile and displacement began to multiply. Needed because it
offered an ethics of restraint in environments where excess
was punished by heat, scarcity, or surveillance. Needed, too,
because Sudanese religious life, especially in Suﬁ-inﬂected
contexts, often emphasized not only law but love, not only rule
but remembrance, not only correctness but presence. Presence
requires anchors. Beauty becomes one of those anchors.
The practice of dhikr exempliﬁes this perfectly. Dhikr is simul-
taneously sonic, bodily, and communal. Groups gather, often at
Suﬁcenters, on Friday evenings. They form circles. They chant

move, swaying, stepping, creating choreographed patterns of
collective motion.
The repetition creates altered states, not through drugs or
dramatic ritual, but through the simple persistence of focused
attention and communal rhythm.
The aesthetic dimension of dhikr cannot be separated from
its spiritual function. The rhythm is carefully calibrated. The
sonic qualities of different names or phrases are understood to
produce different effects. The spatial arrangement—the circle—
creates equality and unity. The movements synchronize individ-
ual bodies into collective expression. This is not “performance”
in the theatrical sense.
This is communal technology for producing and maintaining
spiritual states.
When dhikr happens in a zawiya (Suﬁcenter), the architecture
supports the practice. The space is typically modest but carefully
proportioned. The acoustics allow voices to resonate without
becoming cacophonous. The lighting, often natural light ﬁltered
through small windows or openings, creates an atmosphere
of contained luminosity. Everything serves the purpose: to
create an environment where remembrance can happen easily,
naturally, collectively.
Now we approach Zār, carefully, without the cheap thrill of
exoticism. Zār rituals and their associated aesthetic elements
have been described and debated in various ways, and the
outsider’s gaze has often turned them into spectacle. But within
the Sudanese aesthetic archive, what matters is not whether a
foreign observer ﬁnds Zār “strange.” What matters is what it
reveals: that the body and the unseen have long been treated as
intertwined realities, and that healing may require ritual form,

Zār practices, which involve spirit possession, healing rit-
uals, speciﬁc music, speciﬁc colors, speciﬁc objects, exist in
complicated relationship with orthodox Islam. Some Muslims
condemn them as shirk (polytheism). Others practice them while
maintaining Islamic identity. The tension itself is revealing: it
shows that Sudanese religious life is not monolithic, that people
navigate between official doctrine and lived need, that healing
sometimes requires resources beyond what orthodox practice
provides.
The aesthetics of Zār, its sonic textures, its colors, its objects,
its patterned gestures, belong to a broader Sudanese truth:
that art is sometimes the earliest form of therapy, and that
communal ritual is sometimes the most practical medicine
available when institutions fail. When a person is suffering,
from mental illness, from trauma, from mysterious affliction,
and formal medical care is unavailable or ineffective, Zār offers
an alternative framework.
It names the suffering as spirit
possession.
It provides a ritual process for addressing it. It mobilizes
community support.
It uses music, movement, color, and
symbolic action to create transformation. Whether one believes
in the metaphysics of spirit possession is less important than
recognizing what the practice accomplishes socially and psycho-
logically. It gives suffering a name and a narrative. It provides
agency, the afflicted person is not merely passive victim but
active participant in their own healing.
It creates community, others witness, support, participate. It
uses aesthetic means—rhythm, color, movement—to produce
altered states that may allow psychological breakthrough. This
is sophisticated healing technology, even if it doesn’t conform

THE LENS OF ORIGIN: THE UNWRITTEN ARCHIVE, BEFORE ISLAM,...
environment. The modern mind loves to believe that the unseen
began when metaphysics began, or when scripture arrived,
or when philosophy made it respectable. Sudan’s older truth
is quieter: the unseen was always there, because the unseen
is simply what the world contains beyond the arrogance of
human measurement. To live near the Nile is to know that what
nourishes can also drown. To live near the desert is to know that
what appears empty can kill. When a culture has lived with that
kind of elemental intimacy, its aesthetics become more than
expression. They become etiquette toward reality.
Begin, then, with this refusal: we will not speak of “primitive
art.” Not because we are trying to be politically polite, but
because the term is intellectually lazy. “Primitive” is what
conquerors call what they do not have the patience to learn. It is
what institutions call what they want to keep in their hierarchy’s
basement. It is also what a certain kind of scholarship reaches
for when it wants to feel advanced. But the truth is that Sudan’s
early aesthetic systems—whether carved into stone, shaped
into pottery, woven into cloth, marked onto skin, arranged into
burial architecture—display a sophistication that is not always
legible to modern education because modern education has been
trained to see knowledge only when it is written in the language
of elites. Yet knowledge has many costumes. In Sudan, one of
them was pattern, another was ritual, another was the body
itself.
But what does it mean to treat the body as archive? It means
you do not store memory only in books; you store it in the ways
you move, the ways you adorn, the ways you mark transitions:
birth, initiation, marriage, grief, death. It means the self is not
merely individual but inscribed by lineage. It means aesthetics
are not private taste but communal code. Some marks, some

This is where the phrase, God is a pattern that breathes,
becomes more than poetry. It becomes a key. In Sudan, pattern
is not merely visual. It is ontological. It suggests that reality
itself is structured, that recurrence is not boredom but mercy,
that order is not oppression but coherence. When the world is
violent, the idea that something repeats reliably—prayer times,
verses, Names, geometric cycles—becomes a lifeline.
The pattern breathes because it is lived. It is not a static design.
It is enacted daily. A woven pattern repeats. A dhikr repeats. A
verse repeats. A day repeats. Survival repeats. Beauty repeats.
And through repetition, the self remains held.
Consider the daily rhythm of Islamic practice. Five prayers
punctuate the day at speciﬁc times. Each prayer involves speciﬁc
movements, speciﬁc recitations, speciﬁc orientations (toward
Mecca).
This creates a temporal pattern, a daily geometry of devotion.
For someone living this pattern, time itself becomes structured
differently. The day is not an undifferentiated ﬂow but a series
of marked moments. Each prayer is an opportunity to return, to
recalibrate, to remember purpose.
This repeated return creates psychological stability. When life
is chaotic, when politics are violent, when the future is uncertain,
this reliable pattern offers refuge. You may not control what
happens to you, but you control this: you can pray. You can per-
form ablution. You can orient yourself toward Mecca. You can
recite the verses. You can bow, prostrate, rise. This pattern holds
even when everything else fractures. The aesthetic dimension of
this pattern should not be underestimated. The movements of
prayer have visual elegance, the bow, the prostration, the return
to standing create a kind of choreography. When many people

pray together, their synchronized movements create powerful
visual patterns.
The sonic dimension, the recitation of Qur’anic verses, the
call to prayer, adds auditory beauty. The spatial dimension, the
orientation toward Mecca, the arrangement of bodies in rows,
creates geometric order. All of this serves devotional purpose,
but it also creates beauty. And that beauty is not incidental. It
is part of how the practice sustains itself. Beautiful forms are
easier to return to.
This chapter must also name Sudan’s position in the false
binary of “Arab” and “African.” Sudanese Islamic aesthetics are
often misread because observers want to assign Sudan a single
belonging. But Sudan has long been an aesthetic seam: North
and sub-Saharan currents, Nile corridors and desert routes,
Arabic and local languages, imported scripts and indigenous
marks, Qur’anic recitation and oral praise traditions.
The
Sudanese visual world does not ﬁt the tidy identity politics of
outsiders. It is braided. It is layered. It is not “confused.” It
is complex. And complexity, in postcolonial contexts, is often
treated as a problem rather than as a truth. This book will treat
it as truth.
The question “Is Sudan Arab or African?”
is a colonial
question.
It assumes these categories are stable, mutually
exclusive, and meaningful. But Sudanese people have never
needed to choose. They have been both, neither, and something
else, simultaneously, ﬂuidly, contextually. Sudanese Arabic is
not Egyptian Arabic or Gulf Arabic, it has its own vocabulary, its
own rhythms, inﬂuenced by local languages. Sudanese Islam
is not Saudi Islam or Turkish Islam, it has its own practices, its
own emphases, shaped by Suﬁtraditions and local customs.
Sudanese visual culture draws on North African, Nile Valley,

and sub-Saharan aesthetics without needing to declare alle-
giance to one.
This hybridity, though that term itself can be problematic, is
not weakness. It is strength. It is aesthetic intelligence.
It is the ability to draw from multiple sources, to synthesize
without anxiety, to create something new that honors its an-
tecedents without being limited by them. Sudanese Islamic
aesthetics are remarkable precisely because they are not “pure,”
they are living, adaptive, responsive to local conditions while
maintaining connection to broader Islamic worlds.
So the lens of Sand & Scripture offers an instruction for
reading the rest of the book: do not treat Islam in Sudan as
a mere overlay, and do not treat pre-Islamic continuities as
something Islam “replaced.”
The aesthetic reality is more
subtle. Islam reorganized and sanctiﬁed certain forms.
It reﬁned and redirected certain protective practices.
It
introduced new textual and sonic regimes of beauty. But it did
so within a land already aesthetically intelligent, already trained
by environment, already ﬂuent in pattern, already close to the
unseen.
What emerges is not imitation. What emerges is a Sudanese
visual theology: devotional, practical, communal, restrained,
and deeply aware that beauty is not decoration.
Beauty is
discipline.
And now, because this is a Post-Interpretive book, we end with
the ethical warning. Western institutions and contemporary
cultural discourse often approach Islamic aesthetics with one
of two violences: clinical ﬂattening or sensationalist fear. The
clinical voice reduces devotion into “motifs.” The sensation-
alist voice reduces devotion into “threat.” Both refuse moral
proximity.

Both refuse to stand beside the work as living evidence.
So if you read this chapter and ﬁnd yourself tempted to
categorize—Is this orthodox? Is this folk? Is this African?
Is this Arab?—remember: those questions are often the mind’s
attempt to avoid presence. Presence is harder.
Presence requires you to see that people built these forms to
live with God under difficult conditions, and that any reading
which strips away that lived difficulty becomes a kind of theft.
Let the record show:
in Sudan, scripture did not arrive
to overwrite sand.
It arrived to speak through it, until the
land itself began to look like devotion, and devotion began
to look like survival. And in that fusion, something emerged
that was neither Arab imposition nor African resistance, but a
third aesthetic, one that holds both legacies without choosing
between them, one that makes beauty serve mercy, and one that
understands that in a world of relentless rupture, pattern itself
can be a form of prayer.

The Lens of Oral Memory: The Artwork
That Walks Before the Pen
Sudan has always known something the modern world keeps
forgetting: language is not only written. It is carried. It is
sung. It is thrown across rooms in praise, in grief, in teasing, in
warning, in prayer. It travels through the throat long before it
travels through libraries. And when a culture is shaped by oral
memory, its art does not behave like an illustration. It behaves
like a voice. It doesn’t sit still the way a page sits still. It walks.
It arrives in rhythm. It repeats. It improvises. It shifts according
to audience and circumstance. In such a world, the artwork is
not primarily an object. It is an event of transmission.
Sudan’s literary forms are older than the writing that records
them. Long before the novel arrived as category, before the
short story became a recognized form, literature here moved
through voices. The Ahaji—the folk tale tradition—traveled
through grandmothers before it traveled through books.
The Madih—praise poetry honoring the Prophet, performed
communally with lead vocalist and responding chorus—
circulated through memory and song before any manuscript

preserved it. And the oral poetic tradition that developed across
northern Sudan was not rudimentary verse awaiting elevation.
It was formally sophisticated: structured, rhythmically precise,
carried in colloquial Sudanese Arabic as a living literary form
with its own fully developed conventions.
This is why Sudanese art so often feels like it is carrying
weight rather than displaying content. The West is trained to
treat the visual as primary and the oral as secondary—sound as
supplement, voice as ephemeral, performance as non-archival.
But Sudan’s aesthetic intelligence often reverses the hierarchy.
The oral is not decorative; it is foundational. It is how history
survives when institutions fail. It is how lineage persists when
paper is scarce, when archives are burned, when regimes rewrite
records, when displacement fractures documentation.
The tongue becomes the ﬁrst library. The body becomes the
ﬁrst museum. And when the tongue is the library, the visual
arts inherit a distinct task: to hold rhythm, to hold recitation,
to hold collective breath.
So we must approach Sudanese visual form with an ear, not
only an eye. Because oral cultures encode knowledge through
cadence. They stabilize memory through repetition, rhyme, and
structure. A story that must survive across generations cannot
rely on footnotes.
It must rely on music. It must rely on memorable pattern.
Madih in Sudan is a tradition of sung praise for the Prophet
Muhammad, performed at community gatherings and celebra-
tions, most notably Moulid (an annual festival commemorating
the birth of the prophet), with a lead vocalist and a responding
chorus, often supported by handclaps from the audience.
This is why praise-singing traditions, poetic forms, chants,
and communal recitations do not remain conﬁned to “litera-

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
ture.” They bleed into the visual. They teach the hand to repeat.
They teach the eye to favor rhythm. They teach pattern to behave
like a stanza. They teach color to act like emphasis. They teach
composition to operate like a breath: pause, surge, pause again.
What made Sudanese recitation distinct was not only the text
but the training ground. In the khalwa, children learned in
unison until chanting became body memory. In the Suﬁcircle,
repetition became indistinguishable from breath. The result was
a recitational voice that belonged to more than one occasion—
heard in the mosque, in the home, in the street, carrying the
same disciplined cadence across every threshold.
In this sense, Sudanese art is often not representational in
the naive Western way. It doesn’t simply depict something. It
recites something. It holds the cadence of a people.
This becomes especially visible in craft lineages: weaving,
beadwork, henna, pottery, forms often dismissed as “women’s
work” or “folk practice” by institutions that mistake domestic
survival for aesthetic inferiority. Yet these forms are, in oral
cultures, central repositories of memory. A woven motif can be
a proverb without words.
A repeated geometry can be a chant made visible. A color
choice can signal lineage, region, marital status, ritual function.
A pattern can carry a genealogy more efficiently than a written
chart, because the pattern is embedded in practice, and practice
is remembered through doing.
Oral memory does not store itself in abstraction; it stores itself
in embodied repetition.
This is why the title of the chapter is “The artwork that walks
before the pen.” The pen is late. The pen arrives after the
voice has already built a nation inside the body. The pen arrives
after the praise singer has already mapped the moral universe.

THE LENS OF ORAL MEMORY: THE ARTWORK THAT WALKS BEFORE THE...
The pen arrives after the mother has already taught pattern to
the child without ever calling it art. The pen arrives after the
community has already rehearsed its own survival as ritual, as
song, as repetition. Written history, then, is not the origin of
Sudanese meaning. It is one of its later garments.
And here we must speak of the Hakamat, not as exotic curiosity,
but as evidence of oral tradition’s aesthetic and political power.
The Hakamat are poets and singers of Western Sudan—women
whose power is speciﬁcally vocal, speciﬁcally communal, and
speciﬁcally feared. To call them praise singers is too narrow.
They also ridicule. They incite. They arbitrate.
A Hakama holds charisma, cultural knowledge, and the com-
munity’s trust that her voice carries authority beyond perfor-
mance. She is poet, singer, judge. Her verse deﬁnes community
law without writing any of it down. She praises bravery. She
shames cowardice. She honors generosity and satirizes self-
interest.
She comments on events the community has no other insti-
tution to adjudicate. Many Hakamat are not formally literate,
and this is part of their power: their authority is embodied, not
institutional. It lives in presence, in voice, in the accumulated
recognition that what she says matters. They preserve history
not in documents but in bodies. They hold the community’s
story in the throat. Their art does not hang in a museum. It
circulates, arbitrates, and—when the moral stakes demand it—
starts wars.
This is oral power in its most concentrated form.
The
Hakama’s voice can shift communal action, can shame men into
battle or dissuade them from it, can deﬁne honor and cowardice,
can preserve history and shape present conduct, all without
writing a single word. This is aesthetic intelligence operating at

full political force.
Her art is not representation but intervention. Her perfor-
mance is not entertainment but governance.
Her memory-
keeping is not archival nostalgia but living law.
The ethical complexity of the Hakamat tradition cannot be
ignored. During the Darfur conﬂict, Hakamats were regularly
used by tribal leaderships as a way of inﬂuencing communities,
often in return for payment. When members of both groups
were keen to avert bloodshed between the Rizeigat and Fayreen
communities, it was the female singers who commanded most
inﬂuence; on returning to their village, the Fayreen men who
reached a peace agreement were confronted by groups of Haka-
mat singing songs about cowardice, removing their Islamic
headscarves to indicate their lack of respect for the men and
questioning their manhood, causing the men to take up arms
and return to ﬁght, resulting in dozens of deaths.
This is not a simple story of women’s empowerment or
cultural authenticity. It is a story of how oral tradition carries
moral force, force that can be weaponized, manipulated, paid
for. The Hakamat hold power precisely because their voices are
trusted as carriers of communal values.
When those values prioritize warrior honor over peaceful
resolution, the results can be catastrophic.
Yet this same
aesthetic-political force can be redirected. The Hakamat are
beginning to sing songs of peace; this change has come because
many Hakamat have paid a personal price for the violence, one
singer confessed, “I already lost a brother… If I continue singing
it could be a son this time round”.
The point is not to romanticize or condemn the Hakamat. The
point is to recognize what they reveal: that in oral cultures,
art is never “just” aesthetic. It is infrastructural. It shapes

action. It holds memory. It deﬁnes morality. It can start wars or
end them. And it does all of this without needing to be written
down, because it lives in voice, in performance, in the communal
recognition that certain voices carry weight.
The oral lens also changes how we understand authorship.
Modern art history often fetishizes the individual genius, the
signature, the biography, the solitary breakthrough.
Oral
cultures complicate this.
In oral transmission, creativity is often communal, iterative,
and distributed. A song belongs to a lineage more than to a
single author. A proverb is reﬁned by use. A story is adjusted
by each teller. This means Sudanese aesthetic forms may carry
collective authorship even when an individual hand executes
them. The pattern you see may not be “invented” by one person;
it may be inherited, modiﬁed, and renewed.
The value lies not only in novelty but in ﬁdelity, ﬁdelity to the
rhythm that keeps the community coherent.
The poet Najlaa Eltom describes being surrounded by poets
“not in the traditional sense of published writers or those
who take writing as a profession” but by “a different group
of artists—those who composed songs about their daily lives,
their children, and their grandchildren,” her aunts who created
verses spontaneously. Her mother did not compose herself,
but “was constantly by the radio, immersed in Sudanese music
and Madih, the local tradition of praising Prophet Muhammad,”
while her father “was deeply connected to poetry, often reciting
verses written by relatives and friends; whenever he had some-
thing on his mind, he would express it through poetry rather
than ordinary conversation.”
This lens demands that the reader unlearn a certain Western
hunger: the hunger for the single origin. Sudanese oral aes-

scars, some pigments—whatever one thinks of them ethically
today—were part of a social grammar: they told stories of
belonging, endurance, protection, status, and covenant. In
many places, scariﬁcation is discussed with either horror or
romanticism, both of which are forms of distance, but the
ethical approach is neither. It is witness: to acknowledge that
in societies where the body was vulnerable to environment and
predation, the body also became the ﬁrst site where meaning
could be stabilized. To mark the body was, in part, to refuse
the body’s anonymity. It was to say: I am not merely living. I
belong to a world that recognizes me. And beyond the body, the
land itself was read as a kind of text. Before scripture, there was
weather. Before theology, there was drought.
Before doctrine, there was the Nile’s generosity and its threat.
River-based cosmology is not a poetic ﬂourish; it is an epis-
temology.
It teaches that life is contingent, cyclical, and
distributed. A river does not obey a single ruler, it is a system, it
nourishes and destroys without moral performance. Cultures
formed around such a force develop an intelligence that is
neither purely scientiﬁc nor purely mythic. It is practical meta-
physics: an understanding that unseen causes can shape visible
outcomes, and that one must behave with care toward forces one
cannot command. This is why talismanic thinking—so often
mocked by the modern voice—should be approached here not
as irrationality but as an attempt to negotiate vulnerability. A
talisman is a technology of reassurance when formal power
is absent. It is also a device of agency in a world that often
refuses agency to the weak. When you cannot control disease,
you produce protective marks. When you cannot command the
politics of your region, you anchor your home with ritual. When
the world is full of envy, hunger, and loss, you create objects

thetics often resist origin stories because they are not built for
ownership. They are built for continuity.
Now consider the relationship between oral memory and
space. Oral traditions are not only words; they are gatherings.
They require bodies in proximity. They require shared time.
They require a setting where voice can travel.
This is why
architecture and communal spaces in Sudan carry an aesthetic
logic that is inseparable from sound.
Courtyards, open spaces, shaded areas, communal rooms,
these are not neutral. They are acoustic infrastructures. They
allow recitation, storytelling, praise-singing, and ritual to occur.
Space becomes part of the oral archive. Architecture becomes a
vessel for communal memory, not just shelter from heat.
When the oral is dominant, the visual is often designed
to support it rather than replace it. Visual form becomes a
mnemonic device: patterns that help memory, objects that
anchor stories, symbols that trigger recitations.
In such a
world, the artwork is not fully “read” in silence. It is activated
by speech. It becomes fully itself when someone speaks near
it, when someone sings, when someone remembers aloud.
Museums often fail Sudanese art because museums insist on
silence as a default.
But Sudanese aesthetics often include
silence as a strategy, yes, yet they also include voice as lineage.
The work is not always meant to be approached alone. It is often
meant to be held in community.
Out of the praise-singing traditions of the 1930s, a new form
emerged—TumTum, born in Kosti on the White Nile. Its lyrics
held two registers at once: romance, and the difficulty of female
life. The music was danceable. It spread through urban centers
with the momentum of something people had already been
waiting for.

The ﬁgures who shaped this era worked across composition,
performance, and political commitment simultaneously. Ab-
dallah Abdel Karim—known as Karouma—wrote with proliﬁc
intensity, his voice inseparable from the era’s pulse. Ibrahim al-
Abadi pushed its forms toward new possibility. And Khalil Farah
did both: poet and singer, his song Azza ﬁHawak threading
lyric beauty through the live wire of the Sudanese national
movement.
This lens also illuminates why Sudanese art can feel so in-
tensely ethical. Oral cultures transmit not only history but
values through story. Stories are not merely entertainment.
They are moral rehearsal. They teach what to honor, what
to fear, what to laugh at, what to grieve.
They provide a
people with a shared emotional grammar. When those story
structures migrate into visual form, the art becomes saturated
with communal ethics. A pattern is not neutral; it carries social
memory. A color is not arbitrary; it carries relational meaning.
A motif may be tied to a proverb or a spiritual teaching. The
visual inherits the oral’s responsibility: it becomes another way
of teaching how to live.
By the time of the Mahdist uprising in the late 19th century,
spoken-word poetry was already doing double labor—aesthetic
and political simultaneously, naming events as they happened
and shaping how communities would remember them. Among
the popular vernacular poets of that period were two women:
Bint al-Makkawi and Umm Misaymis. Not minor ﬁgures, not
curiosities.
Women whose voices had sufficient force to move events. That
tradition continued to evolve. By 2018, the same oral-political
energy that had moved through praise-song and epic across
centuries was moving through rap, through protest slogan,

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
through the digital channels the revolution ran on. The form
changed. The function—the voice as weapon, as record, as
communal orientation—did not. And now—because this book
is also about rupture—we must say what happens when oral
cultures meet modern catastrophe. War disrupts gatherings.
Displacement breaks communities. Exile fragments shared
contexts. When oral transmission is interrupted, the visual
arts sometimes take on even greater archival responsibility. A
painting may become a substitute for a story circle that can no
longer gather.
A textile motif may become a portable homeland when the
homeland is inaccessible. A poster may become a public chant
when the chant is forbidden. In these moments, Sudanese art
becomes not only aesthetic but infrastructural: it carries the
oral archive forward when the oral conditions are endangered.
This helps explain the emotional density of so much Sudanese
work, even when it looks formally restrained. The restraint is
not coldness. It is discipline. The work is carrying more than
it shows, because it was trained by a culture where meaning is
often carried rather than displayed. The viewer who expects im-
mediate legibility will call it “subtle.” The viewer with patience
will recognize something more serious: the art is behaving
like memory itself, partial, rhythmic, layered, unwilling to be
summarized without violence.
Sudan is one of Africa’s largest nations, and one of its most
internally varied—linguistically, ethnically, religiously.
Its
literature carries that multiplicity. Poetry has always been the
form nearest the country’s pulse. To read Sudanese literary
culture only through its Arabic inheritance is to read a river by its
surface: it misses the underground tributaries, the oral lineages,
the folktales and epic traditions that have shaped contemporary

writers whether or not those writers name their sources.
So let this chapter offer a new instruction: when you look at
Sudanese art, listen for the oral beneath it. Listen for cadence
in the pattern. Listen for pauses in the composition. Listen
for repetition as refrain. Listen for the work’s relationship to
gathering and communal breath. Ask yourself what kind of voice
the work carries, and what kind of silence it refuses. Because
Sudanese art does not merely represent a culture that speaks.
It is one of the ways the culture continues to speak, even when
the mouth is tired, even when the archive is threatened, even
when the world has grown loud with other people’s narratives.
Let the record show: in Sudan, the artwork often walks before
the pen, because the ﬁrst history was not written, it was carried
in voice, and voice taught the visual how to endure. And in
a world where institutions failed repeatedly, where archives
burned, where regimes rewrote records, where displacement
became chronic, the oral archive survived precisely because
it lived in bodies, in rhythms, in performances that could be
carried across borders and transmitted without permission from
power. The artwork learned from this.
It learned to be portable. It learned to hold memory lightly
enough to travel but ﬁrmly enough to remain recognizable. It
learned that survival sometimes requires you to walk before you
can afford to sit still and be written down.

The Lens of Architecture: Sudanese
Space as Moral Instruction
A Sudanese building is rarely merely innocent.
It doesn’t merely stand; it teaches. It instructs the body before
it persuades the mind. It tells you where to lower your voice,
where to pause, where to gather, where to endure heat without
complaint, where to turn your face toward shade as if shade
were a form of mercy.
In places where the environment is severe and history is
unstable, architecture cannot afford to be a purely aesthetic
performance. It must become ethics made material: shelter,
discipline, protection, and social order joined into form. In
Sudan, long before “spatial design” became a fashionable
language of experience, space was already functioning as a kind
of pedagogy. It taught people how to move, how to gather, how
to withdraw, how to survive.
Much modern architectural discourse speaks in terms of
style: this period, that inﬂuence, this movement, that façade.
Sudanese vernacular architecture, in many of its older and
regionally distinct forms, often speaks ﬁrst through necessity.
134

THE LENS OF ARCHITECTURE: SUDANESE SPACE AS MORAL...
A wall is not an idea before it is protection from sun. A courtyard
is not merely an aesthetic ﬂourish; it is a breathing device. A
dome is not only symbol; it is a way of making weight, enclosure,
heat, and air movement answer to form. A narrow opening is
not stinginess; it is a negotiation with heat. The desert is an
uncompromising critic, and it trains builders more rigorously
than any academy.
It teaches that excess is not always luxury; sometimes it is
risk. It teaches that bodily comfort is not indulgence; in harsh
climates, it is survival. And when survival becomes a ﬁrst design
principle, a culture develops an architectural intelligence that
is both humble and profound: humble because it submits to
reality, profound because it turns submission into elegance.
What the environment demands, Sudanese builders have
often answered with earth, shade, thickness, enclosure, and
restraint. Heat encouraged thick walls: mud, stone, or brick
dense enough to slow the day’s punishment and release it
gradually after sunset. In Nubian and other earthen-building
contexts, limited timber availability, local materials, and inher-
ited construction knowledge encouraged vaults and domes: not
imported wood, but shaped earth, curved into forms that could
hold themselves up through geometry. The land did not ask
permission before teaching these lessons. It simply made some
solutions more durable, more affordable, and more intelligent
than others.
This is why Sudanese space can feel morally legible even
before one knows the theory behind it. The space does not
ask ﬁrst for interpretation. It asks for comportment. You feel
the difference between spectacle and shelter immediately. The
building does not perform only for the passerby; it cares for the
inhabitant. It does not merely ﬂatter the eye; it protects the

In a world where modern architecture often becomes ego
made concrete, Sudan’s older spatial logics remind us of a
forgotten truth: the most digniﬁed building is not always the
one that announces itself loudly, but the one that holds human
life gently.
Consider the Nubian dome and vault: earth-colored, rounded,
modest, structurally intelligent, and quietly resistant to the
tyranny of imported “progress.” What the Nubian vault teaches
is this: shelter does not always require imported material in
order to stand. Mud bricks, shaped and stacked with precision,
generate their own structural logic. Each unit presses against
the next; the curve distributes load without depending on
timber formwork or metal reinforcement. The technique also
responds to heat. Thick earthen materials and vaulted forms
help moderate internal temperature, allowing the building
to remain cooler not through imported machinery alone, but
through the intelligence of mass, air, and shape.
Its beauty does not scream. It does not need the glass tower’s
arrogance. It is a form grown from climate, material availability,
and the wisdom of centuries: how to make a home that stays
cooler, how to build with what the land offers, how to create
volume without waste, how to let air and shade become forms
of mercy.
A dome is an argument the land makes against vanity. It is
the desert teaching the architect: curve is not decoration; curve
is intelligence. The dome does not merely cover; it contains.
It shapes heat, sound, and communal life. It creates a soft sky
inside the home. It reminds the body that shelter can be gentle
without being weak.
When the Egyptian architect Hassan Fathy studied Nubian

architectural discourse, he recognized something industrial
modernity had forgotten how to value: earth already knows
how to make shelter. One does not always need to import what
the ground already provides. His lesson was not nostalgia. It
was correction.
And then there are the tukuls and other vernacular structures,
forms often dismissed by outsiders as “simple” because the out-
sider mistakes European complexity for complexity itself. The
tukul—round, thatched, mud-walled—appears across many
Sudanese and regional vernacular contexts, especially where
rainfall, vegetation, and local building traditions make that
form intelligent. It is built from what grows nearby, from what
the ground holds, from what needs no ship to deliver. The
pitched roof answers rain. The circular form answers material,
structure, repair, and use. Its ornament is not an afterthought;
it is the building admitting that survival and beauty are not
enemies.
But simplicity, in harsh climates, is often the highest sophis-
tication. To build a structure that lasts, that cools, that gathers
people, that can be repaired, that can be remade—this is not
primitive. It is advanced in the only way that matters: it works.
Sudan’s vernacular architecture is a living critique of the
modern world’s obsession with novelty. It suggests that the
true measure of design is not how it photographs, but how it
survives.
Across much of Sudan, one ﬁnds the rectangular or square
earthen house often described as the bayt jalus: ﬂat-roofed,
built from dried clay, sun-dried mud brick, or plaster mixtures
that may include organic materials such as cow dung, locally
referred to in some sources as zibala. Wooden elements are used

used here as poverty alone, but as intelligence: the land teaches
the builder what the land provides.
In parts of Sudanese vernacular architecture, especially in Nu-
bian regions, walls may be elaborately painted with traditional
designs. Houses are often square or rectangular, with ﬂat roofs
and terraces that allow life to continue under the pressures of
heat. Such forms are not merely domestic containers; they are
climatic instruments, social organizers, and visual declarations
of belonging.
Survival, however, is never purely physical. It is also social.
Architecture in Sudan is frequently an instrument of community:
a way of organizing gathering, prayer, mourning, hospitality,
and the rhythms of oral life. A shaded space is not merely shade;
it is where stories travel. A courtyard is not merely open air; it
is where family becomes audible. A threshold is not merely an
entry; it is a moral line between public and intimate, between
outer noise and inner coherence.
The home becomes a small cosmology. It teaches what to
reveal and what to protect.
It teaches that not everything
belongs to the street.
In societies marked by surveillance,
political instability, or social pressure, this lesson becomes more
than cultural preference. It becomes safety.
Many vernacular homes use thick walls, courtyards, shaded
thresholds, and carefully managed openings for thermal regula-
tion and social privacy. Walk near a Nubian house and you may
see what this means in practice: vivid color on white plaster,
geometric forms worked into walls, objects displayed as memory
and address—a house speaking its lineage to everyone who
passes.
This is why Sudanese architecture can become a silent com-

The space itself
participates in restraint. It creates zones of privacy, layers of
access, rooms that hold what cannot be said publicly.
The building becomes an accomplice in survival. It helps life
continue without requiring life to become visible to strangers.
In a world addicted to exposure—where even grief is demanded
as content—Sudanese spatial ethics remind us that dignity
sometimes requires concealment. Not concealment born of
shame, but concealment born of reverence: the understanding
that certain aspects of life are too sacred to be publicly handled.
Now place this within the spiritual geometry of Sudan.
Mosques, zawiyas, tomb complexes, and sacred sites are
not only religious structures; they are moral architectures.
They discipline the body through orientation, repetition, and
communal rhythm.
The vertical gesture of a minaret is not merely a skyline
statement; it is a directional reminder. It says: attention must
rise, even when life is heavy. In urban Sudan, the mosque and the
minaret are not decoration. They help organize space spiritually.
The dome says: gather beneath vastness. The minaret says:
orient. The arabesque says: pattern is one way of approaching
the inﬁnite. Islam did not merely decorate Sudan’s skyline; it
reoriented its spatial imagination.
Yet Sudan is also a land of horizontality—the dune, the plain,
the river’s long sentence. Sacred architecture often exists as a
dialogue between vertical devotion and horizontal endurance:
rise toward God, but remain grounded in the earth’s patience.
This tension, between ascent and endurance, is one of Sudan’s
deepest aesthetic truths.
You can feel it in the way sacred
spaces are often both modest and intense. They do not always
overwhelm with grandeur.
They gather presence through

THE LENS OF ORIGIN: THE UNWRITTEN ARCHIVE, BEFORE ISLAM,...
that hold a promise: that protection can be made visible. Even
if that protection is psychological, it is still a form of care. And
care is not lesser because it is invisible.
Much of civilization is built on invisible agreements: trust,
lineage, prayer, taboo. Sudan’s older aesthetic artifacts are
saturated with these agreements. They do not ask to be “ap-
preciated.” They ask to be understood as evidence of a people
refusing collapse.
At this point the Western reader often asks, impatiently: “But
where is the art?”
The question reveals the problem.
The
Western category of “art” is historically speciﬁc: it assumes
an object made primarily for contemplation, separated from
utility, displayed in spaces dedicated to aesthetic leisure. That
is not the universal condition of beauty. Sudan’s earlier forms
often refuse that separation. A pot is not only a container; it
is a family’s continuity. A textile is not only a surface; it is a
map of belonging. A carved ﬁgure may not be “sculpture” in
the museum sense; it may be a mediator, a guardian, a witness
to rites that keep the community intact. If you insist on the
museum deﬁnition, you will keep misreading what you see. The
correct move is to widen the category until it can hold the world’s
variety without humiliating it.
And now we must speak—brieﬂy, but with gravity—of the
ancient civilizations that make the phrase “unwritten archive”
feel almost like an understatement. Nubia and Kush are not
footnotes. They are not peripheral echoes of Egypt. They are
their own architectures of power and imagination, with their
own aesthetic logics and political structures. To understand
Sudanese art without acknowledging these legacies is like trying
to understand a cathedral while refusing to look at its foundation
stones. Yet these legacies are often ﬁltered through Egypto-

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
rhythm.
Tomb architecture, too, carries this moral geometry. The
dead are not simply absent; they remain as social presence and
spiritual reminder. The structure around death becomes a way of
organizing memory into space, turning grief into form, turning
remembrance into a physical location to which the living can
return.
The qubbas, or gubbas—whitewashed domed tombs often
made of adobe or mud brick and associated with saints, religious
ﬁgures, or important personages—carry this logic. Modern
Western monumentality often treats the tomb as a monument
to the individual. Sudan’s sacred spatial traditions often treat
tombs as nodes in communal continuity, places where the living
negotiate their relationship to history, lineage, mercy, and the
unseen.
The space teaches how to grieve without collapsing, how to
remember without theatricality.
Architecture also reveals the politics of water and scarcity.
Where water is rare, seasonal, or contested, design becomes a
record of resource ethics. The geometry of wells, the place-
ment of courtyards, the organization of shade, the layout
of settlements—these are not merely “vernacular charm.”
They are a material theology of scarcity: a way of living that
acknowledges that resources are gifts, not guarantees.
Modern minimalism likes to claim philosophical elegance.
Sudanese restraint, when born of scarcity, heat, and inherited
environmental knowledge, is often more honest. It is not an
aesthetic posture for magazines. It is a lived discipline. It
teaches that “less” is not always a trend. Sometimes it is the only
way a community stays alive. This is knowledge that cannot be
designed in an office. The placement of vents, the thickness

records.text:
THE LENS OF ARCHITECTURE: SUDANESE SPACE AS MORAL...
of walls, the logic of shade and light—these are answers to
questions the land asks repeatedly. They required centuries
of conversation between builder and environment.
And so, if you want to understand Sudanese aesthetics, you
must understand that the building is not separate from art. The
building is one of the earliest arts. It is the earliest museum. It
is the ﬁrst framing device. It is the space where textiles hang,
where oral memory circulates, where prayer repeats, where craft
is stored, where families survive, where politics is held at the
threshold, when it can be.
This is why I said earlier: Sudan built truth into walls before it
wrote books. Not truth as ideology, but truth as lived instruction.
The wall says: here is where the sun cannot reach you. The
courtyard says: here is where community can breathe. The
threshold says: here is where intimacy is protected. The dome
says: here is how to make shelter intelligent. The sacred space
says: here is how to orient your body when the world disorients
your soul.
The capacity for complex urban form in this region is ancient.
Kerma, whose development reaches back into the third mil-
lennium BCE, became one of the major urban and ceremonial
centers of the Nile Valley. It contained monumental architecture,
organized settlement, religious structures, and urban complex-
ity long before many inherited histories of civilization learned to
treat Africa as a primary site of architectural and urban invention
rather than as background.
Its deffufa—a massive mud-brick ceremonial and religious
structure, elevated above the surrounding settlement and as-
sociated in its surviving form with the later phases of Kerma’s
development—still stands. When you encounter it, understand
what it tells you: this is not the origin of a tradition that

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
later became sophisticated. This is sophistication from the
beginning.
If Western modernity often treats architecture as a perfor-
mance of power, Sudanese spatial traditions often treat archi-
tecture as a discipline of mercy. Mercy toward the body: keeping
it cool, shaded, and gathered. Mercy toward the community:
allowing privacy, hospitality, ritual, and repair. Mercy toward
the future: building in ways that can be maintained, adapted,
rebuilt, and continued.
When architects such as Abdelmoneim Mustafa worked within
the pressures of modern Sudanese architecture, they faced a
collision. The mid-century brought concrete, the modernist
grid, the orthogonal plan, and new institutional ambitions.
These were not inherently wrong. But they arrived alongside
cultural pressure to adopt imported aesthetics wholesale, to let
reinforced concrete replace mud brick not only as material, but
as logic. The challenge was not simply whether to use modern
materials. The challenge was whether modernity could be made
answerable to place.
Yet even as modernization arrived, the ethical lessons of
traditional architecture remained relevant. The modern period
revealed tensions: between imported materials and local re-
sources, between air conditioning and passive cooling, between
global aesthetics and local identity. Dependence on mechanical
cooling is not merely an energy question. At times it is an
architectural confession: the building admitting that it cannot
regulate itself, that it must import comfort because it failed to
produce it through form. Passive cooling intelligence, developed
over centuries, was too often discarded in a generation—not
because it failed, but because new wealth made its abandonment
appear affordable.

THE LENS OF ARCHITECTURE: SUDANESE SPACE AS MORAL...
This tension reveals architecture’s ongoing moral task: to
serve not power or fashion, but human ﬂourishing under spe-
ciﬁc conditions. When buildings abandon climate intelligence
for imported solutions, they abandon one of architecture’s
fundamental responsibilities: to make human life possible
without destroying the systems that sustain it.
Let the record show: in Sudan, space is not a backdrop to art.
It is one of art’s oldest moral teachers, shaping how the body
learns humility, how the community learns continuity, and how
beauty learns to serve survival rather than spectacle.
The dome teaches that intelligence can be curved. The court-
yard teaches that gathering requires breath. The threshold
teaches that privacy is not shame but dignity. The thick wall
teaches that protection from heat is a form of mercy. And the
entire tradition teaches that the most sophisticated architecture
is not the one that announces its complexity, but the one
that makes life possible, generation after generation, without
apology and without collapse.

11
The Lens of Craft: Inheritance in the
Hands
The West calls it craft when it doesn’t know how to kneel.
It reserves the word “art” for what can be framed, sold, hung
under lights, and narrated by institutions that pretend neutrality
while choosing winners. But Sudan has long understood a deeper
hierarchy, one that modern museums often fail to recognize:
the forms that keep people alive are not lesser.
They are
foundational.
In Sudan, weaving, pottery, dyeing, beadwork, henna, met-
alwork, jewelry, and domestic ornament are not peripheral
aesthetic hobbies. They are the architecture of continuity. They
are where beauty becomes practical, where memory becomes
touch, where lineage becomes repeatable, where women—so
often written out of “official” art histories—carry the aesthetic
spine of culture with disciplined hands.
Craft, here, is not a category. It is a covenant.
A covenant between material and community, between the
living and the dead, between the present moment and the
inheritance that refuses to vanish. When a culture is shaped

records.text:
THE LENS OF CRAFT: INHERITANCE IN THE HANDS
by rupture—colonial borders, displacement, war, economic
instability—the most reliable archive is often the one that can
travel: the archive you can wear, carry, remake, repair.
A painting can be conﬁscated. A museum can be burned.
A library can be censored. But a motif carried in a weaving
tradition survives in bodies. A dye practice survives in hands. A
bead pattern survives in domestic rhythm. The home becomes
the safest museum because the home can move, and because
what is transmitted through skill is harder to erase than what is
stored in buildings.
Begin with weaving, because weaving is the mother of pattern
and pattern is one of Sudan’s most durable languages. Across
Sudan’s regions the craft lexicon is wide: pottery and metalwork
and carving and weaving, each discipline shaped by what the
speciﬁc land offers and what the speciﬁc community requires.
Woven cotton moves between the everyday and the ceremonial—
the galabiya worn daily, the cloth weighted with occasion, the
textile that mediates between body, climate, modesty, and
belonging.
The material does not merely serve the body. It carries some-
thing the body alone cannot hold: the accumulated decisions of
people who made under pressure, and still made beautifully.
A woven textile is not merely “beautiful fabric.” It is a social
document, a memory device, sometimes a protective surface,
sometimes a marker of identity, sometimes a ceremonial object,
sometimes simply the labor of staying warm, staying clothed,
staying digniﬁed. In Darfur and other western Sudanese craft
contexts, basket-making carries its own precise vocabulary
of place. Local grasses, ﬁbers, and plant materials become
structure, surface, and pattern.
The dyes and tones often
read like a map of what the landscape provides: plant-based

reds and oranges, indigo blues where indigo traditions are
present, acacia browns and blacks, earth colors drawn from the
environment itself. This is color as geography. This is pattern
as autobiography of the land.
The loom is a quiet philosophy: it teaches patience, repetition,
and attentional discipline. It teaches that beauty is not an event
but a process. It teaches that the hand must submit to rhythm.
And rhythm—whether in dhikr, in oral tradition, in the Nile’s
cycles, in the desert’s demands—is one of Sudan’s oldest tutors.
Weaving is therefore not merely craft. It is a cosmology enacted.
Consider what is actually happening when a woman weaves
baskets in a Darfur market. She may have learned the motions
from her mother or grandmother, which means the teaching
preceded her own memory of having learned it.
If she is
widowed, displaced, or economically responsible for children,
the basket becomes more than an object. It is sold. The income
buys food, pays school fees, sustains a household. What passes
between those hands is not merely skill. It is an economic engine,
a survival structure, a form of insurance whose premium is
patience and whose currency is thread, grass, ﬁber, and time.
This reveals what institutions often miss: craft is not sup-
plementary income. In many lives, it is primary survival. It is
how a grandmother transmits not only technique but livelihood
to her granddaughter. It is how widowhood does not become
destitution. It is how children attend school. This is aesthetic
intelligence operating as social infrastructure.
Pottery, too, deserves to be approached with reverence rather
than condescension. Earlier observers of Sudanese village pot-
tery noted that pots were made by women in some communities
primarily for use in their own households, and that a man’s lack
of pottery could be read as a sign of household incompleteness.
146

THE LENS OF CRAFT: INHERITANCE IN THE HANDS
That observation—seemingly casual—reveals a profound truth:
pottery was so integrated into women’s domestic authority that
its absence could signify not merely material lack, but social
incompletion.
Clay is a humble material, and that humility is precisely what
makes it sacred. Pottery is how water is held. How food is stored.
How daily life becomes possible. The pot is the domestic answer
to scarcity: a technology of containment. The zir—a large
clay water jar cooled by its own porosity—holds water against
the heat and, in some contexts, has also been used as a vessel
for fermenting fasikh: ﬁsh cleaned, salted, sealed inside with
textile, stored in darkness for one or two years until preservation
completes what the climate alone cannot provide.
And when containment becomes vital, the vessel becomes
ethically charged. A beautifully made pot is not simply “nice
design.” It is respect for life’s fragility. It is the decision to craft
the tools of survival with care rather than with negligence.
Much traditional pottery is said to echo naturally occurring
forms, including gourds and other organic containers. This is
not primitive imitation but sophisticated understanding: the
forms that nature has already proven effective under harsh
conditions become templates for human making. The gourd
taught the pot. The land taught the hand.
There is a morality in well-made objects when the world
is harsh. A pot can teach you that dignity is not reserved for
ceremonies. Dignity belongs to daily bread.
The deeper history often placed pottery in women’s hands—
coil and mold techniques organized around domestic rhythms,
transmitted through household practice across long spans of
time. In many craft histories, the later movement toward wheel-
thrown pottery and market specialization could also mark a

shift in gender, economy, and social function: from domestic
production toward commercial production, from communal
use toward market sale, from integrated life-practice toward
specialized trade. This shift should not be simpliﬁed into a single
universal law, but its pattern matters. It shows how technology
can reorganize not only objects, but authority.
Then dyeing—indigo, earth tones, plant color, the language
of color that belongs to place rather than palette theory. Dye
is often discussed in art history as surface effect, as aesthetic
choice. But in craft lineages, dye is also knowledge: knowledge
of plants, water, timing, heat, fermentation, chemistry carried
through tradition rather than laboratories.
It is environmental intimacy turned into color. Indigo, in
particular, has a long, though uneven, history in Sudanese and
Nubian textile contexts. Its presence in archaeological textiles
and later cloth traditions suggests that blue was not simply a
color but a technical achievement, a material memory, a sign
that color itself could become an archive of local practice. A dyed
garment can become a moving record of place.
The color is not merely seen; it is read by those who know
its lineage. This is one of Sudan’s quiet powers: the ability
for the everyday to carry layers of meaning without needing
explanation.
Henna is another misunderstood archive, precisely because
it is ephemeral. Modern institutions tend to value permanence
because permanence is collectible.
But Sudanese aesthetic
intelligence often values the temporary because the temporary
is honest.
Henna is a geometry that lives on the body brieﬂy, then fades.
That fading is not failure. It is truth.
It mirrors the rhythm of life: ceremony, beauty, passing,

return. The body becomes the canvas, but not in the contem-
porary art sense of conceptual spectacle. The body becomes
the site where celebration, protection, femininity, marriage,
and belonging are made visible for a moment, then allowed to
dissolve without panic.
There is a spiritual wisdom in this: to create beauty without
insisting it must last forever. That is an aesthetic discipline
modernity has largely forgotten.
Beadwork and jewelry take this even further: objects worn
close to the body that function as social memory, status markers,
protective tokens, and sometimes economic stability. Across
Sudanese and South Sudanese communities, bead choice is not
merely ornamental. The arrangement of color, which strands
are worn and when, the age of the wearer, the social occasion,
the region, the community—these together can constitute a
legible language: lineage declared, age marked, wealth signaled,
regional belonging announced.
In some communities, color does not decorate the event;
it helps constitute the event. A child’s birth, a marriage, a
rite of passage, a public gathering—these moments are made
visible through what is worn, repeated, gifted, inherited, and
recognized. The body becomes a page, and ornament becomes a
form of social writing.
The milaya belongs especially to this conversation about
portable memory. In South Sudanese contexts, the milaya—
a hand-embroidered bedsheet or textile often decorated with
animals, ﬂowers, domestic scenes, and local motifs—has be-
come more than household cloth. In refugee settings such as
Bidibidi in Uganda, women have carried, stitched, sold, and
remade milayas as both memory and livelihood. Antelopes,
birds, ﬂowers, alligators, and other images become the complete
