logical obsession, as though Nubia matters only insofar as it
relates to Egypt. This is a kind of intellectual colonialism: even
scholarship can be an annex.
The custodial posture insists otherwise.
Sudan’s ancient
forms deserve to be approached as Sudan’s—full stop—without
requiring external validation.
In those ancient worlds, the relationship between art and
afterlife was not decorative.
It was governmental.
Tomb
architecture, ritual object-making, and ceremonial design were
forms of political metaphysics: they organized the community’s
relationship to death, memory, legitimacy.
The dead were not simply gone.
They were present as a
pressure on the living. The living responded with form: burial
practices, objects, inscriptions, arrangements of space meant
to sustain continuity beyond the visible horizon. If modern
aesthetics often asks, “What is beautiful?” ancient aesthetics
often asked, “What endures?” That is a deeper question, and it
produces a different kind of beauty: not beauty as spectacle, but
beauty as scaffolding for permanence.
Here a Post-Interpretive instinct becomes necessary. Because
the temptation is to translate all these practices into symbolism:
“This animal means that virtue,” “This shape represents that
deity,” “This ritual signiﬁes that belief.”
Sometimes such
readings are accurate. Often they are lazy. They allow the analyst
to feel intelligent without being accountable to the lived context
of the object. Symbolism can become a shortcut that replaces
encounter.
But many early Sudanese forms were not created to com-
municate abstract meanings to strangers. They were created
to operate within a community’s shared knowledge. To treat
them as puzzles for the outsider is to invert their ethic. The

visual vocabulary of a world worth recording. When displace-
ment came, women carried what could still carry home back to
them: cloth, pattern, memory, skill.
This is craft as portable homeland. When you must ﬂee with
only what you can carry, the embroidered sheet becomes both
memory and potential livelihood. The aesthetic object becomes
survival tool. The decorative becomes structural.
In contexts where women’s labor is undervalued by official
institutions, adornment becomes one of the few domains where
women can generate and control aesthetic authority. Jewelry can
be inheritance, portable wealth, and a public language of identity
all at once. The bead pattern can carry regional belonging. The
metal object can carry ritual function. The ornament is not
only “pretty.” It is a system of economy, of memory, of social
relation.
And then metalwork itself: forging, hammering, sharpening,
the transformation of resistant matter into usable form. Among
the Zande, whose communities extend across present-day
South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the Central
African Republic, craft was often inseparable from force. Knives,
spears, shields, and other objects were not merely tools of war;
they were objects of mastery—evidence that a people’s material
intelligence can become its civilizational signature.
Alongside metalwork, Zande and neighboring regional craft
traditions have included basketry, net weaving, pottery, carving,
and other forms of material production. The hand moved across
many forms, because the hand that can make is the hand that
can survive.
Here the land’s pedagogy returns again. Heat is not merely
endured; it can be used. Metal is not merely hard; it can be
disciplined. Scarcity is not only a hardship; it can become a

THE LENS OF CRAFT: INHERITANCE IN THE HANDS
constraint that trains ingenuity. A culture that can turn earth,
ﬁber, clay, metal, heat, and patience into objects of use and
beauty is a culture that has mastered the ethics of material
reality.
This is not romantic craftsmanship.
It is survival
intelligence; what I would call functional beauty: beauty that
earns its place by doing work.
Now we must confront the institutional failure that shadows
this entire chapter: the failure of art history to treat craft as
serious aesthetic thought. What the institutional category of
Fine Arts excludes, Sudanese daily life holds centrally: the
galabiya worn through Khartoum’s heat, the turbans and skull-
caps that mark male dignity in public space, the thoub draped
across ceremony and ordinary morning, the leatherwork that
mediates between the body and whatever ground it must stand
on. Yet these are often relegated to “applied arts” or “material
culture”—categories that sound neutral but function hierarchi-
cally.
When museums separate “ﬁne art” from “craft,” they often
separate men’s public production from women’s domestic pro-
duction, elite consumption from communal survival, collectable
objects from living practice.
This separation is not merely
academic taxonomy. It is political.
It decides whose labor counts as culture. It decides which
objects are archived and which are merely “used.” It decides
who becomes “artist” and who remains unnamed. In Sudan,
where so much aesthetic intelligence has been carried through
women’s hands, that institutional separation becomes a form
of erasure. It turns the culture’s backbone into its footnote.
Mo Abbaro was a Sudanese ceramicist and potter who moved
between institutions without letting institutions own him. Born
in Sudan, he studied Fine and Applied Arts at Khartoum Tech-

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
nical Institute before going to London to study ceramics at the
Central School of Arts and Crafts, followed by postgraduate work
in industrial pottery design at North Staffordshire College of
Ceramics. He returned to Sudan to teach ceramics for a period,
then continued his career in Britain, where he taught for many
years and exhibited internationally.
His work matters here because it complicates the false bound-
ary between craft and art. Abbaro did not need to abandon clay
in order to become serious. He made clay serious by allowing
it to retain its intelligence. His ceramics carry the memory of
vessel, curve, containment, and surface; they belong to the same
moral world as the pot and the calabash, even when they stand
within the gallery.
This is what it looks like when a craftsperson refuses to choose
between inheritance and education: the choice becomes the
form. And even when craft forms enter “ﬁne art” institutions,
they often do so by referencing—rather than continuing—the
living traditions. The calabash shape becomes aesthetic citation
rather than functional vessel. The basket becomes form rather
than household tool. The pot becomes sculpture rather than
container. That transformation can be beautiful, but it should
not make us forget the intelligence of the object before it entered
the gallery.
So this book refuses to treat craft as supplementary.
It
treats craft as one of Sudan’s central archives. Not because
it is quaint. Not because it is “authentic.” But because it is
where continuity has been most faithfully preserved, precisely
because it remained tied to daily life rather than to institutional
recognition. Craft survives by being needed. It is protected by
its usefulness.
A painting can be burned as propaganda. A textile tradition

records.text:
THE LENS OF CRAFT: INHERITANCE IN THE HANDS
survives because people still need cloth.
A pottery lineage
survives because people still need vessels.
A dye practice
survives because people still need garments. A bead pattern
survives because social life still needs symbols of relation. In
other words: craft survives because it cannot be fully separated
from living.
When women from South Sudan sit together to work—
threading
beads,
stitching
milayas,
shaping
baskets—
something else happens alongside the making.
The labor
creates a room. A room with no soldiers, no checkpoints, no
official narrative.
The talk that ﬁlls it is not political speech; it is social breath,
the kind that keeps a person human. What they embroider is
not merely craft. It is memory of the parts of life that violence
did not reach—the wedding, the harvest, the child’s ﬁrst steps.
The milaya becomes proof that these things happened. That
they were real.
This reveals craft’s psychological function: it is not only
economic survival or cultural transmission. It is therapeutic
structure. It is the ritual of making as a counter to the chaos
of war. It is the hand’s memory of peace enacted in present
time. The embroidered antelope is not nostalgia; it is active
remembering, the refusal to let war become the only story the
hands know how to tell.
This also changes how we understand Sudanese aesthetics
as a whole. Sudan’s beauty is not primarily museum beauty.
It is lived beauty. It is beauty that appears in thresholds, in
garments, in objects that are touched daily. It is beauty that
does not demand the spectator’s admiration because it is not
made for spectators. It is made for a community.
That makes it ethically purer. Spectator-oriented beauty is

easily corrupted by performance. Communal beauty, tied to
function, is often more disciplined. It has less room for vanity.
It is judged by whether it holds.
And this brings us to a ﬁnal doctrine: in Sudan, inheritance is
not only bloodline. It is skill-line. It is the passing down of how
to make.
How to dye. How to weave. How to mark. How to build.
These crafts do not merely reﬂect continuity—they are con-
tinuity. Each technique transmitted is a refusal to let rupture
have the ﬁnal word.
The skill carried in the hand is the archive that does not
burn. When a culture transmits making, it transmits worldview.
It transmits patience. It transmits attentional discipline. It
transmits the belief that the world can be shaped with care even
when the world is harsh.
That belief, in a postcolonial and wartime context, is not
trivial. It is resistance. It is the refusal to become purely reactive.
It is the insistence that the human can still create coherent form
under pressure.
Let the record show: Sudanese craft is not lesser art; it is the
aesthetic spine of survival, the archive carried in hands, and the
proof that beauty, when it is disciplined, can keep a world intact.
It is the grandmother teaching the granddaughter not merely
how to weave but how to remain economically sovereign.
It is the potter teaching not merely how to shape clay but how
dignity belongs to daily bread. It is the dyer teaching not merely
how to create color but how environmental knowledge becomes
inheritance. It is the henna artist teaching not merely how to
pattern skin but how beauty can be truthful by acknowledging
its own passing. It is the beadworker teaching not merely how
to string ornament but how social memory can be worn close to

And it is all of these practices, together, teaching that when
institutions fail, when borders are drawn, when archives burn,
when displacement scatters, the hands remember, and what the
hands remember can be taught again, can be made again, can
survive again.

12
The Lens of Migration: The Shadow
Canon of Diaspora
Sudanese art has learned to make itself in transit.
Not as a romantic tale of the wandering artist, but as a
structural fact: Cairo, London, Paris, the Gulf, Nairobi, Kampala,
cities that become temporary studios because the homeland,
too often, has been made difficult or dangerous for sustained
making. Exile, here, is not a scenic detour. It is an imposed
condition.
And when a condition repeats across generations, it stops
being biography and becomes material. It enters the work the
way dust enters lungs, quietly, continuously, shaping breath
without asking permission.
After his release from prison, El-Salahi eventually chose
departure: Doha ﬁrst, then, many years later, Oxford. Each
city a different kind of distance from Sudan, each move an
exchange of one form of precarity for another. But despite his
itinerant life, El-Salahi remained deeply attached to his roots.
This is not simply the story of one artist’s personal journey. It is
part of a larger pattern: political pressure or threat, departure,
156

records.text:
THE LENS OF MIGRATION: THE SHADOW CANON OF DIASPORA
years in foreign cities where the work continues under strange
light, eventual recognition in Europe or the United States, often
arriving late, when the artist is already old enough for the danger
of the work to be softened by history.
Diaspora produces a shadow canon: an archive made “else-
where,” yet tethered to Sudan by a cord of longing, anger,
responsibility, and fracture. The diaspora artist works under a
double sky. They paint beneath foreign light while their memory
keeps replaying Sudan’s sun.
They learn to translate their own instincts into environments
that don’t share the same sensory grammar.
The result is
a particular aesthetic of distance:
forms that feel slightly
displaced, images that carry a faint echo of a place that cannot
be re-entered, patterns that behave like portable homes. Even
when the work is formally conﬁdent, it is often metaphysically
unsettled.
Exile trains the imagination to become a suitcase: organized,
careful, portable, haunted.
The Qatar years, late 1970s into the 1980s and beyond were
years of deliberate reduction. El-Salahi drew in black and white.
Much of the world that admired his earlier work did not know
precisely where he was, or how intensely he continued to work.
He would later describe distance as something close to relief:
no audience pressing its expectations on the work, no institution
watching, no immediate demand to perform Sudanese identity
for anyone. Space, ﬁnally, to become more experimental. This
relief, the ability to work without being constantly watched,
without being expected to function as a national emblem is one
of exile’s paradoxical gifts.
Yet it comes at the cost of invisibility, of working in a space
where the work is not always recorded by the institutions that
157

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
claim to archive a culture’s history. Qatar offered safety, time,
and material resources. But it also placed the work outside the
most powerful circuits of art-historical recognition.
The admirers who didn’t know El-Salahi was there were not
necessarily ignoring him. Often, they simply had no way to track
an artist working outside the established circuits of recognition.
This invisibility is structural, not accidental. The art world
operates through networks: galleries know artists, critics know
galleries, museums know critics. When you work outside these
networks, when you work in Doha while many of the validating
networks are in New York, London, Paris, and later the Gulf’s
formal institutions, you can functionally disappear. Your work
continues, but it does not always register. You become a ghost
in your own career, making substantial bodies of work that may
not be “discovered” until someone with institutional access
happens to ﬁnd you.
His palette became a form of faithfulness. He often worked
with black, white, burnt sienna, yellow ochre—colors that recall
earth, skin, calligraphy, and Sudanese visual memory. The
constraint added depth, technically. But it also said something
else: displacement cannot instruct you to forget what color
meant at home. Even in Qatar, even later in Oxford, the earth
tones travel.
The visual memory of skin and soil becomes the portable
archive. This is not nostalgia. It is the stubborn insistence that
displacement cannot erase origin. But notice what this requires:
the constant mental translation of painting Sudanese earth
tones while looking at another landscape, of maintaining visual
ﬁdelity to a place one can no longer safely or consistently inhabit,
of keeping an aesthetic vocabulary anchored to a homeland that
exists partly in memory. The work becomes a bridge between
158

records.text:
THE LENS OF MIGRATION: THE SHADOW CANON OF DIASPORA
the body’s location and the mind’s home. The canvas becomes
the only place where these two geographies can coexist.
And then comes the burden of representation, that cruel gift
exile gives the artist. The moment you leave, you become a
spokesperson in the eyes of those who do not want to do the
work of knowing Sudan beyond headlines. Your name becomes
an entry point to a whole country.
Your paintings are asked to carry a nation’s complexity as if
the canvas were obligated to be diplomatic. You are invited to
speak, exhibit, explain, but what is being requested is often not
dialogue. It is a simpliﬁed Sudan that can be consumed.
A Sudan of tragedy neatly packaged. A Sudan of “resilience”
that ﬂatters the viewer’s conscience. Exile does not only relocate
the body; it relocates the gaze. It places the artist inside foreign
appetite.
In 2013, Tate Modern ﬁnally arrived: around one hundred
works, ﬁve decades, and a landmark retrospective widely de-
scribed as Tate Modern’s ﬁrst major exhibition devoted to
an African modernist, and one of the ﬁrst major British in-
stitutional recognitions of El-Salahi’s full achievement. The
exhibition was framed as revelation: a signiﬁcant ﬁgure in
African and Arab Modernism, now placed within a broader global
art history.
Notice what that framing requires.
The institution arrives last. It names what it ﬁnds. It calls the
naming recognition.
This recognition coming when the artist was in his eighties
reveals how institutions often fail diaspora artists until their
work becomes historically “safe,” until it can be celebrated
without fully confronting the systems that delayed its reception.
The Tate retrospective was honor, and it was overdue recog-

records.text:
THE LENS OF ORIGIN: THE UNWRITTEN ARCHIVE, BEFORE ISLAM,...
correct posture is restraint: to admit what we do not know,
to refuse to ﬁll gaps with elegant speculation, and to let the
object remain partially closed to us without punishing it for that
closure. Because closure is not failure. Closure can be dignity. A
culture is not obligated to be fully legible to the visitor.
And so the chapter’s central claim begins to sharpen: Sudan’s
earliest aesthetic life was not “before art.” It was before the
Western division between art and life. It was before institutions
demanded that beauty justify itself. It was before the colonizer’s
gaze arrived with its measuring instruments and its hunger to
classify. It was a world in which form was intimate with survival,
where the seen and unseen were not opposites but neighbors,
and where the community’s continuity depended on objects
and patterns that carried memory forward without needing a
museum to make them respectable.
This has consequences for how we will approach everything
that comes later. It means that when Islam arrives—when
scripture enters the aesthetic climate—it does not enter an
empty room. It enters a world already ﬂuent in pattern, already
disciplined in ritual, already skilled in encoding the unseen into
form. This is why Sudanese Islamic aesthetics will later feel like
a “third thing,” a whisper between Arab and African categories:
because Sudan was already a thirdness.
The pre-Islamic archive does not vanish; it becomes substrate.
It becomes the soil into which later forms root themselves. No
culture begins when a religion arrives. Religions arrive into
climates, and they are shaped by what they ﬁnd. In Sudan, what
they found was a people already trained in the ethics of pattern.
So we end where we began: with the refusal of reduction. “Pre-
Islamic” is a useful chronological marker, but it is a dangerous
aesthetic insult if it is used to imply incompletion. Sudan was

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
nition.
It was also a symptom of how institutions manage
belatedness.
By 2013, El-Salahi was old enough, established enough, and
far enough from the immediate political dangers of the 1960s
and 1970s that his work could be celebrated through the lan-
guage of historical importance. The revolutionary potential
of his earlier work could be safely historicized. The prison
drawings and the works that emerged from incarceration could
be displayed as testimony to past trauma, rather than as present
accusation.
The institution could congratulate itself on expansion without
having to confront why it took so long to recognize one of the
major modernists living partly within its own orbit.
This pattern repeats across diaspora experience: institutions
ignore artists while they are actively making difficult work,
then “discover” them when history has softened the risk. The
retrospective becomes both tribute and correction. It honors,
but it also reveals neglect. “Look, we include African artists,”
the institution seems to say. But inclusion that arrives late
can function almost like burial: a way to archive the artist into
history without changing the structures that made the delay
possible.
This is why diaspora artists often create under a double
audience: home and elsewhere. Home watches with suspicion:
Have you abandoned us? Have you softened? Have you become
a foreign product? Elsewhere watches with hunger: Perform
your origin. Give us your pain in a form we can understand.
Between suspicion and hunger, the artist must invent a
third posture: ﬁdelity without propaganda, visibility without
surrender.
Many Sudanese works in diaspora therefore develop a disci-

records.text:
THE LENS OF MIGRATION: THE SHADOW CANON OF DIASPORA
plined ambiguity. They refuse to become simple. They refuse
to become easily captioned. They refuse to be reduced to either
nostalgia or indictment. They do not deny the homeland, but
they do not allow the homeland to be turned into a marketing
identity. The work maintains a kind of opacity, not because the
artist is being deliberately obscure, but because opacity is one
way to avoid being consumed by either audience’s hunger.
Since the outbreak of the current war in Sudan in April 2023,
Cairo and other Egyptian cities have become major gathering
points for Sudanese creative exile: ﬁlmmakers, musicians,
writers, heritage workers, photographers, designers, cultural
researchers, and artists trying to remake working lives amid
displacement. To spend time among them is to understand
something about what endurance actually costs—not the dra-
matic breaking, but the sustained pressure of breathing for a
country you cannot safely return to, of keeping Sudan alive in
rooms that were never designed to hold it.
This phrase “breathe for Sudan in exile” captures something
essential about diaspora’s burden. The artist becomes a kind of
lung for the homeland, processing air that Sudan itself cannot
breathe safely. They take in the foreign atmosphere, extract
what can be used, expel what is toxic, and somehow keep
producing the oxygen of culture.
But lungs can collapse under too much pressure. The expecta-
tion to represent an entire nation is exhausting. The artist must
constantly negotiate: how much do I carry? How much can I
refuse to carry? What is solidarity and what is self-erasure?
Cairo has become particularly signiﬁcant as a site of Sudanese
creative exile. It is close enough to Sudan to maintain connec-
tions, far enough to escape immediate danger, large enough
to offer some infrastructure for artists to work, and, for some,

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
relatively more survivable than other cities. But Cairo is also
precarious. Many Sudanese refugees and displaced artists there
face legal uncertainty, economic exploitation, social discrimi-
nation, and the daily fragility of temporary arrangement.
Egypt offers proximity, but proximity is not protection.
Artists work knowing that status can be provisional, that money
can vanish, that housing can be unstable, that visibility can
bring opportunity and exposure at once.
Abushariaa Ahmed’s trajectory reads as the careful construc-
tion of a working life that Sudan could not at that moment hold:
departure in the mid-nineties, years connected to Nairobi and
the Paa ya Paa Arts Centre, a short period in Cologne, then a
longer settlement in Kampala from around 2000, where he built
a full-time artistic practice. His path, like many diaspora paths,
was not a single migration but a sequence of temporary rooms
each one offering walls he could paint, networks he could enter,
and enough stability to continue.
This trajectory—Khartoum to Nairobi to Cologne to Kampala,
with continuing ties to Sudan—illustrates how diaspora is often
not one departure but a series of attempts to ﬁnd stable ground.
Each move reshapes the work. Each city leaves its mark. The
artist becomes a palimpsest of places, carrying traces of every
location in his aesthetic vocabulary. Nairobi offers one kind
of artistic community, Cologne another, Kampala a third. The
artist learns to code-switch not just linguistically but visually,
adapting the work to whatever context offers the best chance of
survival and making.
Salah Elmur arrived in the world in 1966 near the Blue Nile,
in the Khartoum region—water as ﬁrst visual education. He
graduated in graphic design in 1989, the same year the coup
remade Sudan’s political sky. The years after the coup brought

records.text:
THE LENS OF MIGRATION: THE SHADOW CANON OF DIASPORA
pressure, arrest, and departure. Nairobi came ﬁrst; Cairo came
later. The Blue Nile remained, present in the work even when
the work was made nowhere near it.
His mid-1990s departure marks a particular generation:
artists who came of age during or after the 1989 coup that
brought Omar al-Bashir to power. For these artists, the decision
to leave was not always about a single crisis. It was often about
the long-term impossibility of working under a regime that
viewed cultural production with suspicion and narrowed the
space of public expression.
Distance also changes memory in speciﬁc ways. Memory is
not a stable recording; it is reconstructed each time we access it,
and the context of reconstruction shapes what we remember. An
artist in exile reconstructs Sudanese memory through foreign
frameworks. They remember Sudan while living in Cairo, and
Cairo’s dust, Cairo’s light, Cairo’s social dynamics, Cairo’s
political atmosphere inevitably color what they remember.
The Sudan of memory becomes partly Egyptianized, partly
imaginary.
This can sharpen certain details until they become almost
religious: the exact quality of Khartoum’s light at certain hours,
the smell of dust after rain, the sound of the call to prayer
echoing across neighborhoods. These details become precious
because they are what remains. They get polished through
repeated remembering until they shine with an intensity they
may not have had when one actually lived there.
But distance also blurs.
The daily irritations fade.
Petty
conﬂicts become irrelevant. The aspects of Sudanese life that
drove departure can become softened, romanticized, excused.
Exile can cause the homeland to become myth: too pure, too
painful, too symbolic. Every problem becomes the regime’s
163

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
fault. Every difficulty becomes political oppression. The com-
plexity of ordinary social life—the ways people can be kind and
cruel for reasons that have nothing to do with the state—can
fade.
Or it can go the other direction. Exile can cause the homeland
to become indictment: too oppressive, too disappointing, too
heavy to return to without rage. Distance reveals patterns that
proximity normalized. You see more clearly how women are
constrained, how ethnic hierarchies operate, how religious
authority polices daily life. Things once accepted as “just how it
is” suddenly become intolerable when viewed from outside. You
become angry at a version of home that perhaps never existed
as monolithically as memory now insists.
Both distortions leak into the work: either through over-
idealization or through severe austerity. Yet the most honest
diaspora works do something more difficult: they permit con-
tradiction. They allow Sudan to remain complicated. They allow
love and anger to share the same surface. They accept that home
can be both wound and devotion.
When El-Salahi was serving in Sudan’s Ministry of Culture and
Information, the state that employed him imprisoned him. Six
months without trial, in a cell where he made drawings on small
cement casings and buried them in sand before guards could
approach. What came after was departure. Doha. Later Oxford.
A palette stripped to black, white, and earth. And eventually The
Inevitable—vast, fractured, refusing to aestheticize Sudan’s civil
war, a monumental work that absorbed chaos without making
it beautiful, that bore witness without pretending the witness
was safe.
The chaos in The Inevitable mirrors the chaos of the homeland,
but it is chaos mediated by distance, by memory, by political

THE LENS OF MIGRATION: THE SHADOW CANON OF DIASPORA
rupture, by the impossibility of full return.
This is exile’s
particular torment: to witness your homeland’s suffering from
a position of relative safety, unable to intervene, unable to fully
grieve because you are not there, unable to fully celebrate safety
because your people are not safe. The work becomes a container
for this impossible emotional position.
It carries both the chaos of Sudan and the guilty safety of exile.
It refuses to choose between them.
El-Salahi’s memoir charts a geography of conversation—
Khartoum, London, São Paulo, New York, Doha—and in each
city, encounters that were never accidental. Hale Woodruff.
Jacob Lawrence. The Spiral Group, navigating Blackness and
modernism during the Civil Rights era.
Elijah Muhammad.
Ruﬁno Tamayo.
What unites these ﬁgures across their vast differences is the
question El-Salahi carried across every border: how does an
artist make work that is African, modern, and unmistakably
itself without allowing any of those adjectives to become a cage?
This global network becomes part of diaspora’s possibility:
exposure to conversations, movements, and aesthetics that
might not have been available in Khartoum. El-Salahi’s encoun-
ters with African American modernists offered him models for
how to navigate being simultaneously African and modern, how
to claim modernism without accepting its Eurocentrism. The
Spiral Group in particular—Black American artists grappling
with identity, politics, and representation during the Civil Rights
era—offered a parallel struggle to his own attempts to deﬁne
Sudanese modernism.
But these encounters are always haunted by the question: why
did one have to leave to access this? The artist carries a quiet
drumbeat of resentment beneath the gratitude. Resentment not

at the opportunities, but at the fact that opportunity required
departure, that growth required loss, that to become the artist
he needed to be, El-Salahi had to move away from the country
he wanted to serve.
There is also the material reality of diaspora work. El-Salahi’s
early movement was scholarship-shaped: the Slade School in
London from 1954 to 1957, then a UNESCO fellowship to the
United States in 1962, then travel and study across the Americas
in the 1960s. These institutions paid for crossings.
None of them could have anticipated what he would do with
the distances they enabled. Scholarships, grants, and fellow-
ships can enable the work, but they also create dependencies.
The diaspora artist often relies on foreign institutions for
support that should, in a just world, be available at home.
This creates complicated loyalties. You are grateful for the
fellowship, the residency, the invitation, the visa, the studio,
the grant. But you are also aware that institutional support
is never neutral. It brings networks, expectations, languages,
and frames. To accept support is often to enter someone else’s
grammar of value.
The practical challenges are mundane but constant. Shipping
artwork across borders is expensive and complicated. Customs
can damage work or hold it indeﬁnitely. Storage is expensive
when you do not have a permanent home. Insurance is often
unaffordable. Materials may not be available in the new location,
or they may be prohibitively expensive. The studio one can
afford may be smaller, darker, colder, or more provisional than
what the work requires. Artists work around these constraints,
but the constraints shape the work. They limit scale, determine
medium, inﬂuence process.
There is also the language barrier, even for artists working

THE LENS OF MIGRATION: THE SHADOW CANON OF DIASPORA
primarily in visual media. Gallery contracts are in English,
French, Arabic, or another administrative language of the host
country, and mistranslation can be costly. Artist statements
need to be written in the language of wherever one is exhibiting.
The artist has to explain the work in frameworks the local art
world understands, which means translating not just words
but entire conceptual systems. The intellectual labor of this
translation is immense and usually uncredited.
Return is not a single question but a calculation that changes
with each generation, each war, each set of roots laid down
in foreign soil. Ibrahim Shaddad, one of the key ﬁgures of
Sudanese cinema, active across the country’s fragile cinematic
decades and later forced into exile has repeatedly insisted on the
necessity of Sudanese cinema being made from lived proximity
to Sudan, not merely from distant representation.
Not nostalgia. Precision: Sudanese cinema cannot only be
made as an idea from afar. The country must be inhabited in the
body—lived and breathed—or the work risks becoming about
Sudan rather than of it.
This generational split runs deep through diaspora communi-
ties. The older generation, who remember Sudan before certain
ruptures—before al-Bashir, before South Sudan’s separation,
before the current war—carry memory of a Sudan that younger
generations may never have experienced. They feel a moral
obligation to return, to rebuild, to not let the homeland die in
exile. Their art often carries this obligation, this sense of debt
to the dead, to the ancestors, to the idea of Sudan itself.
But younger generations face a different calculation. Many
have spent more years outside Sudan than inside it. They have
built careers, relationships, families in the diaspora. Their
children may not speak Arabic ﬂuently, or may speak another
167

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
Arabic than the one that carries Sudanese intimacy. Return is
not simple homecoming. It would be another displacement, this
time from the life they have built.
And return to what? To a country at war? To a collapsed
economy?
To a political system that has not resolved the
conditions that forced departure?
Neither position is wrong. Both are attempts to solve an
impossible problem: how to remain Sudanese when Sudan itself
is fractured, unsafe, or inaccessible. The art made under these
different pressures differs accordingly.
Older artists’ work often carries explicit commitment to
return, to national project, to Sudan’s future. Younger artists’
work may be more ambivalent, more global in reference, less
bound to speciﬁcally Sudanese contexts. This can look like aban-
donment to the older generation. To the younger generation, it
looks like survival.
The shadow canon, then, is not monolithic.
It contains
multiple generations, multiple cities, multiple relationships
to homeland. What uniﬁes it is the fact of having been made
elsewhere, under the speciﬁc pressures of displacement. This
gives the work certain shared characteristics: a heightened
attention to memory, a tendency toward portable symbols—
pattern, color, motif that can travel—a certain defensive opac-
ity, and an underlying tension between presence and absence,
between here and there.
So we state it cleanly, as demanded: exile is not an accident
in Sudanese art; it is a material. It behaves like pigment. It
behaves like cloth. It behaves like breath. It conditions the
work’s rhythm, its guardedness, its longing, its refusal to be
fully legible. It teaches the artist to build portable altars out of
pattern and silence. It teaches the work to survive in rooms that

THE LENS OF MIGRATION: THE SHADOW CANON OF DIASPORA
were never meant to hold Sudan. It creates an archive that is
scattered but not broken, displaced but not destroyed, distant
but not disconnected.
Let the record show: the shadow canon is not lesser than the
homeland canon. Often, it is the homeland’s continuation by
other means: an archive made under foreign ceilings because
the original roof was set on ﬁre. And when institutions ﬁnally
recognize this work, when retrospectives ﬁnally happen, when
the art market ﬁnally pays attention, this recognition should
not erase the decades of neglect that preceded it. The shadow
canon survived without institutional support.
It will continue after institutional attention fades. Because it
was never made only for institutions. It was made to keep Sudan
alive in the bodies and minds of those forced to live elsewhere.
That work continues, regardless of who is watching.

not waiting for its meaning. Sudan was living it.
The older forms are not relics of ignorance; they are records
of intelligence, an intelligence that did not need academic
language to be real. They are evidence that a society can build a
sophisticated relationship to the unseen without metaphysical
pride, and can build beauty not as luxury but as a discipline that
keeps life coherent.
The Pyramid Fields No One Teaches
There is a speciﬁc ignorance that haunts the Western imagina-
tion when it encounters Sudan’s ancient past, and it centers on
a single fact that should be impossible to ignore but somehow
is: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt. Not metaphorically.
Not “pyramid-like structures.” Actual pyramids. More than two
hundred of them, clustered in the desert at sites like Meroë, Nuri,
and El-Kurru; steep-sided, stone-built, deliberate monuments
to royal power and cosmic order. Yet ask most educated people
to name a pyramid culture and they will say Egypt. Ask them
to name a second and they will say nothing, or reach vaguely
toward Central America. Sudan does not appear. This is not
accidental ignorance. It is curated absence.
The pyramids of Meroë alone should be enough to force a
reckoning. They rise from the sand in clean geometric deﬁance,
smaller than Giza’s colossi but no less intentional, no less
invested with the logic of permanence. They were built between
roughly 300 BCE and 300 CE, at the height of the Meroitic
Kingdom, when Kush had already outlived multiple Egyptian
dynasties and developed its own script, its own trade networks,
its own theological imagination. These were not imitations.
They were responses, aesthetic arguments made in stone about

The Lens of Rupture: The Hand
Continues
War is a force that attempts to erase the human by making the
human routine.
It turns suffering into statistics, and bodies into “develop-
ments,” and villages into “zones,” and grief into a headline
that expires. Sudanese art after war does not always “respond”
to this, because response implies a safe distance, implies the
luxury of reﬂection after the fact. Often the art is made inside
the rupture, with shaking hands, limited materials, and a reality
that does not pause to allow aesthetic reﬂection.
Under such conditions, a drawing is not merely a drawing. It
is proof that someone still had enough interior life left to mark
a surface.
Children who had survived violence in Darfur were given
paper and crayons and asked to draw. They drew what they
had survived: Janjaweed on horseback, Sudanese Armed Forces
in vehicles mounted with guns, green uniforms, burning, ﬂight.
These were not illustrations. They were depositions—speciﬁc,
unmediated testimony that adult witnesses could not always
170

records.text:
THE LENS OF RUPTURE: THE HAND CONTINUES
safely provide. The drawings were taken to the International
Criminal Court and accepted as contextual evidence of war
crimes and crimes against humanity in the Darfur case, includ-
ing proceedings connected to former President Omar al-Bashir
and other high-level suspects. The Darfur drawings are now
held by The Wiener Holocaust Library, placing a child’s crayon
in an institution devoted to the documentation of genocide and
mass atrocity.
Not metaphor. Accounting.
Let that sink in: children’s drawings as contextual evidence
at The Hague. Not as illustration, not as emotional supplement
to “real” evidence, but as documentation of atrocity that could
speak where conventional testimony was dangerous, broken,
or inaccessible. The drawing becomes legal trace. The child’s
hand becomes witness.
This is not metaphor.
This is the
literal transformation of mark-making into testimony under
conditions where traditional testimony has been made perilous.
In refugee camps, where the world becomes tent geometry
and time becomes waiting, drawings often appear as the ﬁrst
act of reclaiming shape. The child draws because the child must
insist that imagination still exists, that the mind can still make
something that was not there before, that interior life continues
despite external devastation. The adult draws because the adult
must insist that memory still has a place to land, that what
happened can be recorded even if it cannot yet be spoken, that
the act of making marks on paper is an act of continuing to be
human.
These gestures are not cute.
They are not heartwarming
stories of resilience for outsiders to consume. They are evidence.
They are the human refusing to be reduced to bare survival
alone. The pencil becomes a fragile tool of dignity, and dignity
171

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
here is not an abstract philosophical concept; it is the concrete
insistence that you remain a person who can make things, not
just a body that consumes aid and waits.
One young boy’s drawing depicts the attack on his village,
carried out by Janjaweed forces on horseback and Sudanese
Armed Forces in vehicles mounted with machine guns and tanks;
the attackers are shown wearing green military uniforms. A
separate drawing obtained after the June 3, 2019 Khartoum
massacre, made by an eight-year-old girl who witnessed the
violence outside military headquarters, records the massacre
through a child’s hand.
Another Waging Peace description
of children’s drawings from Sudan shows two distinct events:
in the upper portion, a Sudanese Armed Forces soldier on a
pickup truck mounted with a machine gun shooting at a woman
fetching water from a borehole; in the lower portion, a plane
bombing a herder accompanied by his goats.
Look at what these children record: not vague trauma, not
abstract violence, but speciﬁc tactical information. The Jan-
jaweed arrive on horseback. The SAF use mounted guns. The
attackers wear green uniforms. A woman is fetching water when
she is shot, which means she is engaged in the most basic act of
survival. A herder is with his goats, which means the violence
touches not only bodies but livelihoods. These drawings record
the destruction of civilian life at the level of gesture, labor, food,
water, animal, road, and ﬂight.
These are not “war drawings” in the sense that they aestheti-
cize violence or transform it into spectacle. They are testimony
drawn by those who survived what should never have been
survivable. The child’s hand shakes but continues. The line is
uneven but present. The proportions are off but the information
is precise. This is what war looks like when ﬁltered through a

records.text:
THE LENS OF RUPTURE: THE HAND CONTINUES
child’s need to make sense of senselessness, to give shape to
what has no shape, to create a record when official records are
being deliberately destroyed.
The drawings operate in a strange legal and aesthetic category.
They are evidence but also art. They are documentation but also
expression.
They must be accurate enough to be credible, but they bear all
the marks of being made by untrained hands under traumatic
conditions. How do you evaluate such work? Standard aesthetic
criteria—composition, technique, originality—become obscene
when applied as if these were ordinary objects of judgment.
Yet to refuse all aesthetic consideration is to deny that these
children were making intentional marks, exercising agency,
creating something.
The ethical challenge for anyone viewing these drawings is
to hold both dimensions simultaneously: this is testimony of
atrocity and must be treated with the seriousness that demands;
this is also a child’s artwork and must be honored as an act of
creation under impossible circumstances. To collapse it into
only testimony erases the child’s agency as maker. To treat it as
only artwork erases the political and legal weight it must carry.
What began in December 2018 as rage against bread prices,
against the cruel banality of a government that could not feed
its people became, by April 2019, something that shook the
foundations of thirty years. And in the space between rage and
revolution, art moved in. Not as commentary. As participation.
Walls became the ﬁrst public forum that could not easily be
shut down. Pavements spoke. Any surface that could hold paint
became a message.
The shift from camp drawings to revolution murals marks a
shift in war’s phase: from active violence to active resistance,
173

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
from recording atrocity to organizing against it. The revolution
art operates differently from the children’s drawings. It is public,
deliberate, strategic. It makes art a tool of political mobilization.
It understands beauty as weapon and wall as broadcast medium.
The iconography did not need to be subtle. Chains—because
thirty years of al-Bashir is not subtle. Doves—because peace in
Sudan has never simply meant absence of conﬂict; it has meant
the end of a particular machinery of violence. The faces of people
from across the country—because the revolution’s claim was
that it belonged to all of them, not just the urban center that
foreign cameras could reach.
The revolution iconography developed rapidly into a shared
visual language. Certain symbols became widespread: breaking
chains as a sign of liberation; the dove as a sign of peace;
the Kandaka ﬁgure, invoking Nubian queens and women’s
leadership; the blue painted nail that emerged as a solidarity
symbol after the killing of Mohamed Mattar; and the Sudanese
ﬂag colors, alongside other palettes that marked grief, anger,
and political position.
This visual vocabulary allowed for rapid communication
across ethnic, regional, and linguistic divides. When official
media cannot be trusted, when the internet is shut down or
throttled, when organizing openly is dangerous, visual symbols
painted on walls become infrastructure. They mark gathering,
memory, refusal. They commemorate martyrs. They provide
rallying points. They document what is happening in real time.
On the exterior wall of a Khartoum morgue—peach-painted,
hospital-adjacent, unremarkable from a distance—a spray-
painted corpse-hand emerges from the earth. The ﬁngernails
are green. On one ﬁnger hangs a tag bearing one word: missing.
Inside the building, approximately 200 bodies remained, many
174

records.text:
THE LENS OF RUPTURE: THE HAND CONTINUES
of them unidentiﬁed protesters from the 2019 revolution. The
smell of decomposition reached the street because power cuts
repeatedly disabled the refrigerators inside. The mural was
created by street artist Medo Kagonka, one of the Khartoum
artists whose work became politically charged during and after
the revolution.
The morgue mural operates at the intersection of art, memo-
rial, and accusation. It is not decoration. It is not even primarily
aesthetic.
It is a public counter to state suppression of information.
When official institutions fail to identify the dead, fail to notify
families, or fail to allow proper burial, the street artist steps in.
The mural becomes a grave marker in a city where many families
are denied the ordinary mercy of certainty.
It becomes the public record of death that the state wants to
hide.
The “missing” tag mimics morgue identiﬁcation tags but
turns them into accusation. These bodies are not simply dead;
their identities have been suspended, their families kept in
agonized uncertainty. The mural makes this suppression visible.
The green ﬁngernails, without needing a single ﬁxed inter-
pretation, darken the image into a hand that is neither living
nor properly buried. It is a hand that returns from the ground
because the living refused to name it.
And the smell matters. The mural exists in a place where
decomposition reaches the street.
It does not let you have
aesthetic distance. You cannot view it purely visually. The
air implicates your body, forces you to physically experience
proximity to the violence and neglect being named. This is
art that does not merely represent sensory experience; it is
embedded in it.
175

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
Assil Diab—who works under the name SudaLove—paints the
faces of murdered protesters on walls near their homes. Not in
galleries. On exterior walls in neighborhoods where families still
live, where security forces still patrol. She returned from Qatar
during the revolution and began painting martyrs’ portraits on
the walls of the buildings where they had lived.
The choice of location is the argument: these deaths are to be
publicly acknowledged, their erasure refused. In one instance,
when security forces threatened her while she was working, the
family of the deceased formed a human wall around her so she
could ﬁnish. She called it “a deﬁant show of strength.”
It was also something more: a community using its body as
the only institution available, when every official institution
had already failed.
This scene encapsulates something essential about war art’s
social function: the artist painting the face of a martyr near
his home while his family stands guard against the forces who
might erase him twice. This is not individual artistic expression
alone. This is collective action that uses art as its medium.
The painting is made possible by community protection. The
community protection is organized around artistic commemo-
ration. Neither can happen without the other.
The family forming a human wall around the artist reveals
that they understand the mural as necessary work, as work
worth risking further violence to complete. They recognize that
having their son’s face painted near their home is a form of
justice when legal justice is absent or delayed. It allows them
to publicly grieve when public grief has been criminalized. It
marks his death as murder, not as accident; as political killing,
not unfortunate incident.
For Diab, painting these portraits was a conscious choice to

THE LENS OF RUPTURE: THE HAND CONTINUES
enter danger. Women painting street art during and after the
revolution faced speciﬁc risks. Before Sudan repealed its Public
Order Law in November 2019, women’s appearance and behavior
in public could be policed. Diab herself worried that wearing
baggy trousers could get her into trouble with the police while
she painted. Her choice to paint anyway—with her technicolor
spray-paint bag and pink gas mask—was not romantic courage.
It was deliberate political risk.
The protests that began in December 2018 carried one de-
mand: that thirty years of Bashir end. By April 2019, they had
succeeded, which is to say, they had removed one ruler while
power remained contested by men in uniform. Then June 3, 2019
arrived: the sit-in site turned killing ground, the military and
security forces demonstrating that removal is not liberation.
Artists recorded it in real time, their work turning darker with
each death, more precise with each atrocity, more urgent as the
world looked away.
The timeline matters: protests began in December 2018,
Bashir was removed in April 2019, and the sit-in was violently
dispersed on June 3, 2019. The art evolves through these phases.
Early protest art is hopeful: breaking chains, doves, future-
oriented symbols. Post-Bashir art becomes more complex as it
becomes clear that military power has not disappeared. Post-
massacre art turns darker, angrier, more explicitly accusatory.
The visual language has to adapt to changing political reality; it
has to serve changing movement needs.
Mohammed Elmekki built his practice around distribution—
graphics designed for phone screens, for rapid sharing, for the
compressed attention of a population following events in real
time. His framing was unambiguous: the work was duty, not
self-expression. As a young Sudanese artist who believed in

what the revolution was doing, he treated ampliﬁcation and
documentation as obligation, keeping visual pressure from
becoming invisible.
The artist’s language here is signiﬁcant: duty, not oppor-
tunity. This is art made under moral obligation. The work
does not ask only, “How can I express myself?” It asks, “How
can I serve the movement?” The artist becomes a node in a
network of communication, using design to spread information,
commemorate martyrs, organize resistance, and maintain
morale.
Elmekki’s graphics function as applied aesthetics: beauty
weaponized for speciﬁc political ends. They are designed for
rapid social media distribution: high contrast, bold shapes,
limited text, powerful imagery that reads quickly even on small
phone screens. They are designed to be screenshotted, shared,
and reshared until they saturate digital space. They are designed
to work within the material constraints of digital circulation:
low bandwidth, interrupted access, compressed attention, and
fear.
This requires thinking about aesthetics in relation to infras-
tructure. The most beautiful mural in the world does little
politically if it cannot be seen, photographed, remembered, or
circulated. The most powerful graphic does little if it cannot
load. Revolution art under censorship has to understand the
material constraints of distribution and design accordingly.
Galal Yousif had already been painting women’s lives before
the revolution gave the walls a new urgency. His practice came
from inside Sudanese social pressure, not from the safe distance
of an observer. When the protests began, the work absorbed
that pressure without abandoning its original concern: the
revolution was also a demand for women’s freedom, not only

THE LENS OF RUPTURE: THE HAND CONTINUES
the removal of a dictator. Reporting from 2019 described Galal’s
murals at the sit-in, many of them showing gaunt ﬁgures
in Sudanese garments with red lines crossing their mouths,
symbols of censorship and oppression.
He described going into the streets and painting as a way to
heal, to break fear, and to document what was happening. The
painting was not supplementary to the uprising. It was among
its central arguments.
This is art as healing technology. But healing here does not
mean only private therapeutic recovery. It means collective
repair, the community painting itself back into coherence after
violence tried to scatter it. The street art becomes a shared
language, a visual vocabulary through which people who might
not trust words can still communicate hope, rage, dignity,
solidarity.
The breaking of fear is key. Fear under dictatorship is not just
an internal emotion. It is political technology.
The regime maintains power partly through fear, through
making people too afraid to gather, too afraid to speak, too
afraid to imagine alternatives. Street art breaks this fear not
by eliminating danger—danger remains real—but by making
visible that others are also unafraid, that one is not alone, that
the regime’s power to frighten is not absolute.
When an artist paints a mural in public daylight, he demon-
strates that public political expression is possible. When crowds
gather to watch, they demonstrate that public gathering is
possible. When people photograph the work and share it, they
demonstrate that communication networks exist outside state
control. Each of these demonstrations chips away at fear’s
power.
The documentation function is equally crucial. Art becomes

THE LENS OF ORIGIN: THE UNWRITTEN ARCHIVE, BEFORE ISLAM,...
what it means to govern, to die, to be remembered. The steep
angle of the Meroitic pyramid is distinct from the Egyptian
proﬁle. It announces itself differently. It refuses to be a copy.
And yet scholarship, for over a century, treated Meroë as Egypt’s
backwater, as though sophistication could only ﬂow north to
south, never the reverse.
This is where the violence of chronology becomes clear. Be-
cause Kush did not simply exist after Egypt’s decline. Kush
existed alongside Egypt, sometimes in conﬂict, sometimes in
alliance, and at one point—during the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty—
Kushite kings ruled Egypt itself. Pharaohs with names like
Piye, Shabaka, and Taharqa came from what is now Sudan and
commanded the entire Nile Valley. They built in both Egyptian
and Kushite styles. They understood both iconographies. They
were not provincial imitators; they were cosmopolitan rulers
navigating a region of multiple powers. To treat them as foot-
notes is to misunderstand the political and aesthetic complexity
of the ancient Nile as a whole.
And the material culture they left behind is not silent. Pottery
from Meroë shows a reﬁnement of technique and a discipline
of decoration that speaks to workshops, apprenticeships, and
aesthetic lineages. The painted ceramics—red and black on buff,
with geometric precision—were not peasant craft.
They were prestige objects, items of display and exchange.
Metalwork, particularly in gold and iron, was another Meroitic
strength. Iron smelting in Meroë was extensive enough that
some archaeologists have called the city “the Birmingham of
ancient Africa” a label that, while reductive, at least acknowl-
edges industrial capacity.
Gold, meanwhile, moved through Meroë’s economy as both
currency and symbol, adorning royalty, ﬁlling tombs, anchoring

a way to document what is happening because official doc-
umentation is controlled, censored, incomplete, or falsiﬁed.
The revolution murals become counter-archive, parallel record,
proof that things happened that the state may later deny. Future
histories of the 2019 revolution will depend partly on these
images because official records will be partial at best and
politically contaminated at worst.
The walls of Khartoum changed faster than the government
could respond.
Murals appeared overnight.
Posters were
rephotographed and circulated before the paste dried. Graffiti
spoke names that had been kept quiet for thirty years. The city’s
surfaces became its most honest newspaper—a counter-archive
running parallel to official silence, faster than state censors,
louder than any press release.
The tightly controlled public sphere is not an overstatement.
Under Bashir, public space was monitored; public criticism of
the government was dangerous; and artists often avoided openly
political public work. The revolution claimed public space partly
by claiming the right to mark it, to paint it, to make it visually
speak resistance.
This claiming of space through art was not secondary to “real”
political action. It was political action. Transforming walls
from blank or state-marked surfaces into movement-marked
surfaces changed whose space it was. When a neighborhood’s
walls are covered with revolution murals, the state no longer
controls that space visually. The movement does. This matters
psychologically and strategically.
But this chapter refuses spectacle. It refuses the aestheticiza-
tion of suffering. It refuses the foreign gaze that approaches
war art like a theatre of horror: hungry for images that can be
shared, captioned, consumed, turned into proof of one’s own

THE LENS OF RUPTURE: THE HAND CONTINUES
political consciousness.
Sudanese war-born art must not be treated as content for
empathy. It must be treated as human residue that survived the
attempt to erase it.
A poster is not merely propaganda; it is an act of communal
coherence, a way to maintain shared purpose when everything
else is fragmenting. A mural is not merely protest decoration;
it is a refusal of disappearance, an insistence on visibility when
the regime wants certain deaths invisible. A camp drawing is
not merely “resilience”; it is the minimal evidence that the self
remained intact enough to leave a mark, to claim: I was here, I
saw this, I survived to tell it.
What made 2018 distinct from 1964 or 1985 was not only
scale. It was also composition, speed, media, and visibility.
Earlier uprisings had major centers—trade unions, professional
associations, particular cities, and organized political forma-
tions. The 2018–2019 uprising also had organization, especially
through professional associations and neighborhood resistance
structures, but its body was broader and more visibly plural:
young people in provincial towns, workers and students, women
at the front of the image, regions speaking through the same
demand in different accents. The demand was singular, that
thirty years end, but the body making it was plural in a way that
changed the visual language.
This breadth shaped the iconography. The art had to speak to
and for different regions, ethnicities, classes, and generations.
This is why the iconography often reached for symbols of pre-
Islamic Sudan, including Nubian queens; symbols of diverse
Sudanese geography, including river, desert, and mountain; and
symbols of shared suffering, including martyrs from different
regions.
The visual vocabulary had to build unity without

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
erasing difference, had to assert “we are all Sudanese” without
demanding that anyone abandon particular identity.
War reshapes visual language structurally. It compresses,
because there is no time for elaborate composition when you
need to paint before security forces arrive. It sharpens, be-
cause symbols must be immediately readable to crowds moving
quickly through dangerous spaces. It makes symbol do more
work with less time: a single image must carry political message,
emotional appeal, tactical information, and aesthetic force.
It also forces the aesthetic into public urgency: art becomes
not the slow discipline of the studio but the fast ethics of the
street. The artist cannot afford to be precious about technique
when people are dying. The work serves or it fails its moment.
This creates a different relationship between maker and work—
less about self-expression alone, more about collective need.
Yet even here, even under these pressures, the deepest Su-
danese intelligence remains visible: the refusal to surrender
dignity. The human does not only cry. The human composes.
Even under bombardment, even in displacement camps, even
facing erasure, the hand continues to draw, the wall continues to
speak, the pattern continues to insist that beauty is not a luxury
but a fundamental human right; that to make art under war
is not frivolous distraction, but essential proof of humanity’s
persistence.
The murals that accumulated across the sit-in’s weeks were
not incidental to what happened there. They were its visual
memory, the most concentrated record of what the movement
believed and demanded. When regime forces cleared the camp
in June 2019, they painted over murals and erased visual records
from the site. But documentation had already begun. Pho-
tographs, digital archives, social media circulation, and memory

THE LENS OF RUPTURE: THE HAND CONTINUES
itself preserved what the walls could not hold forever. Human
rights lawyers and artists later emphasized that on June 3,
security forces not only killed protesters but wiped and painted
over the murals.
The documentation of erased murals becomes its own form
of resistance. The regime can paint over the walls, but it cannot
paint over every photograph, every shared image, every map,
every witness, every memory of what was there. The work lives
on in reproduction, documentation, and collective refusal.
This is crucial: war art survives not only in its physical form
but in its documentation, its circulation, its entry into collective
memory. Even destroyed murals continue to function politically
and aesthetically through their archived images.
Let the record show: Sudanese war art is not “about war” as a
theme, not distant aesthetic meditation on violence. It is war’s
failure to fully erase the human, each gesture a thin, stubborn
line drawn against oblivion, each mural a refusal of forgetting,
each drawing proof that interior life persisted when everything
exterior was being destroyed. The work does not transcend
violence. It marks the places where violence tried to erase and
failed, where humanity reasserted itself through color and line
and the determination to make something beautiful in the midst
of everything ugly.

The Lens of Silence: Withheld
Testimony as Strategy
In Sudan, silence is not empty. It is armored. It is a shield that
has learned language. Censorship does not only ban speech; it
trains the body to hesitate. It teaches the tongue to become
careful.
It teaches families to communicate in glances, in
metaphors, in half-sentences that carry full histories.
Under regimes of surveillance and under social conditions
where consequences arrive quickly and unpredictably, testi-
mony becomes a dangerous luxury.
So Sudanese art, like
Sudanese speech, often learns to survive through omission. Not
the omission of ignorance, but the omission of safety.
For thirty years under Omar al-Bashir’s regime, artists, writ-
ers, journalists, activists, and ordinary citizens learned to speak
with caution.
The direct statement could bring censorship,
harassment, interrogation, detention, or professional conse-
quence. The explicit critique could get a newspaper conﬁscated,
an exhibition pressured, a public event cancelled, or a name
placed under security attention. Sudanese authorities repeatedly
censored media, restricted expression, and cracked down on

THE LENS OF SILENCE: WITHHELD TESTIMONY AS STRATEGY
activists and journalists during the Bashir years, especially when
political criticism touched state violence, corruption, religion,
or justice.
So art developed its own encrypted language: images that
appeared decorative to the censor but carried heavier meaning
to those who knew how to read. This is not metaphor as poetic
ornament. This is metaphor as survival technology.
The mechanics of this coding are sophisticated. You cannot
make it so obvious that the censor catches on, but you cannot
make it so obscure that your intended audience misses it. You
walk a knife-edge between legibility and protection. A bird in a
painting may remain only a bird to the censor; to a viewer who
knows the poem, the martyr, the exile, the banned song, or the
political wound being echoed, it may become something else
entirely. The image survives because it refuses to confess too
quickly.
This places particular demands on the audience. The art does
not hand you its meaning. It withholds, deﬂects, encodes. To
follow it, you must bring cultural knowledge, political aware-
ness, historical memory. You must know what cannot be said
directly in order to recognize when it is being said indirectly.
What emerges is a community of readers bound by shared
code: people who recognize the references, who understand
what is being withheld and why. This is not without its own form
of closure. The work opens toward those who already know, and
that opening is also, inevitably, a boundary.
Coded artworks emerge from this ecology with speciﬁc formal
characteristics. Symbols become double-edged tools: a bird
that can mean ﬂight, disappearance, exile, or burial depending
on context, color, and composition. A tree that can mean root-
edness, family lineage, hanging, knowledge, or loss depending

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
on how it is rendered. A pattern that can read as ornament to
the untrained eye and as warning, mourning, or resistance to
those who know how to read it.
Abstraction, in particular, becomes shelter. When you paint
abstractly, the censor cannot easily reduce the work to a single
prosecutable statement. What is this painting about? It is about
color, form, composition. It is not “about” anything that can
be neatly articulated as political critique. Yet for viewers who
share the context, formal choices carry weight: the violent red
that dominates the canvas, the fragmented composition that
refuses coherence, the empty spaces that feel like absences,
the repetitive marks that feel like compulsion, trauma, or the
desperate attempt to hold something together.
This is one reason Kamala Ibrahim Ishaq’s Crystalist work
remains so important. Ishaq, a pioneering Sudanese painter
and one of the ﬁrst women to graduate from the College of Fine
Arts in Khartoum, helped form the Crystalist Group in the 1970s
and developed a practice that challenged the male-dominated
Sudanese art scene. Her work often explored women’s bodies,
spiritual experience, psychological states, and social constraint
through distortion, translucency, and ambiguity rather than
straightforward narrative.
Her engagement with Zār is central here. Ishaq studied and
painted Zār ceremonies, where women—and sometimes men—
gather in ritual, spiritual, and therapeutic contexts involving
possession, bargaining with spirits, performance, and healing.
These ceremonies are not simply aesthetic subjects. They are
intimate social and spiritual worlds, tied to women’s experience,
bodily distress, psychological pressure, and communal forms
of care.
By working through distortion, crystalline form, and symbolic

THE LENS OF SILENCE: WITHHELD TESTIMONY AS STRATEGY
density, Ishaq created a visual language that could hold women’s
constrained lives, women’s spiritual practices, and women’s
psychological realities without reducing them to documentary
explanation. Is this painting about Zār ceremonies? It may be. Is
it about transformation, pressure, possession, emotional strain,
or women’s social life? It may be that too. The work can be read
multiple ways, and this multiplicity is part of its force.
The work can say what it cannot declare. It can carry grief
without indicting a single hand. It can carry critique without
ﬂattening itself into slogan.
It can protect the privacy of
the practice while acknowledging its aesthetic and spiritual
importance.
When you paint a grieving mother, you do not need to specify
who killed her son. The grief itself becomes accusation: against
whoever created the conditions for grief, against systems that
make mothers bury children, against political arrangements
that normalize violence. The work points without naming.
This is not evasiveness. This is ethics under threat.
Metaphor becomes protection in literal ways.
If security
forces, officials, or hostile observers examine a work for ev-
idence of sedition, ambiguity matters. A painting of a bird is
easier to defend than a poster naming a general. A fractured
red ﬁeld is harder to prosecute than a written accusation. Ambi-
guity is not only aesthetic choice. Under certain conditions, it
becomes legal, social, and bodily strategy.
This creates interesting tensions around interpretation. The
artist may want some viewers to understand the political dimen-
sions while protecting themselves from accusation by author-
ities. This means the work must be simultaneously open and
closed: readable to initiates, opaque to outsiders.
This is the opposite of how Western art discourse often

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
imagines itself: as universal, accessible to any educated viewer,
transcending particular contexts. Sudanese coded art often re-
fuses this universal accessibility. It requires entry into particular
knowledge systems to be fully read.
The domestic sphere becomes particularly important in
this ecology of coded expression.
The home is not outside
surveillance—regimes can recruit informants, monitor families,
and punish kinship networks—but it can offer more cover than
the street, the gallery, the newspaper, or the radio. Women’s
craft, ornament, speech, and domestic practice can therefore
become zones where memory, grief, and coded testimony travel
relatively unnoticed.
A woven pattern can carry information that would be dan-
gerous if written. The pattern looks decorative, traditional,
apolitical. But if you know the maker, the occasion, the deviation
from ordinary usage, or the context of its making, you may read
more than surface. A wedding pattern used outside a wedding
might signal celebration that cannot be publicly acknowledged.
A mourning color, rhythm, or motif might signal a death that has
been officially denied. The pattern becomes code, and the home
becomes the space where this coded communication circulates.
Henna designs can work similarly.
Applied to women’s
bodies for celebrations, transitions, and ritual occasions, henna
appears as cultural practice: traditional, feminine, domestic.
But the speciﬁc patterns chosen, the timing of application, the
refusal or insistence on adornment during periods of mourning
or fear—all of these can carry meaning to those who know how
to read.
When women gather for henna nights or other intimate forms
of sociality, they create spaces that are partly protected from
the dominant public gaze. What is said in these spaces, what is
188

marked on these bodies, operates in a register that may appear
apolitical but can still carry political and social content.
This is not to romanticize women’s domestic labor as inher-
ently resistant. Much domestic work is simply work: survival,
duty, the daily repetition of tasks necessary to maintain life. But
under conditions of censorship, the domestic sphere’s relative
privacy can make it available for forms of coded communication
in ways the public sphere is not. Women may become carriers
of certain kinds of memory precisely because their work is
dismissed as merely decorative, merely functional, merely
private.
Silence is especially charged for women because the social cost
of visibility is not evenly distributed. A man who speaks publicly
faces censorship, imprisonment, violence.
A woman who
speaks publicly can face all of that plus reputational destruction,
sexualized threat, social ostracism, and family shame. During
the Bashir era, Sudan’s public order regime policed women’s
public behavior and appearance with particular severity; the law
was only repealed in November 2019.
So women’s testimony frequently travels through coded chan-
nels: craft, domestic form, ornament, rhythm, the aesthetics
of the home. What the public sphere forbids, the domestic
sphere preserves in pattern. What the official archive refuses,
the private archive carries quietly.
Here, silence is not consent. It is strategy. It is survival that
refuses to become spectacle. It is the determination to maintain
witness even when witness cannot be spoken.
The ethical complexity emerges when we consider what
silence protects and what it costs. Silence protects the speaker
from immediate harm: arrest, violence, social punishment,
family exposure. But silence can also allow the conditions that

trade with Rome, with Arabia, with the interior of Africa. These
were not isolated villages. These were nodes in a network.
But here the archive becomes contested, because much of what
we know about Meroë comes not from Meroitic voices but from
Greek, Roman, and Egyptian sources, external perspectives that
saw Kush through the distortions of empire. Classical writers
like Herodotus, Strabo, and Pliny describe the region with a mix
of fascination and condescension, calling its people “Ethiopi-
ans” (a Greek term meaning “burnt-faced”) and attributing
to them both great wealth and barbarism, depending on the
writer’s mood.
These accounts cannot be dismissed—they contain useful
details—but they also cannot be trusted as neutral. They are
the conqueror’s ethnography, the trader’s rumor, the rival’s
caricature. They tell us more about how outsiders wanted to see
Kush than about how Kush saw itself.
What makes this loss sharper is that the Meroitic script—an
alphabetic writing system developed around 300 BCE—remains
only partially deciphered. We can identify phonetic values for
many signs. We can read names and a few formulaic phrases. But
the grammar, the syntax, the full semantic range of the language
remains largely opaque. This means that Meroë’s own voice; its
literature, its theology, its administrative records, its poetry if it
had any is still locked inside inscriptions we can see but not fully
hear. The irony is bitter: a civilization sophisticated enough
to invent its own writing system is still forced to speak to us
primarily through the secondhand accounts of its neighbors and
enemies. The unwritten archive, in this case, is not unwritten.
It is unread.
And yet even in this silence, the material speaks. Temple
reliefs at sites like Naqa and Musawwarat es-Sufra show deities

require silence to continue. If no one speaks, if all testimony
remains coded and hidden, the regime faces less pressure
to change. This creates impossible positions: speak and be
destroyed, or stay silent and watch destruction continue.
Many Sudanese artists navigate this by ﬁnding threshold posi-
tions: ways to speak that are just legible enough to matter, just
coded enough to survive. They push boundaries incrementally,
testing what can be said, how much directness a regime, faction,
institution, or community will tolerate at a given moment.
These calculations shift constantly based on political conditions.
During periods of relative opening, artists can be more direct.
During crackdowns, coding intensiﬁes.
The 2019 revolution created a brief period when silence
became less necessary. For a few months, artists could speak di-
rectly. Street art could mock al-Bashir, commemorate martyrs,
name violence, and depict military power with open accusation.
The work from this period is striking in its directness. Finally,
the ability to say clearly what had been said in code for decades.
But that openness was fragile. After the violent dispersal
of the sit-in on June 3, 2019, the revolutionary visual ﬁeld
darkened. Reporting and scholarship on Sudan’s uprising note
that protest art shifted after the massacre: brighter colors gave
way to harsher palettes, martyrs, rape crimes, military violence,
and grief. Security forces also painted over or erased murals
after the sit-in, turning the destruction of art into a second act
of suppression.
As military power remained central and the transitional period
failed to secure a stable freedom of expression, silence returned
as a necessary skill.
Artists who had become accustomed
to direct speech had to re-enter the old languages of code,
metaphor, and strategic withholding. Some faced harassment,
