THE LENS OF SILENCE: WITHHELD TESTIMONY AS STRATEGY
intimidation, public pressure, or the forced erasure of their
work. The precise consequences varied, but the lesson was
familiar: openness had limits, and those limits could be enforced
violently.
The 2023 war intensiﬁed this dynamic. Artists working inside
Sudan cannot always say what they are witnessing. The risks
are too high, not just for themselves but for their families, their
communities, and anyone identiﬁable through their testimony.
Social media has become a major battleﬁeld in the SAF–RSF
war: a space of propaganda, intimidation, hate speech, military
narrative, and public accusation. Reports since the war began
have documented the weaponization of social media, online
incitement, and the circulation of violent or self-incriminating
footage by armed actors and supporters.
So the work develops a particular texture during this war
period. It shows enough to acknowledge reality—yes, this is
happening; yes, we see it—but not so much that it exposes
people to danger. It walks a knife-edge between testimony and
protection.
This is not cowardice. This is the complex calculation of how
to bear witness without getting yourself or others killed.
Some artists choose complete silence. They stop posting, stop
making work public, retreat from visible artistic practice. This
is also a choice that should be respected, not criticized. The
demand that artists “speak out” often comes from those who
face none of the consequences of speaking.
It is easy to demand bravery from a safe distance. The artists
living through war must decide for themselves what level of risk
is sustainable.
And the ethic of this chapter is simple: do not punish withheld-
ness by demanding disclosure. Do not treat silence as deﬁciency.

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
The modern critic often approaches art like a courtroom: tell
me what happened. Explain yourself. Provide evidence. Make
yourself transparent. Prove your political commitment by being
legible to me. But Sudanese silence is often a moral decision: I
will not deliver my people’s vulnerability to your appetite for
clarity. I will not give you the speciﬁc details that could be used
to harm speciﬁc people. I will not satisfy your curiosity at the
cost of someone’s safety.
The critic’s job, then, is not to extract confession. It is to
witness the shield. It is to recognize that opacity is sometimes
the only ethical option available, that withholding is an active
choice deserving respect, not a passive failure deserving criti-
cism. It is to understand that silence can be loud; that it can be
its own form of testimony about conditions so dangerous that
testimony becomes impossible.
This requires a different kind of criticism, one that respects
boundaries, that understands that not everything is meant to be
legible to everyone, that recognizes withholding as intelligent
strategy rather than aesthetic failure. The Post-Interpretive
approach insists: some things are kept deliberately unclear, and
that opacity is not a problem to be solved. It is a boundary to
be honored. It is a door marked “do not enter” that should be
respected, not forced open.
The reader trained in Western transparency will ﬁnd this
frustrating. They want the work to “open up.” They want
“access.” They want the artist to make themselves vulnerable
for the reader’s beneﬁt, to provide the full story, to eliminate
ambiguity. But access is not a right when access itself has been
weaponized. Interpretation has historically functioned as a tool
of extraction: the colonizer interpreting the native culture, and
in the process claiming to understand it better than the people

who live it; the ethnographer explaining Indigenous practice,
and in the process ﬂattening it into data; the critic decoding
the artwork, and in the process claiming ownership over its
meaning.
All of these interpretive acts can function as forms of violence
when they insist on making visible what was strategically kept
hidden.
When the critic demands that the work reveal its
political content, the critic may not realize they are asking
the artist to expose themselves or others to danger. When the
viewer wants full explanation, they may not understand that
full explanation could compromise speciﬁc people. The desire
for transparency is not innocent. It has costs that are borne by
others.
So Sudanese silence teaches a harder lesson: that understand-
ing is not always the goal. Sometimes the goal is simply to
remain near the work without demanding that it surrender itself.
Sometimes the ethical stance is: I see that you are not telling
me everything, and I respect that decision.
I will not interpret your silence as an invitation to dig deeper.
I will not mistake your opacity for a puzzle that exists for me to
solve. I will accept that there are things I am not meant to know,
and I will be at peace with not knowing them.
This is particularly important for work emerging from con-
texts of trauma.
Survivors of violence often cannot speak
about what happened, not because they have forgotten, but
because the memory is too raw, too dangerous, too likely to
re-traumatize. Trauma does not create a narrative that can be
neatly told.
Trauma fragments narrative, breaks causality, makes time
non-linear, creates gaps that cannot be bridged by explanation.
Demanding that art “process” or “express” trauma in ways that

make it legible to viewers is demanding that the artist re-open
wounds for the viewer’s beneﬁt.
Silence, in these contexts, is not avoidance.
It is self-
protection. It is the psyche’s wisdom about what can be spoken
and what must be held.
The work may carry traces of trauma without naming it di-
rectly. It may be present in the formal choices: the fracturing of
composition because the self is fractured; the darkness of palette
because the world has gone dark; the violence of brushstroke
because the body remembers violence; the emptiness of space
because something that should be there is missing.
These are somatic responses: the body speaking through the
hand even when the mouth stays closed. The hand knows things
the mind cannot articulate. The mark on the canvas carries
weight the artist may not be able to explain verbally.
To read these traces requires sensitivity, not interrogation.
It requires sitting with uncertainty rather than rushing toward
conclusion. It requires being comfortable with not understand-
ing fully, with sensing that something heavy is present without
needing to name exactly what it is.
There is also the question of what silence protects cultur-
ally. Some practices, some stories, some aesthetic forms are
considered private by the communities that hold them. They
are not meant for outsiders. They are speciﬁcally not meant
to be explained in ways that outsiders can access. This is not
obscurantism. It is sovereignty. It is the community’s right
to maintain boundaries around what they share and what they
keep.
When critics demand that Sudanese art “explain itself,”
they may be demanding that communities surrender their
sovereignty, that they make their private practices public, that

THE LENS OF SILENCE: WITHHELD TESTIMONY AS STRATEGY
they translate their internal logics into forms palatable to
outsiders. The refusal to do this is not failure to communicate.
It is refusal to submit to the assumption that everything must
be made available to everyone.
This becomes especially charged around religious practices,
women’s practices, and practices involving altered states of
consciousness or spirit possession. Zār ceremonies, for instance,
are often painted or referenced in Sudanese art, especially in
the work of Kamala Ibrahim Ishaq. But Zār is not simply a
public performance. It is a ritual and healing practice with social,
spiritual, gendered, and psychological dimensions. To explain it
fully to outsiders, or to make it fully “accessible,” risks violating
its privacy, reducing it to spectacle, or changing the nature of
what is being held.
So art that references Zār often maintains a certain reserve.
It shows enough to acknowledge the practice’s aesthetic and
spiritual importance, but not so much that it exposes what
should remain private. This is not teasing the viewer. This
is honoring the practice by refusing to commodify it, by not
turning it into content for outsiders’ consumption.
The work becomes a threshold. You can stand at the edge.
You can sense that something is happening inside. But you
are not invited all the way in unless you have earned that
invitation through relationship, initiation, trust, or belonging to
the community that holds the practice. The artwork marks the
boundary rather than erasing it. This is ethical making: making
that knows when to stop, that knows when to protect rather
than expose.
Let the record show: silence in Sudanese aesthetics is not
emptiness. It is an intelligence forged in danger, a form of
speech that refuses to make itself easy to harm. It is strategy

developed over decades of navigating censorship, surveillance,
and violence. It is knowledge about what can be said and what
must be withheld.
It is respect for practices that should remain private. It is
protection of people who are vulnerable. It is refusal of the
colonial demand for transparency.
And the critic’s task is not to break the silence but to under-
stand why it exists, to honor what it protects, to accept that
some things are kept deliberately out of reach: not as failure but
as dignity, not as withholding but as wisdom, not as absence but
as presence of a different kind. The silence speaks, if you learn
how to listen. But learning to listen means accepting that you
will not understand everything, that opacity is sometimes the
most honest form of communication available, that the shield
is as important as what it shields.

The Lens of the Ghost: What Sudan
Tried to Forget
Sudan keeps an archive, and like all the most important things, it
is almost impossible to suppress. It rises through the work with
the quiet insistence of a truth that has grown tired of waiting to
be acknowledged: slavery, that most proﬁtable of inheritances,
trailing its hierarchies and silences behind it like a court train
no one will admit is still being worn; the politics of Arabization,
which discovered, as such politics often do, that identity is most
efficiently managed when rebranded as culture.
The South, whose beauty was never really suppressed so much
as misﬁled under the wrong heading by those who preferred its
brilliance at a comfortable distance. Nubia, which the power-
ful converted into scenery while living Nubian communities
remained inconveniently present; ethnic tension, which polite
society has often agreed not to discuss, and which has therefore
been forced to conduct itself as atmosphere.
None of these are topics. They are the furniture of the room,
and the room has been arranged by people who claimed they
were simply letting in the light.
197

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
Slavery’s ghost moves through Sudanese visual culture in
ways that are rarely acknowledged directly. This is not ancient
history. Slavery and the slave trade in Sudan were formally at-
tacked and gradually dismantled under Anglo-Egyptian colonial
rule, with 1924 often marking a decisive legal and administrative
moment in that abolition process; but the social hierarchies
produced by enslavement and slave raiding did not vanish when
legal status changed. Informal bondage, racialized servitude,
stigma, and the afterlife of slave descent continued to shape
social life long after formal abolition. That means there are
people alive today whose grandparents or great-grandparents
lived in a world where slavery, servitude, or slave descent were
not abstract historical concepts but social facts.
The hierarchies it established—who is considered beautiful,
who is considered civilized, who is granted full humanity—
persist in aesthetic choices that seem merely formal.
Color choices in painting are never just about color. When a
painter consistently renders skin in lighter tones, when darker
skin appears primarily on laborers or marginal ﬁgures, when
beauty standards visually favor Arab features over African
features, these are not neutral aesthetic decisions. They carry
historical weight.
They reproduce hierarchies that slavery inscribed. The eye
has been trained by history to see certain bodies as more worthy
of aesthetic attention, more suitable for heroic portrayal, more
properly “Sudanese.”
But to speak about slavery directly in Sudan is to risk frac-
turing national unity, to risk opening wounds that the official
narrative insists have healed. The nationalist project often
requires the ﬁction that “we are all Sudanese now,” that shared
citizenship has erased historical violence, that independence

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE GHOST: WHAT SUDAN TRIED TO FORGET
created a clean slate. To insist on slavery’s ongoing effects is to
be accused of divisiveness, of stirring up old conﬂicts, of being
unpatriotic.
So the art often cannot speak the word “slavery,” but it
carries the weight anyway. It appears in the careful way certain
artists render Black Sudanese bodies, with dignity that pushes
against historical degradation, with complexity that refuses
stereotyping, with centrality that challenges marginalization.
It appears in the choice to paint subjects from marginalized
regions, to honor aesthetic traditions from communities his-
torically targeted by raiding, enslavement, or racial contempt,
to insist on beauty in bodies that history tried to render as less
than human.
It appears also in silences: in the absence of direct engage-
ment with slavery’s history, in the way certain narratives are
sidestepped, in the topics that remain unaddressed.
These
silences are not innocent. They reﬂect the ongoing difficulty of
reckoning with a past that implicates powerful lineages, com-
fortable class positions, national myths of unity, and ongoing
forms of racial hierarchy.
The politics of Arabization haunts the work in similarly unspo-
ken ways. For decades, Sudanese state formation was shaped
by the privileging of Arabness, Arabic language, and Islam
as central markers of national identity. This was not merely
cultural preference. In the postcolonial state, Arabization and
Islamization operated through education, administration, law,
media, and war, especially in relation to South Sudan and
other non-Arab or non-Muslim communities. Scholars have
described the conﬂation of Arabic, Arabness, and Islam in
twentieth-century Sudan as central to the country’s citizenship
crisis.

THE LENS OF ORIGIN: THE UNWRITTEN ARCHIVE, BEFORE ISLAM,...
and kings in procession, their iconography blending Egyptian
motifs with distinctly Meroitic elements: gods with multiple
arms, lions with exaggerated musculature, queens; yes, queens,
because Meroë had a tradition of powerful female rulers called
kandakes depicted with the same martial authority as kings.
These are not marginal images. They are state propaganda,
theological instruction, visual law. They organize the cosmos
on stone so that the living know their place within it. To stand
before these reliefs now, half-eroded by wind and time, is to
stand before an aesthetic system that knew exactly what it was
doing: asserting order, continuity, and legitimacy in a world
that constantly threatened all three.
Pottery, Cattle, and the Grammar of Survival
Move south and west from the Nile’s royal centers, and the
aesthetic archive changes texture. Among the Nilotic people,
Dinka, Nuer, Shilluk, and others, whose lives were organized not
around monumental stone but around cattle, migration, and the
ﬂood rhythms of the Sudd, a different kind of formal intelligence
emerges.
Here, the body becomes the primary site of aesthetic elabora-
tion. Scariﬁcation patterns, the shaping of the skull in infancy,
the cultivation of speciﬁc physical postures and gestures, all
of these are forms of design, ways of making the self legible
within a community’s code. This is not decoration for its own
sake. In societies where wealth is counted in cattle, where
political authority is negotiated through oral performance and
kinship, and where the environment offers few permanent
materials for monumental building, the body becomes the most
reliable surface for the inscription of identity. A young man’s

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
The violence of this was both explicit and implicit. Explicitly:
military campaigns against non-Arab and non-Muslim regions,
especially in the long wars with the South, were frequently
accompanied by civilizational language, Islamic-nationalist
rhetoric, and the demand that difference submit to a central
state project. Implicitly: educational systems privileged Arabic;
state institutions rewarded assimilation into dominant cultural
forms; media centered Arab-Islamic Sudanese aesthetics; and
non-Arab languages and identities were often pushed into the
margins as regional, tribal, or backward.
The art world was not exempt from this pressure.
What
counted as “Sudanese art” was often what aligned with Arab-
Islamic aesthetics or could be incorporated into them. The
Khartoum School, while genuinely revolutionary in many ways,
still operated within this terrain.
Its synthesis of African and Islamic forms was a major inter-
vention, but it also often centered Arabic calligraphy, Islamic
visual inheritance, and an idealized African element as the
organizing language of national modernism. The “African”
component was sometimes drawn from ancient, symbolic, or
generalized forms rather than from sustained institutional
recognition of living non-Arab Sudanese cultures. The Khar-
toum School’s achievement remains real; so does the question
of what its synthesis included, what it translated, and what it
left peripheral.
Non-Arab,
non-Islamic
aesthetic

remained

A Dinka
scariﬁcation pattern becomes anthropology. Arabic calligraphy
becomes art. A Beja weaving technique becomes craft. Islamic
geometry becomes design. The categories themselves carry

the weight of Arabization:
they structure what counts as
worthy of serious aesthetic attention and what is relegated
to ethnographic curiosity.
This creates painful positions for non-Arab Sudanese and
historically Sudanese/South Sudanese artists. To succeed in
the national art world often required learning to speak in
visual languages legible to Arab-dominated institutions. Or one
could refuse this and remain marginal, working within one’s
own community’s aesthetic traditions but without national
recognition, institutional support, or the resources that national
recognition brings.
Some artists navigate this by code-switching, making
work in multiple registers, producing work that ﬁts national
frameworks for exhibition and sale while also making work
in community-speciﬁc forms for different audiences. This is
survival strategy, but it is exhausting. It requires constantly
negotiating between aesthetic systems, constantly translating,
constantly justifying why a particular tradition deserves
attention.
The suppressed beauty of the South is the ghost that the 2011
separation should have forced Sudan to confront but largely did
not. South Sudan’s independence was treated by many in the
North as loss, betrayal, or failure of national unity. But it could
also have been understood as symptom of the North’s failures:
failure to include, failure to protect, failure to recognize South
Sudanese cultural forms as equally central to the history of the
country that once claimed them.
The aesthetic brilliance of South Sudanese traditions—
elaborate beadwork systems that encode social information
in color and pattern, scariﬁcation traditions that mark bodies
with aesthetic and spiritual meaning, body arts that use ash and

pigment to create extraordinary visual effects, architectural
forms adapted to swamp, savannah, and forest environments,
musical traditions with their own scales, rhythms, and
instruments—remained underrepresented in institutions that
claimed to represent “Sudanese” art before separation.
Even now, after separation, there is too little sustained en-
gagement with South Sudanese aesthetics as part of the his-
torical ﬁeld from which Sudanese modernity emerged. The
narrative often treats 2011 as a clean break: now there is
Sudan and there is South Sudan, and their art histories are
separate. But this erases centuries of entanglement, shared
and violent history, movement, intermarriage, trade, war,
displacement, and the ongoing presence of South Sudanese
people and practices in Sudan.
It also risks erasing the violence that made separation polit-
ically imaginable. The narrative rarely asks: what conditions
made remaining impossible? What exclusions, what sustained
violence, what refusal of recognition made independence appear
to many as the only viable option? These questions remain
largely unasked, which means the conditions that produced
them remain largely unaddressed.
The art that does engage with the South can fall into problem-
atic patterns. It either romanticizes the noble traditional culture
untainted by modernity or pathologizes the violent tribalist, the
underdeveloped primitive, the victim needing rescue. Both are
failures to see South Sudanese aesthetic production on its own
terms, to recognize it as sophisticated cultural practice rather
than exotic other or tragic victim.
Nubia’s ghost is perhaps most visible because Nubian culture
has been partially recuperated as national heritage, but in a
strange, ﬂattened way. Ancient Nubian civilization is celebrated

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE GHOST: WHAT SUDAN TRIED TO FORGET
as proof of Sudan’s historical importance. The pyramids at
Meroë appear in tourism campaigns, museum displays, national
imagery, and public narratives of ancient greatness. Archaeo-
logical sites become objects of national pride. Museums display
Nubian artifacts with reverence.
But this celebration is highly selective. It celebrates ancient
Nubia, safely archaeological, available to be claimed by the
nation-state as heritage.
It does not equally protect living
Nubian communities, who have faced repeated displacement
from dam projects, cultural and linguistic pressures, economic
marginalization, and the loss or ﬂooding of ancestral lands.
The Merowe Dam, built at the Fourth Cataract, displaced
tens of thousands of people—commonly estimated between
roughly 50,000 and 70,000—especially the Manasir, Amri, and
Hamadab communities along the Nile. These communities
are often discussed within the wider history of Nubian and
Nile Valley displacement, though it is more precise to name
the affected communities rather than simply calling them all
“Nubians.”
The disconnect is stark: the state and nation celebrate ancient
Nubian temples while living Nile communities are displaced
from their lands.
It displays Nubian artifacts in museums
while Nubian languages and place-names face pressure, loss,
or decline. It uses Nubian imagery as heritage while political
demands for compensation, representation, and cultural protec-
tion are often ignored. This is heritage as appropriation: taking
the aesthetically useful aspects of Nubian culture while refusing
full responsibility for living communities.
Nubian artists work within this contradiction. Their aesthetic
forms are sometimes celebrated as “authentically Sudanese,”
proof of Sudan’s ancient civilization, proof of African achieve-

ment, useful for national image. But they can be dismissed as
“regional” or “ethnic” when they assert speciﬁcally Nubian
concerns, when they demand recognition not as heritage but as
ongoing cultural practice.
The art becomes a negotiation: how to honor the civilizations
that built the pyramids of Meroë while also acknowledging
communities displaced by dams? How to claim pride in Nubian
heritage while also insisting on justice for living Nubians?
How to make work that is recognizably Nubian without being
ghettoized as merely ethnic rather than nationally signiﬁcant?
The characteristic Nubian aesthetic—bright colors, geometric
patterns painted on house walls, speciﬁc forms of pottery, weav-
ing, and domestic decoration—becomes fraught territory. Is
this tradition to be celebrated or folklorized? Is it living culture
or heritage preserved like a museum piece? The line between
honoring and freezing, between recognition and appropriation,
is constantly negotiated.
Ethnic tension remains perhaps the most dangerous ghost
because it is recent, raw, and violently unresolved. Darfur’s
genocide and mass atrocities exposed what the state had long
denied: that citizenship does not erase ethnic hierarchy, that
“we are all Sudanese” is an aspiration rather than a settled
fact, and that state and militia violence can be organized along
racialized and ethnic lines.
The systematic targeting of Fur, Masalit, Zaghawa, and other
non-Arab groups in Darfur was not an aberration. It intensi-
ﬁed existing hierarchies of land, race, ethnicity, state power,
and armed impunity. The Sudanese government and allied
Janjaweed militias carried out mass atrocities against these
communities between 2003 and 2005, and since the 2023 war,
the RSF and allied militias have again targeted many of the same

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE GHOST: WHAT SUDAN TRIED TO FORGET
communities. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum
notes that the RSF is rooted in the Janjaweed and that recent
atrocities in Darfur have targeted civilians based on ethnicity.
Artists working with Darfur’s violence face an impossible task.
How to represent atrocity without sensationalizing it, without
turning genocide into spectacle? How to honor victims without
reducing them to victimhood, without denying their complexity
as people who had lives before and beyond the violence? How to
acknowledge the ethnic dimension without reinforcing ethnic
division, without suggesting that ethnicity is inherently divisive
rather than something made divisive by political manipulation?
Many choose silence or heavily coded reference. The work
carries weight without naming what it carries.
A painting
might show destruction without specifying whose destruction.
A sculpture might evoke loss without detailing who was lost. The
work becomes container for grief that cannot be fully articulated,
for rage that cannot be safely expressed, for accusation that
cannot be directly leveled.
This is strategic silence again, but driven by different pres-
sures than censorship alone. It is driven partly by the trauma
being too large to represent directly: how does one make an
artwork adequate to hundreds of thousands of deaths, to mass
rape as a weapon of war, to entire villages burned, to ongoing
displacement of millions? Any representation risks inadequacy,
risks diminishing the scale of what happened.
It is driven partly by ongoing danger.
The militias that
committed violence in Darfur were not fully dismantled. Many
ﬁghters and commanders associated with Janjaweed structures
became part of the RSF, the paramilitary force now waging
war across Sudan. To explicitly name their crimes can invite
retaliation.
The ghosts are not safely historical.
They are

walking around with guns. They are in power. They are capable
of killing again.
It is driven partly by the difficulty of addressing ethnic vio-
lence in a national art context. To make work explicitly about
Darfur’s ethnic dimension risks being accused of tribalism,
divisiveness, or anti-Arab sentiment. Some national narratives
reduce the violence to land and resources alone, as if ethnicity
were secondary or incidental.
To insist on the ethnic and
racialized dimension challenges that story, which can mean
risking exclusion from institutions, funding, recognition, or
safety.
The 2023 war has reopened these ghosts simultaneously.
RSF violence in Darfur has repeated many of the patterns of
earlier atrocities: ethnicized targeting, mass killing, sexual
violence, displacement, and attacks on non-Arab communities.
The power struggle between SAF and RSF also reﬂects deeper
questions about who gets to deﬁne Sudan, whose violence
becomes state violence and whose violence becomes rebellion,
whose vision of Sudan gets to prevail, and whether the country
can exist beyond an Arab-Islamic nationalist frame.
The destruction of cultural infrastructure during the war
reﬂects the vulnerability of Sudan’s memory itself. Museums
have been looted or damaged, universities burned or occu-
pied, archives endangered, laboratories desecrated, and artists,
scholars, museum workers, and cultural custodians forced to
ﬂee. Reports from 2023–2025 documented looting, vandalism,
combat damage, and destruction affecting the National Museum
and other cultural institutions in Khartoum and beyond, with
RSF control and looting widely reported in relation to the
National Museum. The damage is not merely collateral in a
narrow sense. Whether deliberate, opportunistic, or produced

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE GHOST: WHAT SUDAN TRIED TO FORGET
through combat, it strikes at the infrastructure through which
Sudan remembers itself.
This is where the Post-Interpretive posture becomes explicit
and urgent. I will not solve the ghosts. I cannot solve them. I do
not have that power, that knowledge, that moral authority.
To claim I could solve them would be to claim a position
outside the haunting, a place from which I could analyze dis-
passionately and offer solutions. But there is no such place. To
write about Sudanese art is to write from inside the haunted
house. The ghosts move through my own categories, my own
assumptions, my own desire for coherence.
I will not turn the ghosts into neat arguments. This chap-
ter will not end with solutions, with recommendations, with
the critic’s typical move of identifying the problem and then
proposing how to ﬁx it. That move assumes that problems
of this magnitude can be ﬁxed through cultural intervention,
that addressing ghosts in art history somehow addresses the
material conditions that created them.
This is fantasy. This is the critic’s delusion of relevance.
I will not offer the reader the comfort of resolution, because
comfort has often been the accomplice of erasure. The modern
reader wants closure because closure is control. If the chapter
ends with clear conclusions, the reader can ﬁle it away as
understood, as handled, as no longer requiring attention.
But the haunted archive refuses control. It insists that some
histories remain morally unﬁnished, and that the ethical task is
not to ﬁnish them with language, but to stay beside them until
the reader’s desire to “understand” collapses into humility.
To stand beside a ghost is to accept that the ghost is not an
object.
It is a demand.

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
It demands that we recognize the limits of our explana-
tions.
Slavery’s ongoing effects cannot be fully mapped or
measured. Arabization’s violence cannot be undone by better
cultural policy. The South’s separation cannot be retrospectively
prevented. Nubian displacement cannot be compensated by
heritage recognition. Ethnic violence cannot be resolved by art
criticism. These are problems that exceed the reach of aesthetic
intervention.
The ghosts demand that we stop using interpretation as a way
to keep pain at a safe intellectual distance. When we interpret
slavery’s residue in visual culture, we risk turning it into an
interesting analytical problem rather than ongoing injustice.
When we analyze Arabization’s aesthetic effects, we risk treating
it as historical process rather than continuing violence. The
move to interpretation can be a move away from implication, a
way to study the wound without acknowledging our proximity
to the systems that produced wounds.
The ghosts demand that we acknowledge how institutions—
colonial, national, cultural—have curated forgetting with pro-
fessional skill.
Museums decide what to display and what
to store.
Archives decide what to preserve and what to let
decay. Curricula decide which artists to teach and which to
omit. Funding bodies decide which work to support and which
to starve. All of these decisions shape what is remembered and
what is forgotten, and none of them are neutral.
Sometimes forgetting is not accidental. Sometimes it is policy.
The state that claims ancient Nubian heritage while displacing
living Nile communities is not simply confused. It is strategic.
The art institutions that celebrate the Khartoum School while
ignoring non-Arab aesthetic traditions are not merely ignorant.
They are reproducing hierarchies.
The critics who discuss

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE GHOST: WHAT SUDAN TRIED TO FORGET
Sudanese modernism without addressing slavery’s legacy are
not only forgetful. They are avoiding discomfort.
Sometimes forgetting is pride. Sometimes it is the price of an
identity that cannot survive truth. To build a uniﬁed Sudanese
national identity has often required papering over certain divi-
sions, creating a narrative of shared heritage that elides whose
heritage is actually shared and whose is marginalized. The cost
of this identity is the truth it must suppress.
Sudanese art often functions as a custodian of erasure: it
carries what the official narrative tries to smooth over. It does
this not always through explicit imagery, but through atmo-
sphere, omission, fracture, residue. The ghost appears as a gap
in the archive: the artists who never received recognition, the
traditions that were never documented, the aesthetic practices
that were dismissed as craft.
The ghost appears as stubborn motif, the recurring image
that makes no sense until you understand the history it is trying
to carry. The ghost appears as silence that feels too heavy to
be merely aesthetic: the topic that is consistently avoided, the
region that is consistently underrepresented, the experience
that ﬁnds no visual form.
The work becomes a site where the unreturnable remains
present, not as explanation, but as pressure. You feel something
in the work that you cannot name. You sense absence. You
recognize that something is being withheld or something has
been lost. This pressure is the ghost making itself felt. It does
not appear as a clear image that can be identiﬁed and discussed.
It appears as disturbance in the ﬁeld, as the place where the
work does not cohere, as the tension that cannot be resolved.
The reader who wants this chapter to “explain” the ghosts has
misunderstood the project fundamentally. Explanation would

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
scariﬁcation marks his passage into adulthood. A particular
pattern on the forehead or torso signals lineage, clan, and
sometimes individual achievement. The marks are painful. They
are permanent. They are meant to be. Because permanence is
the point. In a world of seasonal migration, of ﬂoods that erase
settlements, of conﬂicts that scatter populations, the body is
the one archive that moves with you.
Western observers have often reacted to these practices with
discomfort, reading them as “mutilation” or “primitive self-
harm.” But this reaction reveals more about Western anxieties
around bodily autonomy and aestheticized pain than it does
about the practices themselves. The ethical stance here is not
to celebrate or condemn from a distance, but to recognize that
different cultures negotiate the relationship between pain, iden-
tity, and beauty in different ways. In many Nilotic communities,
the willingness to endure scariﬁcation was understood as a test
of courage, a public demonstration of one’s readiness to endure
hardship.
The aesthetic outcome—the patterns themselves—was in-
separable from the ethical act of enduring. Form and fortitude
were the same event. Cattle, too, carry aesthetic weight in these
cultures, though this is often invisible to outsiders who see only
economic function. A prized ox is not merely valuable; it is
beautiful. Its color, its horn shape, its comportment; all of these
are subjects of intense attention and verbal artistry. Cattle songs,
composed and performed by young men, describe individual
animals with the same precision and emotional investment that
a European poet might reserve for a lover or a landscape. This is
not metaphor, the ox is not standing in for something else, the
ox is itself the occasion for aesthetic attention.
To dismiss this as “just agriculture” is to miss the point
12

require a position outside the haunting, a place from which one
could analyze dispassionately, a perspective untouched by the
history being discussed. But there is no such place.
If you are reading this as a Western academic, you may
inherit colonial structures that helped create these ghosts:
categories that separated “Arab” from “African,” hierarchies
that ranked civilizations, institutions that extracted artifacts
and knowledge.
If you are reading this as Sudanese diaspora, you may carry
these ghosts in your own family histories, your own ambigu-
ous identities, your own negotiations between belonging and
exclusion. Your own family may have been slave-owning or
enslaved, Arabizers or Arabized, perpetrators or victims, or
some complicated combination of these. You do not get to
analyze this from outside. You are implicated.
If you are reading this as Sudanese in Sudan, you live daily
with the consequences of what remains unresolved. You nav-
igate ethnic tensions that cannot be named, you participate
in hierarchies you may not consciously recognize, you inherit
structures you did not personally create but that structure your
life regardless. You are inside the haunted house, whether you
acknowledge the ghosts or not.
No one gets to be innocent observer. This is crucial. The
fantasy of neutral analysis is a fantasy of innocence: the belief
that we can study the ghosts without being touched by them,
that we can remain clean while handling dirty history.
But the ghosts do not grant this distance. They implicate ev-
eryone who comes near. They demand: what is your relationship
to this?
How do you beneﬁt from the structures that created me? What
are you willing to give up to address the injustice I represent?

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE GHOST: WHAT SUDAN TRIED TO FORGET
These are not rhetorical questions. These are demands for
ethical reckoning. And most of us fail them.
Most of us—myself included—want to acknowledge the
ghosts without changing the material structures they haunt. We
want to be thoughtful about history without sacriﬁcing present
comfort. We want to be on the right side intellectually while
remaining on the comfortable side materially.
So the reader must be trained here, must be confronted with
the insufficiency of reading as response. If you feel impatient,
if you want the chapter to “resolve,” that impatience is the very
habit that makes ghosts necessary. The desire to be ﬁnished is
the desire to be innocent, the wish to acknowledge history and
then move on, to feel that understanding equals absolution.
This book does not grant innocence. It does not grant absolu-
tion. It grants proximity.
Proximity means staying near the ghosts without demanding
they become comprehensible. It means acknowledging that
slavery’s residue shapes contemporary aesthetics without pre-
tending we can trace every causal line, without claiming to fully
understand how historical violence becomes internalized as
aesthetic preference. It means recognizing that Arabization’s
violence continues without claiming we can neatly separate
“Arab” from “African” identity, without pretending that ad-
dressing cultural violence solves structural violence.
It means honoring Nubia’s living presence without ﬂattening
it into nationalist symbol, without turning living communities
into heritage assets. It means sitting with ethnic tension’s
ongoing reality without rushing toward false unity, without
pretending that calling everyone “Sudanese” erases the hierar-
chies that make that identity unequal. It means accepting that
South Sudan’s separation was a symptom of Sudan’s failures
211

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
without claiming to know how those failures could have been
avoided.
The aesthetic consequence of haunting is fracture. Work that
carries ghosts cannot be smoothly coherent. It contradicts itself
because the reality it emerges from is contradictory. It contains
ruptures it cannot explain because the ruptures in the social
world cannot be explained. They can only be witnessed. It
gestures toward something it cannot name because naming
would require making explicit what may remain strategically
unclear, emotionally impossible, or historically unresolved.
This fracture is not failure.
It is honesty.
It is the work
refusing to lie about the coherence of Sudanese identity, refusing
to pretend there is one uniﬁed Sudanese culture, refusing to
suggest that Sudanese history has been resolved. The fracture
is evidence of the ghosts’ presence. The work breaks where the
ghosts press against it. The composition fails where the ghost
disrupts it. The narrative stutters where the ghost interferes.
Western art history tends to read fracture as postmodern
fragmentation, as deliberate aesthetic strategy, as the artist
choosing to fragment as stylistic move. But Sudanese fracture is
not always chosen. Often, it is inherited. It is not simply strategy.
It is symptom.
The work fractures because the ground beneath it is fractured.
The artist does not always decide to create ruptured composi-
tion; the rupture erupts through the work because the historical
ﬁeld is ruptured.
To smooth the work into coherence would be to lie about the
ground. To unify the composition would be to falsely claim that
Sudanese reality is uniﬁed. To resolve the tensions would be to
suggest that the historical tensions have been resolved.
The fracture is the truth the work cannot avoid. It is the

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE GHOST: WHAT SUDAN TRIED TO FORGET
ghost’s mark, the place where haunting becomes visible.
Let the record show: Sudan’s ghosts are not puzzles to be
solved; they are moral presences to be endured, until the reader
learns the ﬁrst mature lesson of witnessing: that some histories
demand humility, not mastery. The haunted archive does not
ask for understanding. It asks for acknowledgment.
It asks that we stop pretending we can know completely,
explain fully, resolve ﬁnally. It asks that we learn to live with
what cannot be settled, to make art near what cannot be spoken,
to stay present with what refuses to be made comfortable.
The ghosts will not be solved by this chapter. They will not
be explained away by better interpretation. They will not be
resolved by more sensitive curatorial practice.
They remain because the conditions that created them remain.
They haunt because the violence that generated them continues
in new forms. They press against the work because they press
against the world, because Sudan has not yet fully reckoned with
slavery, Arabization, ethnic hierarchy, displacement, and the
suppressed beauty of marginalized communities.
The work can only carry this. It cannot solve it. And the critic
can only witness the carrying, can only stay near the weight, can
only refuse the false comfort of claiming to understand what
cannot be understood from outside.
This is the lesson of the ghost: stay humble, stay near, stay
honest about your limits. The ghost exceeds your categories.
Let it.
213

Epilogue: The Custodian’s Oath
I did not write this book to capture Sudan.
Capture is what empires do.
I wrote it to stand near what survives—near the forms that
carried breath through heat, carried memory through rupture,
carried dignity through displacement, carried beauty through
war, carried silence through danger. I wrote it to refuse the crude
habit of turning Sudan into a narrative that comforts outsiders.
This is not a book of ownership. It is a book of proximity.
So I end with an oath, not as theatre, but as discipline. I will
not treat Sudanese art as a resource for my cleverness. I will not
translate it into slogans to satisfy impatient readers.
I will not mistake interpretation for intimacy.
I will not
aestheticize suffering. I will not ask the work to perform its
wounds for my certainty.
I will approach each object, each motif, each silence, each
fracture, as evidence of a people’s ongoing struggle to remain
coherent in a world that has repeatedly tried to dismantle them.
I will remember that institutions are not neutral, that archives
are political, that forgetting is often curated, and that the critic’s

EPILOGUE: THE CUSTODIAN’S OATH
ﬁrst responsibility is not to speak, but to listen. I will remember
that beauty is not decoration but discipline, that silence is not
emptiness but shield, that craft is not lesser but foundational,
that the domestic is not peripheral but primary, and that exile
is not accident but material.
And when the ghosts arrive, when the archive trembles with
what cannot be safely named; I will not force resolution. I
will stay beside the haunting until my own appetite for control
dissolves. I will accept that humility is sometimes the only
honest aesthetic conclusion.
Let the record show: the custodian does not arrive to own
meaning. He arrives to protect presence, so that what survived
history’s violence is not violated again by the violence of our
language.

THE LENS OF ORIGIN: THE UNWRITTEN ARCHIVE, BEFORE ISLAM,...
entirely: these cultures do not separate the utilitarian from the
beautiful. They understand that life itself can be the medium of
art.
Pottery, meanwhile, travels between the domestic and the
ceremonial. In many Sudanese cultures, ceramic production was
and remains the domain of women, and the vessels produced
carry both functional necessity and symbolic density. A water
jar is shaped to balance on the head during long walks from well
to home.
But it is also shaped to please the eye, to assert the skill of its
maker, to ﬁt within a community’s sense of proper proportion.
Some pots are burnished to a high sheen, their surfaces catching
light in ways that transform the everyday act of fetching water
into a moment of visual encounter. Others are incised with
geometric patterns—lines, dots, crosshatching—that echo the
scariﬁcation on bodies, the weaving in baskets, the arrangement
of space in a homestead. Pattern, in this context, is a language. It
does not need to “mean” something external to itself. It means
coherence. It means continuity. It means that the world, despite
its volatility, can still be organized.
The Christian Interlude and the Architecture of Conversion
And then there is the archive that even specialists often overlook:
Christian Nubia.
Between roughly the sixth and ﬁfteenth
centuries CE, the kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria, and Alodia
converted to Christianity; not the Christianity of Rome or
Byzantium exactly, but a distinct Coptic-inﬂuenced tradition
that developed its own theological emphases, its own liturgical
language (Old Nubian), and its own visual culture.
Churches were built along the Nile, their walls covered in
13

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
frescoes depicting saints, biblical scenes, and ecclesiastical
hierarchies. These were not crude provincial copies of Mediter-
ranean models. They were sophisticated adaptations, works
that took Byzantine iconographic conventions and translated
them into a Nubian key.
The frescoes at Faras, uncovered in the 1960s before the site
was ﬂooded by Lake Nasser, remain among the most striking
examples. Figures rendered in rich ochres, deep blues, and
luminous whites stare out from the walls with an intensity
that suggests not passive devotion but active spiritual combat.
Angels hold swords, saints hold scrolls. Kings are depicted
alongside bishops, the sacred and the political braided together
in paint. The style is hieratic—ﬂattened, frontal, iconic—but it
is not lifeless.
There is a tension in these images, a sense that they are doing
work, that they are not merely illustrating scripture but enacting
protection, establishing presence, organizing space.
What makes Christian Nubian art particularly important for
this book’s argument is that it complicates any narrative that
treats Sudan’s aesthetic history as a simple progression from
“traditional” to “Islamic.” Christianity was not a marginal
episode. It was a sustained cultural formation lasting nearly
a millennium, longer than Islam has existed in some parts of
northern Sudan.
And when Islam did arrive, it did not erase Christian Nubia
overnight. There were centuries of coexistence, of trade, of
intermarriage, of slow transformation. The aesthetic legacy
of Christian Nubia, its attention to ﬁguration, its use of archi-
tectural space as theological argument, its tradition of literacy
and manuscript production did not vanish. It sank into the
substrate, where it would later resurface in unexpected forms: in
14

THE LENS OF ORIGIN: THE UNWRITTEN ARCHIVE, BEFORE ISLAM,...
the decoration of Quranic manuscripts, in the layout of religious
schools, in the visual grammar of authority.
But Christian Nubian art also suffered a speciﬁc kind of era-
sure: colonial scholars, when they encountered it, often praised
it primarily as evidence that “civilization” had reached Africa.
The implicit logic was insulting; that Christianity brought
art, that without external religion there could be no aesthetic
sophistication. This misreads the evidence entirely. Christian
Nubia was impressive not because Christianity arrived, but
because Nubia already had the social organization, the craft
traditions, the architectural knowledge, and the political will to
make Christianity its own. The frescoes at Faras were painted
by Nubian hands, commissioned by Nubian rulers, viewed
by Nubian congregations. They were not imports, they were
syntheses.
What the Silence Protects
There is always a point in this kind of historical accounting
where the evidence runs out and speculation begins. We do not
have diaries from Meroitic queens. We do not have manifestos
from Dinka poets. We do not have treatises on aesthetics from
Nubian bishops. The archive is fragmentary, and the fragments
are unevenly distributed: more stone survives than wood, more
gold than cloth, more monumental than domestic. The result is
that we see power more clearly than we see dailiness.
We see kings more clearly than farmers. We see ritual objects
more clearly than children’s toys.
This unevenness is not
neutral. It shapes what we think we know about these cultures.
It makes them seem more remote, more ceremonial, less human
than they were.

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
But the silence also protects something.
It protects the
cultures from being fully consumed by external interpretation.
It ensures that some portion of their world remains unavailable
to the analyst’s hunger. This is not romanticizing absence. It
is acknowledging that incomplete knowledge can be a form of
respect, a way of not pretending to possess what we do not.
So when we speak of the “unwritten archive,” we are speaking
of two things at once: the knowledge that was indeed preserved
without alphabetic text, carried forward in practice and pattern
and memory; and the knowledge that has been lost, that we
can gesture toward but not recover, that leaves gaps in the
historical record which we must resist the urge to ﬁll with
elegant invention. Both kinds of unwriting matter. Both make
demands on how we proceed.
The ﬁrst asks us to recognize intelligence in forms we have
been trained to dismiss. The second asks us to hold our certainty
lightly, to speak carefully, to admit when we are guessing.
And this is where the chapter ends: not with mastery, but
with acknowledgment. Sudan’s earliest aesthetic archive is vast,
varied, and unevenly known. It includes monumental stone and
intimate scars, gold and clay, script and song.
It was never waiting for validation. It was already complete
on its own terms. And when later forms arrived—Christian,
Islamic, colonial, modern—they did not replace this archive.
They entered into conversation with it, sometimes violently,
sometimes generatively, but always encountering a culture that
had already developed its own answers to the questions: What
endures? What protects? What makes a life coherent in a world
that refuses coherence?
The next chapter will attend to what happened when scripture
arrived with new rules about representation. But this chapter

The Lens of the Land: River­Cosmology
and Desert Intelligence
Sudan does not begin with a monument.
It begins with a
climate. Before the museum, before the manuscript, before
the argument, there is heat that makes arrogance ridiculous,
and water that makes survival feel like a prayer you must repeat
daily.
To approach Sudanese art without approaching Sudan’s el-
ements ﬁrst is to read a sentence while refusing its grammar.
The Nile is not a setting. The desert is not scenery. They are
teachers. They are the ﬁrst curators. They trained the eye long
before critics arrived with their soft lamps and clever language.
The Nile, in Sudan, is a kind of grammar because it organizes
meaning through rhythm, recurrence, and consequence. It
is not simply “a river.” It is an ordinance: it decides where
life gathers, how communities settle, what forms travel, what
materials endure, what crops grow, what bodies can remain.
Grammar does not merely enable speech; it disciplines it. In the
same way, the Nile disciplines Sudanese form. It teaches that
abundance and danger are not opposites. The same current that

THE LENS OF THE LAND: RIVER­COSMOLOGY AND DESERT...
nourishes can undo. The same generosity that grants continuity
can also impose fear. When your largest blessing is also your
most patient threat, you learn an intelligence that does not
romanticize nature. You learn reverence without illusion. And
reverence, when it is honest, becomes aesthetic restraint.
If the Nile is grammar, then rhythm is its ﬁrst lesson. Water
moves in cycles, and cycles train attention. Sudanese aesthetic
systems—especially those rooted in pattern, repetition, and
modular design—did not emerge only because “people liked
decoration.” They emerged because repetition is the only stable
law in a world where politics shifts, borders shift, regimes shift,
and even the soil can betray you. Pattern becomes a pact with
continuity. To repeat a shape is to say: something still holds.
Something still returns.
In a land where so much can be taken, the return itself
becomes sacred.
Modern audiences often treat repetition as “ornament,” as
if the repeated motif were a pleasant extra on the surface of
life. Sudan teaches a harsher truth: repetition is often how life
stays intact. A woven pattern repeats because hunger repeats,
because seasons repeats, because prayer repeats, because grief
repeats, because the body repeats its vulnerabilities.
The
aesthetic becomes a mirror of reality’s discipline. And out of
that mirroring comes a strange mercy: if the world insists on
repeating its hardships, the human being insists on repeating
beauty back at it, not as denial, but as deﬁance.
Then there is the desert, which is not a place so much as an
ethic. The desert does not negotiate. It does not ﬂatter. It does
not apologize. It offers you the brutal clarity of minimalism:
take what you need, leave what you cannot carry, respect
shade as if it were a currency, and understand that excess is

not glamorous, it is dangerous. In that sense, the desert is a
philosopher older than any school.
It teaches that form must earn its place, it teaches that a line
matters because it costs, it teaches that a structure matters
because it stands against heat.
It teaches that the body’s
relationship to space is moral, because space can either shelter
you or expose you.
This is where Sudanese minimalism is born. Not the curated
minimalism of galleries, but the existential minimalism of a
land that will punish waste. Sudan understood restraint before
modernism packaged it as taste.
The white cube may congratulate itself on simplicity, but the
desert is the original critic: it strips you down until you can
no longer hide behind ornament for ornament’s sake. And yet
Sudan does not become barren. It becomes precise. It learns the
difference between emptiness and clarity. The desert does not
teach absence. It teaches necessity.
And necessity, paradoxically, is one of the oldest sources of
beauty.
Consider what heat does to architecture.
It makes shade
more valuable than display. It makes thickness, courtyards,
ventilation, and orientation into aesthetic decisions. A wall is
not just a wall; it is a defense against sun. A dome is not only a
symbol; it is a way of managing air and space. The desert makes
geometry practical, it gives rise to an architectural intelligence
where elegance is measured by how well a structure protects
human breath. That kind of elegance is not decorative, it is
ethical, it refuses spectacle because spectacle does not cool the
body.
It refuses unnecessary complexity because complexity, under
heat, becomes punishment. This is why Sudanese space so

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE LAND: RIVER­COSMOLOGY AND DESERT...
often “teaches posture.” The environment forces the body into
humility. You stand differently when the sun is relentless. You
move differently when water is limited. You build differently
when survival is an ongoing negotiation.
The Nile and the desert together create a dual pedagogy: one
of ﬂow, one of constraint. One teaches continuity through
movement. The other teaches continuity through restraint.
Sudanese aesthetics learns from both. The result is an art culture
deeply ﬂuent in tension: between abundance and scarcity,
between fertility and severity, between curve and line, between
the lushness of river-life and the austerity of desert-life. This
tension is not a theme, it is the ground, and because it is the
ground, it appears everywhere: in patterning that feels both
organic and strict; in color palettes that hold sand tones and
sudden blues; in textiles that move like water but repeat like
law; in ornaments that are not indulgent but encoded.
When you begin to see nature as text, you stop treating
environment as mere “inﬂuence.” Inﬂuence is too soft a word.
Inﬂuence implies choice, preference, the optional. Sudan’s
environment is closer to sovereignty. It doesn’t “inﬂuence”
form, it governs it. The critic must therefore change posture.
You do not describe a river the way you describe a museum wall
label, you read it as a set of instructions. You read the desert
as a set of constraints that produce elegance. You read scarcity
as a training regimen for the eye: it teaches you to value the
small, the durable, the repeatable, the repairable. Repair, here,
becomes a concept worth holding tightly. In environments
where materials are scarce or hard-won, you do not discard
easily. You mend. You patch. You reweave. And those acts
of repair are themselves aesthetic acts, because they carry the
visible trace of time and use. Sudanese material culture has

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
long understood what contemporary art sometimes pretends
to discover: that the scar can be a form of truth. The patched
textile is not inferior to the pristine one. It is often more honest.
It tells you that life continued. It tells you that continuity was
chosen. This is an aesthetic of endurance, not perfection, and
endurance is a deeper form of beauty than shine.
This is also why water scarcity produces a distinct relationship
to the idea of “waste.” In many modern consumer cultures,
waste is hidden: the trash removed, the excess normalized,
the disposability disguised as convenience. Sudan’s landscapes
do not allow such denial. Scarcity makes waste visible. Waste
becomes shameful not because of moral posturing but because
of lived consequence. When you have had to carry water, you
do not treat objects lightly. When shade is earned, you do not
build carelessly. When food is contingent, you do not pretend
that abundance is eternal. These conditions don’t merely shape
ethics, they shape taste. They produce a visual culture that
understands necessity as form, and form as gratitude.
Now consider the Nile again, not only as ﬂow but as memory.
Rivers are archives without pages, they carry silt from elsewhere,
they carry seeds, they carry the residue of what happened up-
stream. In that sense, the Nile is a teacher of interconnectedness,
it instructs that no place is isolated. What happens in one region
reaches another. This is not simply hydrology; it is a model for
social reality.
Sudanese art—especially in its oral and craft traditions—
often functions like a river: carrying fragments of lineage,
migrating motifs, borrowed rhythms, inherited marks, and
making them coherent without insisting on purity. Purity is
a colonial obsession. Rivers are mixed. Sudanese art is often
mixed. It does not apologize for hybridity because hybridity
22

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE LAND: RIVER­COSMOLOGY AND DESERT...
is the land’s logic.
And so, when later scholars attempt to
categorize Sudan as “Arab” or “African,” they enact a violence
against the river’s truth. The river does not choose one identity.
It travels. It accumulates. It integrates. The desert, too, doesn’t
belong to one category. It stretches across borders like a refusal.
Sudan’s environment therefore undermines the neatness of
political identity projects. It teaches that the land itself is post-
categorical. This is why Sudan’s aesthetics often feel like “a
third thing”: because the land is a third thing, and the people
learned their visual intelligence from it.
But there is a danger here: the danger of romanticizing. To
speak of rivers and deserts poetically can become an escape
from history’s uglier textures. So let this be said with disci-
pline: the environment’s pedagogy has been intensiﬁed by
political violence.
Scarcity is not only natural; it has been
weaponized. Water and land are contested. Communities are
displaced. The desert expands not only through nature but
through mismanagement and war. The Nile’s blessing becomes
a site of geopolitical struggle. In such conditions, aesthetics
become even more ethically charged. Beauty is not a luxury; it
is a way of maintaining the human when systems attempt to
reduce people into numbers. A woven pattern becomes a refusal
to be erased. A pot becomes a refusal to starve quietly. A house’s
geometry becomes a refusal to surrender dignity.
This is why I keep returning to the word pedagogy. Sudan’s
environment does not merely “inspire.” It trains. It shapes. It
disciplines. It teaches the eye what matters. It teaches that
the smallest gesture—shade, water, repetition—can be the
difference between life and collapse.
From this training emerges a unique aesthetic posture: one
that does not worship excess, one that does not trust perma-
23

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
nence, one that values the durable and the repeatable, one that
treats repair as beauty, one that recognizes that the most sacred
forms are often the ones that keep you alive. And once you learn
to read nature as text, you begin to understand why Sudanese
art so often feels like it is speaking in a low voice. The land itself
speaks in a low voice. It is not performative, it does not shout, it
persists, and that persistence becomes the model for the work.
A river does not need applause.
A desert does not need
validation. Sudanese art, at its deepest, inherits that same
sovereignty: it does not beg to be understood. It asks only
to be approached with patience. In Sudan, environment isn’t
background, it is curriculum, and every serious aesthetic gesture
is a lesson learned from water, heat, and the discipline of what
cannot be wasted.
The Two Niles and the Geography of Difference
There is a geography lesson that matters here, one that is often
ﬂattened in casual discourse about “the Nile.” Sudan is not fed
by one river but by a conﬂuence. The Blue Nile descends from
the Ethiopian highlands, carrying volcanic silt and seasonal fury,
its ﬂoods are dramatic, its contribution to Egypt’s agricultural
fertility historically greater than its calmer sibling.
The White Nile rises from the lakes of East Africa, ﬂowing
through the vast wetland of the Sudd in South Sudan before
reaching Khartoum. These two rivers meet at the Mogran, the
conﬂuence that gives Khartoum its name and its reason for
being. Stand at that meeting point and you can see the difference
with your eyes: one river dark with sediment, one lighter, each
maintaining its character for kilometers before they fully merge.
This conﬂuence is not merely hydrological trivia.
It is a

records.text:

structural fact that shapes Sudanese reality. The Blue Nile brings
fertility but also unpredictability, its ﬂoods could be blessing or
catastrophe.
The White Nile brings steadiness, a more reliable ﬂow, but
less of the rich sediment that renews soil. Communities along
each river developed different relationships to water, different
agricultural calendars, different vulnerabilities. And because
vulnerability shapes culture, it also shapes form. The pottery of
the Blue Nile regions, the architecture of the White Nile zones,
the textiles produced in areas dependent on seasonal ﬂooding
versus those in more stable zones, all of these carry the trace of
their speciﬁc relationship to water.
What this means for aesthetics is that “Sudanese art” is
already plural before you even introduce ethnic or religious
difference. The land itself imposes variation. A weaver working
near the Ethiopian border is working in a different environmen-
tal grammar than a weaver near the Sudd. The clay available
in one region differs from the clay in another. The dyes that
can be extracted from local plants vary. The rhythms of labor—
when hands are free for craft, when they must turn to planting
or harvest—shift according to the river’s calendar.
To speak of “Sudanese aesthetics” as a singular entity is there-
fore already a simpliﬁcation. What we are really speaking of is a
family of practices shaped by related but distinct environmental
pedagogies.
And then there is the question of the cataract. The Nile in
Sudan is interrupted by six cataracts—stretches where the river
becomes unnavigable, where granite intrusions force the water
into rapids and narrow channels. These cataracts are not merely
obstacles to trade; they are also political boundaries, cultural
dividers, and linguistic frontiers.
25

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
Each cataract creates a zone of relative isolation. Communi-
ties between cataracts develop distinct dialects, distinct craft
traditions, distinct architectural styles. The river that connects
also separates.
This paradox—that the same feature which enables com-
munication also imposes fragmentation—is fundamental to
understanding Sudan’s internal diversity. The cataracts also
produce a speciﬁc kind of aesthetic knowledge: the knowledge
of portage, of carrying goods and boats around obstacles, of
maintaining networks despite interruption. This is not just
logistics; it is a model for cultural continuity under conditions
of rupture.
Sudanese aesthetics, especially in the northern riverine re-
gions, often display this sensibility: they know how to maintain
coherence across breaks, how to resume a pattern after inter-
ruption, how to signal continuity even when the material or
political conditions have changed. A textile tradition may be
disrupted by migration or war, but when it resumes, it picks up
the thread. The pattern remembers, even when individuals have
been displaced.
Heat as Sculptor: Architecture’s Debt to the Sun
If water is Sudan’s ﬁrst teacher, heat is its most demanding
examiner. To build in Sudan is to build against temperatures
that regularly exceed 40 degrees Celsius, that turn metal too hot
to touch, that make unshaded stone dangerous. Architecture,
in this context, is not primarily about beauty in the decorative
sense. It is about thermodynamics. It is about creating micro-
climates. It is about organizing space so that human bodies can
survive.
26

THE LENS OF THE LAND: RIVER­COSMOLOGY AND DESERT...
This is where the genius of traditional Sudanese architecture
becomes visible, not in ornament, but in intelligence. Consider
the Malqaf, the wind-catcher: a tower designed to capture
prevailing breezes and channel them down into interior spaces,
creating ventilation without mechanical assistance.
The Malqaf is geometry in service of breath.
Its form is
determined entirely by function, yet the result is often striking,
a sculptural element rising above the rooﬂine, announcing its
purpose through shape. This is architecture as atmospheric
engineering, as the management of invisible forces. The beauty
that emerges is not applied; it is consequent. The structure is
elegant because it is efficient.
Or consider the courtyard house, a form found across Sudan’s
urban centers: thick exterior walls that absorb and slow the
transmission of heat, a central open space that allows hot air
to rise and escape, rooms arranged around this void so that no
interior space directly faces the punishing afternoon sun. The
courtyard becomes a breathing lung for the entire structure.
It is also a social space, where families gather in the evening
when temperatures fall, where children play in relative safety,
where domestic work can occur in partial shade. The form is
simultaneously thermal, social, and aesthetic. To separate these
functions is to misunderstand the logic of the design.
What makes this architectural tradition particularly impor-
tant is that it represents a pre-industrial solution to prob-
lems that contemporary “green architecture” is only now re-
discovering. The language may be different—contemporary
architects speak of “passive cooling,” “thermal mass,” “cross-
ventilation”—but the principles are identical to those employed
by Sudanese builders for centuries. The difference is that tradi-
tional Sudanese architecture never pretended these techniques
27

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
were innovations. They were simply the conditions of survival,
and survival produced a vernacular of great sophistication.
But heat does not only shape architecture. It shapes the body’s
relationship to time. The hottest hours of the day—roughly
from noon to four—are hours when labor becomes dangerous,
when the prudent retreat into shade and stillness. This creates a
daily rhythm fundamentally different from the industrial time-
discipline of colder climates. Work happens in the early morning
and late afternoon. Midday is for rest, for waiting, for the kind
of stillness that looks like laziness to the European eye but is
actually thermal intelligence.
This rhythm, in turn, shapes the pace of social life, the timing
of markets, the hours when communal activities occur. And
pace, we should note, is an aesthetic category. The slowness
imposed by heat is not merely practical; it becomes a cultural
value, a way of moving through the world. Sudanese social
interactions often carry this rhythm: they do not rush, they
unfold with deliberation, they allow silence and pause without
anxiety. This is not universal—urban centers have their own
frantic energy—but the traditional model remains inﬂuential.
When you see this slowness in the pacing of oral storytelling, in
the extended time given to greetings and farewells, in the way
tea is prepared and consumed as a ritual rather than a caffeine
delivery system, you are seeing the aesthetic residue of heat’s
discipline.
28

Materials and Their Limits: The Aesthetics of What
Endures
Every environment offers a palette of materials, and that palette
constrains and enables in equal measure. Sudan’s material
palette has historically been deﬁned by what the land provides
and what can be obtained through trade.
Clay is abundant
near the Nile. Certain grasses and reeds grow in riverine zones.
Stone, particularly granite and sandstone, is available in speciﬁc
regions.
Wood is scarcer, the region’s trees are often acacia or other
hardwoods that grow slowly and are too valuable for casual use.
This scarcity makes wood a prestige material, reserved for doors,
roof beams, furniture for the wealthy. The absence of extensive
forests also means that monumental stone architecture, which
in other regions might use wooden scaffolding and supports,
must employ different construction techniques.
Clay, therefore, becomes the democratic material, available
to rich and poor alike, plastic enough to take almost any form,
durable when ﬁred. Pottery in Sudan is not a minor craft; it is
a foundational technology. Water storage, food preparation,
grain storage, all depend on ceramic vessels.
But beyond
utility, pottery becomes a site of aesthetic elaboration. Women
potters—and pottery has traditionally been women’s domain in
many Sudanese cultures—developing signature styles, regional
variations, family techniques passed down through generations.
The shapes are often determined by function: a water jar must
balance on the head, a cooking pot must withstand direct heat,
a storage vessel must seal against pests.
But within these functional constraints, inﬁnite variation
emerges. The surface treatment of pottery reveals this most

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
clearly. Some traditions favor burnishing, rubbing the leather-
hard clay with a smooth stone until it achieves a lustrous surface
that is both beautiful and less porous. Others incise geometric
patterns while the clay is still soft, creating textured surfaces
that catch light and shadow.
Still others apply slips—liquid clay of contrasting color—to
create zones of dark and light, often in patterns that echo body
scariﬁcation, textile weaving, or architectural decoration. These
are not random choices, they are aesthetic arguments about
what matters, about what deserves emphasis, about how an
object should announce itself in the world.
Then there is the question of color.
The desert’s palette
is limited: ochre, sienna, umber, white, black.
But within
those limitations, Sudanese aesthetics have learned to create
remarkable variety. Natural dyes from plants—indigo for blue,
henna for red-brown, various barks and roots for yellows
and darker browns—allow textiles to introduce color that the
landscape itself does not provide.
The blue of indigo-dyed cloth becomes particularly charged in
a landscape of sand and heat. It is the color of shade, of water, of
relief. To wear indigo is to carry coolness against the skin. This
is not metaphor. The color becomes associated with its thermal
properties, and aesthetic preference becomes entangled with
bodily comfort.
Metalwork presents a different set of constraints.
Iron,
copper, and gold have all been worked in Sudan historically, but
access to these materials required either local mining—which
was possible in certain regions—or trade networks. The result
is that metal objects carry prestige.
They are not everyday items.
A silver bracelet, an iron
blade, a copper vessel, these are objects that move through

THE LENS OF THE LAND: RIVER­COSMOLOGY AND DESERT...
economies as stores of wealth, as bride-price, as inheritance.
Their aesthetic elaboration often reﬂects this value: engraved
decoration, hammered patterns, careful attention to ﬁnish. But
the decoration is rarely excessive. Metal is too valuable to waste
on purely ornamental excess. The decoration that appears tends
to be integrated with structure, reinforcing joints, marking
ownership, or carrying protective inscriptions.
This brings us to a critical point about Sudanese aesthetics
and materials: the culture of maintenance. In environments
where materials are precious and replacement difficult, objects
are expected to last. They are also expected to be repairable. A
ceramic vessel cracks, and rather than discard it, you bind it
with leather strips or metal wire. A textile tears, and you patch
it with contrasting fabric, creating a visible history of repair.
These repairs are not hidden as ﬂaws. They become part of the
object’s biography, evidence of its utility and its owner’s care.
This aesthetic—what we might call the aesthetic of visible
mending—runs counter to consumer culture’s preference for
the pristine and the disposable. It insists that use-value and
beauty-value are not opposed. An object that has been main-
tained, that shows the trace of human care over time, gains a
dignity that the new object does not yet possess.
The Sudd and the Problem of Permanence
Move south, into the territory that now forms South Sudan, and
the environmental pedagogy shifts dramatically. Here the Nile
becomes the Sudd, one of the world’s largest wetlands, a vast
swampy expanse where the White Nile loses itself in papyrus,
reeds, and seasonal ﬂooding. The Sudd is neither solid land
nor open water. It is a third thing, a landscape in constant
31

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
negotiation between states. Islands appear and disappear. Chan-
nels shift. What was navigable one season becomes impassable
the next. To build in such an environment is to build with the
knowledge that permanence is impossible. Structures must
be temporary, portable, or built on stilts. Materials must be
local and renewable, grasses, reeds, mud that can be reapplied
annually.
This is not architecture in the monumental sense.
It is
architecture as seasonal practice, as ongoing maintenance
rather than one-time construction. The aesthetic that emerges
from this condition is utterly different from the stone-and-
permanence tradition of the northern riverine zones.
It is
an aesthetic of ﬂexibility, of lightness, of forms that can be
assembled and disassembled as needed.
The Dinka, Nuer, and other Nilotic groups developed archi-
tectural forms perfectly suited to this environment: circular
houses with conical thatched roofs, built on raised platforms
during ﬂood season, with walls of woven reeds that allow air
circulation while providing some privacy and protection from
insects. These structures are often described by outsiders as
“simple” or “primitive,” but this reveals only the observer’s
prejudice. The structures are sophisticated responses to speciﬁc
conditions. They are thermally intelligent, the thatch provides
insulation, the open weave allows breeze. They are materially
intelligent, built entirely from renewable local resources. They
are socially intelligent, the circular form creates no corners, no
hierarchy of space within the dwelling, reﬂecting egalitarian
social structures.
But what happens to visual culture when permanence is not
an option? The answer is that it migrates to other mediums. If
you cannot build monuments, you invest aesthetic energy in the
32
