THE LENS OF THE LAND: RIVER­COSMOLOGY AND DESERT...
body, in song, in cattle, in oral performance.
The Dinka and Nuer are famous for their cattle culture, and
within that culture, aesthetics reach an extraordinary level of
elaboration. Cattle are bred not only for milk or meat but for
color patterns, horn shape, and comportment. Young men com-
pose songs praising particular oxen, songs that display verbal
artistry comparable to any written poetry. The ox becomes a
living artwork, a mobile aesthetic object that testiﬁes to its
owner’s taste, wealth, and poetic skill.
This should trouble any deﬁnition of “art” that requires
permanence or museums. The Sudd teaches that beauty can
be utterly ephemeral, a cattle song performed once, a dance
that exists only in the moment of its performance, a body
decoration that will wash away with the next rain. These are
not lesser forms of aesthetic practice. They are forms adapted
to an environment that will not support the archive. They are
intelligence refusing to be erased simply because it cannot be
stored.
When Rivers Become Political: The Dam and the Drowned
Archive
No discussion of the Nile in Sudan can avoid the political. Water
is never neutral. The construction of the Aswan High Dam
in Egypt, completed in 1970, fundamentally altered the Nile’s
behavior in Sudan.
The dam created Lake Nasser, which extended far into Su-
danese territory, ﬂooding archaeological sites, displacing Nu-
bian communities, and ending the annual ﬂood cycle that had
structured life along the river for millennia. Entire villages
vanished underwater. Temples were relocated or lost.
33

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
An aesthetic heritage—the Nubian architectural tradition,
with its distinctive painted houses and decorated courtyards—
was partially drowned, partially displaced, partially abandoned.
This was not natural disaster. This was political choice. Egypt’s
need for hydroelectric power and ﬂood control took precedence
over Sudan’s cultural continuity.
The ﬂooded zone included some of the richest archaeological
territory in Sudan, sites like Buhen, Semna, and portions of the
area around the Second Cataract. International teams conducted
salvage archaeology, and some monuments were moved (the
temples of Abu Simbel being the most famous example), but
much was lost. Not only ancient sites, but living communities.
Not only monuments, but the everyday material culture of
villages: the houses, the granaries, the courtyards where women
painted geometric patterns on walls as both decoration and
spiritual protection.
The displaced Nubians were relocated to new settlements
in less fertile areas. The new houses were often standardized
concrete structures, designed for efficiency rather than cultural
continuity. The traditional painted decoration—bold geometric
patterns in red, white, yellow, and black—appeared in some new
houses, but the social context that had sustained the practice
was fractured. When you displace a community, you do not
only move bodies. You disrupt the transmission of knowledge,
the apprenticeship relationships, the social occasions that gave
practices their meaning. Some traditions adapt. Some attenuate.
Some die quietly.
This history matters for understanding contemporary Su-
danese aesthetics because it introduces a quality that the earlier
environmental discussion might seem to lack: rage. The river’s
pedagogy, when weaponized by politics, produces not only
34

adaptation but also resistance.
Nubian artists and cultural activists have worked for decades
to document, preserve, and revive displaced traditions. The
painted house becomes, in diaspora and displacement, not just
decoration but deﬁance. It says: we are still here. Our aesthetics
did not drown. This transforms the meaning of the work. What
was once simply beautiful becomes also testimonial. The pattern
now carries an argument, and this is where environmental
determinism must be refused even as environmental pedagogy
is acknowledged. Yes, the desert teaches restraint. Yes, the
river teaches rhythm. But people are not passive recipients of
environmental instruction. They argue back. They adapt. They
make the environment a site of meaning-making even when—
especially when—that environment has been turned against
them. Sudanese aesthetics are shaped by climate, yes, but they
are also shaped by the refusal to let climate become destiny.
A people who have survived droughts, ﬂoods, displacement,
and damming do not simply “reﬂect” their environment. They
contend with it. And that contention is visible in the work.
Color, Light, and the Discipline of the Eye
There is a ﬁnal environmental lesson worth holding: the lesson
of light. Sudan’s light is not gentle. It is harsh, high-contrast,
unforgiving. Shadows are sharp-edged. Midday sun bleaches
color until everything becomes a version of white and gold. Dust
in the air during Haboob season turns the sky ochre and obscures
visibility to a few meters. This is light as force, light as weather.
Such light trains the eye differently than the soft, diffuse light
of northern Europe that so much art history takes as its norm.
In harsh light, subtlety becomes invisible. Soft pastels wash

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
out. Gentle gradations disappear. The eye learns to value strong
contrast, bold pattern, clarity of form.
This is why Sudanese aesthetics so often favor geometric
precision over organic ambiguity, why pattern is often high-
contrast rather than tonal, why color, when it appears, tends
toward saturation rather than subtlety. But harsh light also
creates moments of extraordinary beauty, the brief window at
dawn and dusk when the sun is low and the light turns amber,
when the landscape glows, when even the desert becomes brieﬂy
tender. These liminal hours are not merely picturesque; they
are survivable.
They are when the body can move without
punishment. They are when labor resumes. And they are when
the eye, freed from the assault of midday glare, can register
beauty without squinting. This daily rhythm—from harsh to
gentle and back—creates an aesthetic awareness that values
transformation, that understands beauty as contingent on the
angle of light, on the time of day, on the moisture in the air.
Dust, too, becomes an aesthetic medium. During the Ha-
boob—the massive dust storms that roll across Sudan from
the desert—the air itself becomes material. Visibility drops.
The world becomes monochrome. Architecture disappears into
atmosphere. These are not pleasant experiences, but they are
formative ones. They teach that the world is not stable, that
clarity is temporary, that vision itself is a privilege that can be
revoked. When the storm passes and the air clears, the return
of visibility feels like a gift. The eye becomes grateful. And
gratitude, we should remember, is an aesthetic condition as
much as an ethical one.
This leads to a ﬁnal thought about environmental pedagogy:
it produces not only forms but also postures. It trains not only
the hand but also the stance of attention. To live in Sudan is to

THE LENS OF THE LAND: RIVER­COSMOLOGY AND DESERT...
learn patience, to wait for water, to wait for the heat to pass, to
wait for the dust to settle.
That patience becomes embedded in how beauty is ap-
proached. Sudanese aesthetics, at their most disciplined, do not
demand immediate legibility. They reward sustained attention.
They ask you to wait, to return, to sit with the work long enough
for its logic to emerge. This is the river’s lesson: that meaning
unfolds in time.
This is the desert’s lesson: that clarity requires stillness. And
this is the light’s lesson: that what you see depends on when
you look.
So the chapter ends not with conclusions but with recogni-
tions. Sudan’s environment is not background. It is pedagogue,
and every form that emerges from this land carries the trace of
its teaching.
Water and heat, scarcity and light, ﬂood and drought, these
are not obstacles to beauty. They are its conditions. And those
conditions have produced an aesthetic intelligence that does not
need the West’s approval to know its own value.

The Lens of the Body: Scar, Pattern, and
Totem
Some cultures decorate. Others defend themselves with beauty.
Sudan, for long stretches of its aesthetic life, belonged to the
second kind, because when the world is unstable, the surface
is not a vanity. It is a shield. The modern eye, trained to treat
pattern as “design” and marks as “style,” approaches Sudanese
form with the wrong innocence.
It assumes the visible is
optional. But in many Sudanese contexts, the visible was a kind
of contract with the unseen: a way of negotiating vulnerability,
staking belonging, warding envy, gathering protection, holding
memory where paper could not, and where institutions never
promised to preserve you.
A mark, in this tradition, is not an illustration of an idea. It is
an act. It does something. It binds, it warns, it consecrates,
it claims, it remembers. That is why I want this chapter to
sit, with discipline, inside the phrase “marks that keep the
world intact.” Not marks that “represent” the world, not marks
that “express identity,” not marks that function as aesthetic
entertainment.
Marks that keep the world intact, because

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE BODY: SCAR, PATTERN, AND TOTEM
in a climate of scarcity, illness, social fracture, and the slow
violence of history, intactness is not guaranteed. It is made. It is
maintained. It is defended. And one of the oldest tools for that
defense was form.
This is the point where the outsider—especially the museum-
trained outsider—becomes dangerous.
They arrive with a
hunger to translate every pattern into a symbol, every animal
into an allegory, every scar into “culture.” But the drive to
interpret is often a way of avoiding intimacy. It keeps you clever
and distant. It turns human technologies of survival into puzzles
you can solve and ﬁle away.
A Post-Interpretive posture requires another approach: you
don’t conquer these marks with meanings. You stay near them
long enough to feel their seriousness. You admit what you
cannot know. You refuse to reduce what was functional into
what is merely “interesting.”
Begin with scar, not as spectacle, but as inscription. Modern
discourse loves extremes: either it condemns bodily marking as
barbarity or it romanticizes it as authenticity. Both stances are
forms of theft. They treat people’s lived practices as material
for our moral performance. The custodial stance is quieter: it
acknowledges that in many contexts, the body itself became an
archive because other archives were unavailable, untrusted, or
irrelevant. The body was the one surface that traveled with you
when you migrated. The body was the one object that could not
be conﬁscated without violence. The body was where lineage
could be carried in plain sight. To mark the body, then, was
to refuse anonymity. It was to insist: I am recognized. I am
placed within a world. I am not merely a disposable life drifting
through heat.
Scariﬁcation, tattooing, and other bodily inscriptions are

often discussed as “identity.” But identity is too modern a
word, too individual, too psychological, too abstract. What
these marks often encoded was relation: to clan, to ancestry,
to marital status, to social role, to rite of passage, to protective
cosmology.
In societies where the individual is not imagined as a free-
ﬂoating self but as a node in a web of obligations, the body
becomes a public document. Not in the bureaucratic sense—
something cold and administrative—but in the communal sense:
something that says you have been held, initiated, recognized.
This does not make every mark admirable or ethically simple.
It makes them intelligible as evidence of how communities
manage continuity.
The speciﬁcity matters here. Among the Dinka and Nuer,
parallel lines across the forehead—what was called sholoukh
in northern Sudan or gaar among the Nuer—served as clan
markers, visible from a distance. A child would undergo this at
the threshold of adulthood, the cuts made with a blade or thorn,
the healing process managed with ash or other substances to
raise the keloid scars. The pain was part of the pedagogy: you
learned endurance by enduring. You learned membership by
bearing its mark. The body remembered what language could
not always carry across generations fractured by conﬂict and
displacement. But these were not abstract symbols ﬂoating
in a void of pure meaning. They had practical consequences.
In contexts where written documentation was scarce or inac-
cessible, where colonial administrators imposed borders that
cut through kinship networks, where slave raids and violence
made verbal testimony fragile, the body’s inscription became
a form of credential. To be marked was to be accountable, to a
lineage, to a community, to a set of expectations. It was also,

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE BODY: SCAR, PATTERN, AND TOTEM
in some cases, to be protected: certain marks were believed to
have apotropaic power, warding off illness or the evil eye. Scars
above the temples might relieve headaches.
Marks near vital organs might shield against spiritual harm.
Whether these beliefs “worked” in a biomedical sense is less
important than understanding that they worked as systems of
care, as attempts to manage vulnerability in a world that offered
few guarantees.
We must also acknowledge what is no longer present. The
practice of facial scariﬁcation has declined dramatically across
Sudan in recent decades, driven by urbanization, education,
shifting aesthetic norms, and a younger generation’s rejection
of what many now perceive as outdated or disﬁguring. Elders
who bear these marks often speak of them with ambivalence:
pride in their cultural heritage mixed with relief that their
children will not have to carry the same visible difference in
a world increasingly hostile to such markers.
This decline is not merely a story of “modernization” erasing
“tradition.” It is a story of people making calculated decisions
about visibility, about the costs and beneﬁts of being legible in
particular ways. To be marked, in an earlier era, was to be placed.
To be marked, in a globalized present, might be to be excluded.
But scar, in Sudan’s broader aesthetic climate, is not only on
the body. It appears as a principle. The land itself is scarred by
borders, by displacement, by conﬂict, by drought.
Sudanese art learns early that fracture is not an exception. It
is a condition. So scars appear everywhere: in patched textiles,
in repaired pottery, in architecture adapted and readapted, in
patterns that repeat because repetition is the only reliable law.
When you understand this, you stop treating repair as lesser.
Repair becomes a signature of endurance. The patched cloth is

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
a kind of testimony: it declares that something worth keeping
was kept. It says, with quiet deﬁance, that loss did not get the
ﬁnal word.
This is where the aesthetic intelligence of mending reveals
itself. In a consumer culture that valorizes the new and the
unblemished, repair is often invisible labor, relegated to the
domestic and the feminine, dismissed as “making do.” But in
contexts where materials are scarce and objects are expected
to last across generations, repair is a creative act. It requires
attention to structure, to pattern, to the relationship between
part and whole. A woven basket with a replaced section must
maintain its integrity. A textile with a patched tear must still
drape and fold. The angareeb bed frame, with its woven rope
surface, will be re-strung when it sags, the old rope removed
and new rope woven in the same pattern. The object’s biography
accumulates these interventions, and the object becomes richer
for them, not despite the fact that it has been repaired, but
because repair is evidence of value. Only what is loved gets
mended.
Now pattern. Pattern is Sudan’s great discipline, its long
grammar of attention. In Western modernity, pattern often
becomes “decorative”—a surface pleasure, a design choice, an
ornament to be consumed. But in many Sudanese contexts,
pattern is closer to ritual than decoration. It regulates space. It
regulates time. It regulates the body’s relationship to the home,
to the community, to prayer, to work.
It is the aesthetic equivalent of repetition in worship: a
way of stabilizing the mind and the world through ordered
recurrence.
This is why Sudanese patterning—whether in
textile, architecture, henna, beadwork, or talismanic scripts, so
often carries a seriousness that the museum’s lighting cannot
42

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE BODY: SCAR, PATTERN, AND TOTEM
capture. Under the spotlight, it looks like “style.” In life, it is
closer to infrastructure.
Consider the Thoub, the long rectangular cloth that Sudanese
women drape around their bodies. At ﬁrst glance, it might seem
like a simple garment: a length of fabric, variously colored and
patterned, worn in ways that signify modesty, elegance, and
cultural belonging. But the Thoub is a technology.
It is roughly ﬁfteen to twenty feet of material that must be
wrapped, folded, and secured without pins or fasteners, in a
way that allows movement while maintaining coverage. The
skill required to wear a Thoub well is considerable: you must
understand how fabric moves, how different weights of material
behave, how to compensate for wind or for the physical demands
of work. Young girls watch their mothers and grandmothers
and learn through observation and practice. The Thoub becomes
an extension of the body’s intelligence.
And the patterns on that Thoub are not incidental. In tra-
ditional embroidery, geometric shapes—diamonds, triangles,
hexagons—are arranged in interlocking formations. These are
not random designs. They are motifs that have traveled through
generations, carried forward through memory and repetition.
They surface in textiles, in architecture, in henna, in beadwork.
Across different materials and forms establishing a continuity
of vision, a shared vocabulary through which a world learns to
recognize itself.
When you see a familiar motif repeated, you are not just seeing
something pretty. You are seeing memory made tangible.
Pattern also acts as a social memory device. It carries lineage
without needing genealogy charts. Certain motifs travel through
families, regions, and crafts like inherited names. A woven
rhythm can hold centuries without ever being written down.
43

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
This is a kind of intelligence that modern literacy sometimes
fails to respect: the ability to store history in the hands. When
you see a pattern repeated across generations, you are not
merely seeing taste. You are seeing continuity enacted. You
are seeing memory made material. And this is why craft—
often dismissed by art history—matters so profoundly in the
Sudanese archive: because craft is where pattern becomes a
living archive rather than a dead object.
This becomes clearer when we look at henna.
Henna
application—the dyeing of hands and feet with paste made
from crushed henna leaves—is widespread across North Africa
and the Middle East, but Sudanese henna has its own character.
The designs are bold, dark, often covering large areas of skin
rather than delicate tracery.
They favor geometric abstraction and ﬂowing curves, some-
times incorporating ﬂoral elements but never in a naturalistic
way. These are not “pictures” of ﬂowers. They are distillations,
essences, forms that gesture toward the organic world while
remaining ﬁrmly rooted in the language of pattern.
And henna, like scariﬁcation, is a threshold practice.
It
marks transitions: marriage, festivals, celebrations. A bride’s
hands and feet will be hennaed the night before her wedding,
in a ceremony attended by women, accompanied by song and
storytelling. The henna itself is believed to have protective and
beautifying properties. But more than that, it is a social practice
that gathers women together, that transmits knowledge from
older to younger, that turns the body into a site of collective
attention. The designs require skill and patience. The paste must
be applied carefully and allowed to dry. The longer it remains on
the skin, the darker the stain. The hennaed woman must wait,
still and attentive, while the mark sets. This waiting is part of

records.text:
THE LENS OF THE BODY: SCAR, PATTERN, AND TOTEM
the ritual. It slows time. It makes beauty something that cannot
be rushed.
What matters here is not just the aesthetic outcome but
the process. The application of henna is an act of care: one
woman tending to another’s body, making it beautiful for a
signiﬁcant occasion. And because henna fades—because the
mark is temporary, lasting only a few weeks—there is no illusion
of permanence. The mark acknowledges its own transience. It
says: beauty is ﬂeeting, and that is why we must make it again
and again. The temporariness is not a limitation. It is a feature.
It insists that care must be ongoing, that the world does not
maintain itself without repeated effort.
Now to the threshold itself; the space where the human and the
non-human meet, where the domestic and the cosmic intersect.
In many Sudanese contexts, thresholds are sites of power and
vulnerability. The entrance to a home —the doorway between
rooms, the boundary between inside and outside—these are
places where protection is needed. And so they are marked. Not
always visibly, but marked nonetheless.
This is where we encounter the talismanic: amulets, prayers
written on paper and folded into leather pouches, Quranic verses
inscribed and worn on the body, objects placed at doorways,
gestures performed at certain times. The Western secular gaze
often struggles here. It wants to categorize these practices as
“superstition” and move on. But this dismissal reveals more
about the limits of secular thought than about the practices
themselves. What the talismanic acknowledges is that human
life is not sovereign. It is subject to forces—illness, envy, mis-
fortune, spiritual disturbance—that cannot be fully controlled.
The talismanic is an attempt to negotiate with those forces,
to manage fear without surrendering to despair.
45

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
Consider the Hijab, not the headscarf, but the small leather
pouch containing written prayers or Quranic verses, worn on
the body or hung in the home.
These objects are common
throughout the Islamic world, including Sudan. They are made
by religious specialists who have knowledge of which verses
offer protection against which dangers.
The writing itself is sacred: the ink, the paper, the script.
The object is then enclosed, kept close, treated with reverence.
Whether you believe it “works” in a metaphysical sense is
less important than understanding what it does socially and
psychologically.
It externalizes care. It makes protection visible and tangible.
It gives people something to hold onto when the world feels
precarious. And the world, in Sudan, has often been precarious.
Drought, famine, disease, conﬂict, displacement—these are not
abstractions. They are lived realities that have shaped Sudanese
life for generations.
In such conditions, the desire for protection is not irrational.
It is deeply human. The talismanic acknowledges that there
are limits to what individuals can control, and it provides a
technology for managing that helplessness. It is a way of saying:
I am doing what I can. I am not passive. I am taking action, even
if that action is symbolic.
This brings us to the unseen, and to animals. Then totem.
The word itself is hazardous, because it carries the colonial tone
of anthropology: the outsider naming the sacred in order to
classify it.
But we can still speak carefully of animal symbolism, not
as quaint folklore, but as cosmological relation.
In many
Sudanese and Nilotic contexts, animals are not “symbols” in
the Western sense, stand-ins for abstract ideas.
They are

THE LENS OF THE BODY: SCAR, PATTERN, AND TOTEM
neighbors in a shared ecology. They are sources of food, labor,
danger, protection, and spiritual resonance. Cattle, birds, river
creatures, desert animals, these are not decorative motifs. They
are lived presences.
When animals appear in visual form, they often carry the
weight of intimacy: the sense that human life is not autonomous,
not separate, not sovereign. It depends. It is entangled. The
animal becomes a reminder that the world does not revolve
around human language.
Among pastoral groups like the Dinka and Nuer, cattle are
central, not just economically but cosmologically. A man’s
relationship to his cattle is profound: he knows each animal
individually, names them, sings to them, grieves when they
die.
Cattle provide milk, meat, leather, dung for fuel and
building. But they are also markers of wealth, vehicles for social
transactions like marriage, and objects of spiritual signiﬁcance.
Cattle imagery appears in songs, in body decoration, in the way
young men style their hair to resemble cattle horns. This is
not metaphor. It is an acknowledgment that human identity is
shaped by relationships with non-human beings.
Birds, too, carry signiﬁcance. The hoopoe, the crane, the dove,
these appear in folktales, in proverbs, in decorative motifs. Birds
are messengers, travelers between earth and sky, ﬁgures of
freedom and fragility.
In a landscape as vast and open as Sudan’s, where the sky is a
constant presence, birds become natural symbols of the soul’s
movement, of aspiration, of the precariousness of ﬂight. But
again, this is not purely symbolic. Birds are real. They migrate,
they feed, they nest, they die. Their presence in human thought
reﬂects an attentiveness to the actual world, not an escape into
abstraction.
47

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
And this is where the unseen enters again, not as superstition,
but as a dimension of lived reality. The Sudanese archive is full
of protective intelligence: amulets, talismanic papers, marks
placed on thresholds, objects carried on the body, gestures
repeated at certain times, ritual practices meant to manage
illness, envy, misfortune, and spiritual disturbance.
The modern secular mind often mocks these practices because
it thinks knowledge is only what can be proven in laboratories.
But even if one insists on secular explanation, these practices
still reveal something crucial: they are systems of care. They are
ways of managing fear without surrendering to despair. They
are attempts to negotiate the limits of control in a world that
frequently reminds you how little you command.To dismiss that
is to dismiss the human. It is also to misunderstand art. Because
art, at its deepest, has always been bound to the question of
helplessness.
Some cultures answered with theology. Some with philosophy.
Some with empire.
Sudan, often, answered with marks, marks that made protec-
tion visible, made continuity tangible, made belonging legible,
made the unseen negotiable.
At this stage, the careful reader may feel uneasy. They may
fear we are drifting into mysticism. Let them.
The unease is instructive. It reveals how modernity trains us
to trust only what is loud, official, and legible. But Sudanese aes-
thetic intelligence often lived precisely in what was unofficial,
quiet, and relational. It lived in the home, in the threshold, in
the body, in the hand. It lived in women’s practices as much as
in men’s monuments. It lived in what was transmitted through
doing rather than through claiming.
This is why we must resist the impulse to elevate only certain

THE LENS OF THE BODY: SCAR, PATTERN, AND TOTEM
forms of Sudanese art—the monumental, the authored, the
collectible—while ignoring the rest. The museum loves what
it can frame. It struggles with what is ephemeral, embodied,
collective, and domestic.
But the majority of Sudanese aesthetic production has always
happened in those dismissed spaces. Women sitting together,
applying henna. An elder teaching a young person how to weave
a basket. A potter repairing a cracked vessel. A woman embroi-
dering a Thoub. These are not minor activities. They are the
foundation of aesthetic life. And they have been systematically
undervalued because they are associated with women, with craft,
with function, with the everyday.
What would it mean to take them seriously? It would mean
acknowledging that a perfectly applied henna pattern is as
signiﬁcant as a painting. It would mean understanding that
the skill required to weave an intricate textile pattern is as
demanding as sculpture. It would mean recognizing that the
knowledge embedded in these practices—passed down through
generations, adapted to changing circumstances, maintained
despite immense pressures—constitutes an archive as impor-
tant as any written text.
And now we must make a crucial distinction: marks can
protect, but marks can also be forced. Not every inscription
is chosen. Some scar is violence. Some pattern is imposed.
Some bodily modiﬁcation happens under coercion or social
pressure. A custodial book cannot romanticize. It must remain
morally awake. So the ethic here is not to celebrate every mark
as beautiful, but to understand why marking became central
in the ﬁrst place: because unmarked life, in many conditions,
is vulnerable to erasure. The desire to be inscribed is often the
desire not to disappear.

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
This ethical complexity is especially important when we
consider children. Many scariﬁcation practices were performed
on young people who had no real choice in the matter. Parents
made decisions on behalf of their children, based on cultural
norms and social pressures.
Some adults who underwent
scariﬁcation as children speak of it with regret. Others with
pride. Some with both.
The truth is that cultural practices are never simply liberatory
or simply oppressive. They are both, simultaneously, and the
work of a custodial stance is to hold that complexity without
collapsing it into easy judgments.
What we can say is this: the decline of facial scariﬁcation in
Sudan is, for many, a relief. It represents a loosening of social
pressures, an expansion of choice, a world in which people can
decide for themselves how they want their bodies to appear. But
the decline also represents a loss, not necessarily of the practice
itself, but of the social worlds that practice sustained.
When scariﬁcation disappears, so do the rituals around it,
the songs, the knowledge of healing, the intergenerational
transmission. Something is gained, something is lost. This
is the nature of change.
That desire becomes even more poignant when we remember
Sudan’s long history of being misnamed by others—Arabized
here, Africanized there, “peripheral” everywhere. In such a
world, the local mark becomes an act of sovereignty. It says:
we name ourselves. We keep our own codes. We carry our own
archive on skin, cloth, and clay. We do not require external
recognition to be real. The mark becomes a refusal of epistemic
colonization.
It becomes a way of preserving a world that
outsiders would rather simplify.
This is what outsiders often miss: the way aesthetic choices

THE LENS OF THE BODY: SCAR, PATTERN, AND TOTEM
in Sudan have been shaped by the experience of being misread,
misrepresented, and marginalized. Colonial ethnographers ar-
rived with their cameras and their categories, eager to document
“primitive” practices before they vanished. They photographed
scariﬁed bodies as evidence of “tribal” culture, stripping those
bodies of context, of dignity, of complexity. Those photographs
then circulated in museums and textbooks, becoming the basis
for how the world understood Sudan. The people in the pho-
tographs became specimens. Their marks became data.
Against this history, the act of maintaining one’s own aes-
thetic practices—on one’s own terms, in one’s own contexts—
becomes an act of resistance. It says: you do not get to deﬁne us.
You do not get to turn our lives into your archive. We will keep
our marks, our patterns, our totems, and we will decide what
they mean. We will transmit them to our children or we will let
them fade, but either way, it will be our decision.
This is why the question of who gets to interpret Sudanese
aesthetics is not a trivial one.
When Western scholars and
curators approach Sudanese objects, they bring assumptions.
They assume that visual forms can be read like texts, that
meaning is stable, that the observer’s interpretation is as valid
as the maker’s intention.
But what if the mark is not meant for you? What if its meaning
is deliberately opaque to outsiders? What if part of its function
is precisely to create boundaries, to signal belonging to those
who know and exclusion to those who don’t?
The custodial posture acknowledges these limits. It says: I can
describe what I see, but I cannot claim to know what it means
from the inside. I can offer context, but I cannot provide cer-
tainty. I can hold the object with respect, but I cannot possess its
signiﬁcance. This humility is not weakness. It is epistemological

maturity. It is the recognition that not everything is legible to
everyone, and that illegibility is sometimes protective.
So let this chapter end with an ethical instruction for the rest
of the book: when you encounter a Sudanese pattern, do not
rush to treat it as mere design. When you encounter a scar, do
not turn it into spectacle. When you encounter an animal motif,
do not reduce it to metaphor.
Ask instead what it protected, what it preserved, what it
transmitted, what it kept intact. Because in Sudan’s aesthetic
history, beauty has often been a form of care, care made visible,
care made durable, care made repeatable.
Let the record show: Sudan’s marks were never merely aes-
thetic choices. They were survival architectures—inscriptions
against disappearance, patterns against chaos, and quiet totems
reminding the human that the world is larger than its explana-
tions. They were ways of saying: we are here. We persist. We
remember. And we will continue to make marks, even when the
world tries to erase us, because marking is how we prove that
we were not merely passing through.
We were present. We mattered. We made something that
lasted.

The Lens of Aftermath: Art After the
Border Was Drawn
Sudanese art, once empire arrives, is forced to learn a new
grammar: the grammar of fracture. Not the honest fracture
of nature—drought, ﬂood, migration, seasons—but the bureau-
cratic fracture of power: lines drawn by hands that will never
carry water, names assigned by mouths that will never speak the
local tongue with tenderness, and categories enforced by offices
that treat living people like administrative problems. The border
is not merely a line on a map. It is an instruction written onto
the imagination: this is where you end, this is where you begin,
this is what you are allowed to be. Every Sudanese brushstroke
after this moment carries an invisible pressure, the pressure
of being seen through someone else’s lens, of being measured
by someone else’s criteria, of being asked to “develop” into an
ideal that was never born from your own soil.
Rupture is what happens when a culture is forced to translate
itself while under surveillance. The colonial project did not only
seize land and resources; it reorganized time. It rearranged
the past into “primitive,” the present into “backward,” and the

future into “civilized”—a future that always looked suspiciously
like the colonizer’s mirror.
This is how imagination is colonized: not by banning every
form outright, but by humiliating what already exists, by teach-
ing a people to doubt the dignity of their own forms, by turning
inherited aesthetics into superstition and imported aesthetics
into aspiration. You can steal a country’s imagination without
ever burning a painting if you successfully convince the people
that their own visual language is unworthy of seriousness.
The Anglo-Egyptian period and the broader colonial and post-
colonial administrative reality around it introduced a particular
kind of aesthetic violence: the violence of institutional taste. It
wasn’t only censorship in the dramatic sense, though censor-
ship matters, and punishment matters, and fear matters. It was
the quieter disciplining of what counted as “art,” what counted
as “education,” what counted as “culture.” An institution does
not need to shout to control you; it can simply decide what
gets funded, what gets displayed, what gets taught, what gets
archived.
It can decide which forms are “craft,” which are “ﬁne art,”
which are “heritage,” which are “primitive,” which are “mod-
ern.” These labels appear neutral. They are not. They are
weapons with clean hands.
The condominium agreement of 1899 established a curious
ﬁction: that sovereignty was shared between Britain and Egypt.
In practice, this meant British control masked by Egyptian
participation. But the ﬁction mattered aesthetically because
it created a double alienation. Sudanese were governed by the
British but through Egyptian intermediaries.
They were subjects of an empire that pretended not to be one.
This duplicity entered the aesthetic realm as a kind of enforced

THE LENS OF AFTERMATH: ART AFTER THE BORDER WAS DRAWN
multilingualism: to be legible to power, you had to speak in
registers that were foreign twice over, once to the British, once
to the Egyptians. Your own visual language, your own aesthetic
priorities were rendered irrelevant to the mechanisms that
distributed resources, recognition, and institutional validation.
And so Sudanese art after the border is drawn becomes a
work of double survival. First, it must survive the material
consequences of empire, extraction, displacement, economic
reorderings, the rearrangement of labor and education. Second,
it must survive the psyche consequences: the internalized
whisper that says, your forms are not enough; your symbols are
not sophisticated; your beauty is not legitimate until someone
else applauds it.
That whisper is perhaps the most enduring colonization,
because it outlives the colonizer. It becomes a voice inside
the artist’s own mind.
It is why so many postcolonial art
histories are not simply histories of invention, but histories of
negotiation: negotiation with inherited forms, negotiation with
imported modernities, negotiation with the gaze that demands
“African authenticity” one day and “global contemporaneity”
the next.
Consider what it meant for a young Sudanese person in the
early twentieth century to learn “art” in a colonial school.
Art education, as introduced by the British, was not neutral
pedagogy. It was cultural evangelism. It taught that painting
meant easel painting, that sculpture meant ﬁgurative represen-
tation in bronze or stone, that beauty meant European academic
standards, that progress meant abandoning local aesthetic
traditions in favor of imported techniques. The School of Design,
opened in 1947 at Gordon Memorial College, was the site where
this pedagogy took institutional form. It was also, paradoxically,

the site where resistance would eventually crystallize, because
once you teach people the colonizer’s language, they can use it
against you.
But before that resistance, there was adaptation. There was
the slow, often painful process of Sudanese artists learning to
navigate between worlds. Some embraced Western techniques
wholeheartedly, hoping to prove that Sudanese could achieve
excellence in any medium.
Others maintained ﬁerce loyalty to local forms, refusing the
colonizer’s categories altogether. Most inhabited the uncom-
fortable middle: learning European methods while trying to
preserve something of their own aesthetic inheritance, code-
switching between visual languages depending on context and
audience.
Rupture, then, is not only political. It is aesthetic. It splits
the archive into categories that do not belong together, and it
forces the artist to choose between them as though choice were
freedom. But the truth is harsher: the artist often chooses under
pressure, under scarcity, under the threat of misrecognition.
Some artists respond by embracing imported forms, hoping to
enter global intelligibility. Some respond by intensifying local
forms, turning tradition into a fortiﬁed identity. Many respond
by doing something subtler: encoding.
They build works that can speak in two registers at once,
legible enough to survive institutional scrutiny, local enough
to remain faithful to the soil. This is where Sudanese pattern
becomes a political instrument without losing its ancient dig-
nity, where abstraction becomes a safehouse, where metaphor
becomes the language of the living.
The policy of divide and conquer left aesthetic traces. When
the British formally separated north and south in 1924, they

were not simply creating administrative districts. They were
fracturing a cultural continuum. They were deciding which
forms would be classiﬁed as “Islamic,” which as “African,”
which as “Arab,” which as “tribal.”
These categories hardened into institutional reality through
museums, through ethnographic surveys, through educational
curricula. A Dinka mask and a Khartoum textile, both produced
within the territory called Sudan, would be ﬁled into different
conceptual universes—one “tribal art,” the other “Islamic
craft”—as though they did not share a sky.
This fracture entered the consciousness of Sudanese artists
as a question: what does it mean to be Sudanese? The question
was not abstract. It was existential.
If your country is deﬁned by a border imposed from outside, if
your identity categories are assigned by administrators who
know nothing of your lineage, if your aesthetic traditions
are classiﬁed according to someone else’s taxonomy, then
making art becomes an act of self-deﬁnition against imposed
deﬁnitions. It becomes a refusal of the categories that would
simplify you into manageability. Colonial censorship rarely
operates like a villain in a novel. It operates like an administrator.
It asks for permits. It controls printing. It shapes curricula. It
punishes certain gatherings, it regulates public speech, it trains
communities to self-censor so thoroughly that direct testimony
becomes reckless. Under these conditions, art does not vanish.
It mutates, it learns to be indirect without becoming vague. It
learns to carry pain without naming it. It learns to build a world
inside itself because the public world is unsafe. This is why, in
Sudan, silence is not a lack of content. Silence is a strategy, an
intelligence, a protection mechanism reﬁned over generations.
When a people learns that speech can get you killed, beauty

becomes a quieter way of telling the truth.
But we must be careful not to romanticize this either. Encod-
ing is not merely cleverness; it is evidence of constraint. It is
what happens when directness is punished. A coded artwork
is often a work made under duress, even if it is beautiful. So
the lens of rupture asks us to read beauty with moral alertness.
When we encounter elegance, we must ask: was elegance chosen
freely, or was it demanded by danger?
When we encounter abstraction, we must ask:
is this a
modernist preference, or a survival tactic? The same formal
decision can be both. The ethical reader does not rush to decide.
The ethical reader stays long enough to feel the weight of what
might have been impossible to say out loud.
Think about what it means to make art in a context where
your exhibitions can be shut down, your teaching positions
revoked, your very presence in the capital city questioned. This
was not hypothetical. Throughout the colonial period and into
independence, Sudanese artists navigated a landscape where
cultural production was always potentially political, where any
assertion of Sudanese identity could be read as anti-colonial
agitation, where the simple act of painting in a style that
referenced local traditions rather than European academicism
could be interpreted as resistance.
Rupture also changes the relationship between the artist and
the audience. In a culture shaped by surveillance and political
volatility, the audience itself becomes complex. There is the
local audience, which may recognize the code. There is the
institutional audience, which may pretend not to recognize it,
or may punish it if it does. There is the foreign audience, which
may exoticize it, or demand that it perform “Sudanness” in a
way that reduces it to trauma and sand. The artist stands at the

THE LENS OF AFTERMATH: ART AFTER THE BORDER WAS DRAWN
intersection of these gazes, and the work becomes a negotiation
between them.
This is not a comfortable place to create from. It produces
a particular tension in Sudanese art: the tension between the
need to remain truthful and the need to remain safe; between the
desire to speak and the necessity of restraint; between ﬁdelity
to the local and the hunger for international platforms that may
offer resources but also distortions.
And then there is the border itself as an artifact of the psyche.
A border is a form of forced storytelling. It tells you that your
history is now segmented. It tells you that your relations across
land are now “foreign.” It tells you that movement that was
once ordinary is now suspicious. It tells you that kinship is
now subject to paperwork. These changes do not remain at the
level of politics. They enter the aesthetic. They create an art
of fragmentation: not fragmentation as avant-garde play, but
fragmentation as lived reality. When movement is disrupted,
the archive becomes discontinuous.
When families are displaced, memory becomes portable.
When identities are politicized, self-description becomes
dangerous.
The artwork, under these conditions, becomes
a site where continuity can be reassembled, or at least mourned.
Consider the Gezira Scheme, launched in 1925: a massive
irrigation project that transformed land between the Blue and
White Niles into cotton plantations for British textile mills.
This was economic extraction, yes. But it was also aesthetic
extraction. It changed the relationship between people and land,
turning agricultural labor into industrial production. It created
new class formations, new patterns of migration, new forms
of dependency. And it severed older aesthetic practices tied to
seasonal rhythms and communal agriculture.
59

records.text:
Preface
I am not writing this book to prove that Sudan has art, as though
beauty requires a passport stamp from empire before it can be
believed.
I am writing because Sudanese art has spent too long being
treated as either folklore, softened for foreign appetites, or as
“politics”; hardened into slogans that let institutions pretend
they’ve understood the suffering they merely visited. Between
those two violences, the work itself is left unattended: the cloth,
the pigment, the geometry, the breath of pattern, the disciplined
silence that learned to survive in public. Interpretation, when it
arrives too quickly, becomes a second occupation. It enters with
conﬁdence, it names what it has not sat with, and it leaves the
viewer feeling informed rather than changed.
This book refuses that speed. It refuses the museums habit
of turning living forms into legible trophies. It also refuses
nostalgia, the sentimental kind that treats Sudan as a lost
paradise rather than a present, breathing complexity.
Sudanese art is not a decorative annex to history; it is one of
history’s most stubborn witnesses. It carries fracture without
advertising it. It carries devotion without asking permission.
It carries memory without ﬂattening it into “inﬂuence.” If
you approach it with the wrong posture—hungry for meanings,
impatient for summaries—you will mistake its restraint for
absence. But restraint is not emptiness. In Sudan, restraint
v

records.text:
THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
When you reorganize how people relate to land, you reorga-
nize what beauty can mean.
This is why Sudanese art after rupture often feels haunted
even when it is vibrant. It carries the afterimage of what was
interrupted. It carries the grief of what could not continue. It
carries the fatigue of being forced to deﬁne oneself repeatedly
for others. The colonizer’s question “who are you?” is not
innocent. It is a demand for legibility, and legibility is often a
precondition for control.
To answer that question too eagerly is to enter the colonizer’s
game. Many Sudanese works respond by refusing the terms of
the question. They do not provide identity as a neat package.
They provide presence. They provide texture. They provide a
world that cannot be simpliﬁed without violence.
Rupture also fractures the hierarchy of forms. Under colonial
regimes and their afterlives, certain forms are elevated and
others are diminished. “Fine art” is celebrated in ways that
align with European models, while local craft traditions are
relegated to ethnography. The museum and the anthropology
archive become twin instruments of classiﬁcation: one granting
prestige, the other granting curiosity.
Both can be violent.
Prestige can be violent when it demands assimilation. Curiosity
can be violent when it treats a culture as specimen.
Sudanese aesthetic life, which historically did not separate
art from life so sharply, is forced into this hierarchy, and the
result is a kind of institutional amputation: living traditions are
extracted from their contexts and displayed as “heritage,” while
contemporary works are pressured to perform “modernity”
according to imported terms.
The lens of rupture insists that we treat this hierarchy as
suspect. It asks us to see that what was called “craft” was

often where the deepest aesthetic intelligence lived, precisely
because it remained tied to continuity, labor, and communal
transmission. It asks us to see that what was called “modern”
was often not purely invention but negotiation with the colo-
nizer’s standards. And it asks us to see that what was called
“traditional” was not static but adaptive, an evolving language
that changed to survive. Colonial power loves to freeze the
colonized into timelessness, because timelessness is easier to
control than a living, changing culture. Sudanese art refuses that
freezing, even when it is forced into museums and textbooks
that pretend to categorize it cleanly.
Women’s aesthetic labor deserves particular attention
here.
Throughout the colonial period, women maintained
practices—textile work, henna application, basketry, pottery,
body adornment—that carried aesthetic knowledge across
generations.
These practices were systematically devalued
by colonial administrators and their taxonomies. They were
“domestic,” “decorative,” “craft,” never “art.”
Yet they
were the practices that maintained cultural continuity when
institutions failed.
They were the practices that encoded
memory when official archives excluded Sudanese voices.
They were the practices that transmitted pattern, color theory,
compositional sophistication, without needing museums or
galleries.
To dismiss women’s aesthetic labor as “merely craft” is to
accept the colonizer’s hierarchy. It is to agree that what happens
in institutional spaces matters more than what happens in
homes. It is to privilege the authored object over the commu-
nally maintained tradition. The lens of rupture asks us to reverse
this priority: to recognize that in contexts where institutions are
colonial impositions, the unofficial, the domestic, the feminine

often carry the most authentic continuities.
There is another wound inside the rupture: the fracture of the
imagination itself. Colonialism is often discussed as a political
and economic project, but its deepest aim is spiritual: to reshape
what a people believes is possible. When you control education,
you control aspiration. When you control public narrative, you
control dignity. When you control the archive, you control what
can be remembered without shame. Sudanese artists working
under and after these regimes were not merely responding to
external control; they were also battling internalized diminish-
ment. To make work at all under such conditions is already an
act of resistance. To make work that remains faithful to the soil
while speaking to modern conditions is a rarer courage.
But then came independence in 1956, and with it, a new ques-
tion: what does Sudanese art become when the colonizer leaves
but the colonial structures remain? This is where the Khartoum
School emerges as both achievement and complication. The
School—founded by Ibrahim El-Salahi, Ahmed Mohammed
Shibrain, Osman Waqialla, and others in the late 1950s and early
1960s—represents the ﬁrst major effort to articulate a distinctly
Sudanese modernism.
These artists had been trained in colonial institutions. They
knew European techniques.
But they also knew Sudanese
traditions: Arabic calligraphy, Nubian motifs, Islamic geometry,
African patterns.
Their project was synthesis: to create a
visual language that could be recognizably Sudanese while
engaging with international modernism.
This was delicate
work. To emphasize local traditions too heavily risked being
dismissed as “ethnic art” or “heritage”—categories that denied
contemporaneity. To embrace international modernism too
fully risked losing connection to the soil.

THE LENS OF AFTERMATH: ART AFTER THE BORDER WAS DRAWN
The Khartoum School artists walked this line with sophisti-
cated intelligence. El-Salahi’s paintings combined calligraphic
elements with abstraction. Shibrain developed a visual language
based on Arabic letterforms distilled into pure design.
Waqialla explored Sudanese-Kuﬁcalligraphy as modern
graphic form. These were not nostalgic gestures. They were
assertions that Sudanese aesthetic traditions could be as
legitimate a foundation for modernism as European ones.
The name “Khartoum School” itself was coined by Denis
Williams, an Anglo-Guyanese artist teaching at the College
of Fine and Applied Arts in the late 1950s. Williams recog-
nized something distinctive happening: a group of artists who
shared not a rigid manifesto but a sensibility, a commitment
to expressing Sudanese identity through forms that respected
both local heritage and contemporary innovation. The fact that
the name came from an outsider is telling, it suggests how
much Sudanese artists were still operating within frameworks
of external validation, still needing foreign recognition to
legitimate their work.
And this is where the encoded resistance that appears not
as slogans but as structure. In Sudan, resistance often wears
the mask of patience. It is not always loud. Sometimes it is a
refusal to abandon a motif. Sometimes it is the insistence on a
certain palette tied to place. Sometimes it is the preservation of a
rhythm that survives despite institutional pressure. Sometimes
it is the very act of continuing to make, to weave, to draw,
to inscribe, when the world is trying to reduce you to a crisis
statistic. Colonial and postcolonial violences produce a certain
hunger in outsiders: the hunger for “political art” that can be
easily read, easily cited, easily turned into moral performance.
Sudanese art often refuses that hunger.
It resists not only

oppression, but also the foreign appetite for legible suffering.
Think about what El-Salahi’s “Reborn Sounds of Childhood
Dreams” (1961) accomplishes.
On ﬁrst viewing, it appears
abstract: monochromatic forms, calligraphic gestures, geo-
metric structures. But look closer and you see references to
Sudanese visual culture, mask-like faces, pattern systems,
spatial arrangements that echo domestic architecture. The
painting is modern without rejecting tradition, abstract without
losing speciﬁcity. It speaks to international audiences while
remaining rooted in local knowledge. This is encoding at its
most sophisticated: the work appears legible in multiple visual
languages simultaneously, and the viewer you are determines
which language you hear.
The Khartoum School’s achievement was real. For the ﬁrst
time, Sudanese artists gained international recognition not as
exotic curiosities but as serious contributors to modern art. El-
Salahi would eventually have a retrospective at Tate Modern,
the ﬁrst African artist so honored. But the School also reveals
the persistence of colonial frameworks. These artists succeeded,
in part, by translating Sudanese aesthetics into forms legible to
European-trained eyes. They worked within gallery systems,
museum structures, critical discourses that were all imported.
The very category “Sudanese modernism” accepts European
modernism as the standard against which Sudanese contribu-
tions are measured. And then the School fractured. In 1975,
it effectively disbanded. Kamala Ibrahim Ishaq broke away
to found the Crystalist Group, which rejected what they saw
as the Khartoum School’s alignment with post-independence
government ideologies.
El-Salahi was accused of anti-government activities and
imprisoned by the Nimeiri regime, later going into self-imposed

exile in the UK. The fragmentation was not merely personal or
aesthetic. It reﬂected deeper tensions about what Sudanese art
should be, whom it should serve, how it should navigate between
local and global, between political engagement and aesthetic
autonomy.
The Crystalist Group’s manifesto—published in Al-Ayyam
newspaper in 1976—argued that the world is like a crystal:
transparent, with interdependent components. They rejected
singular objective truth in favor of multiple truths intertwined
with perception, feeling, and pleasure.
This was radical in
Sudan’s political context. It was a refusal of didactic art, of
propaganda, of nationalist simpliﬁcation. It was an insistence
that art could be playful, exploratory, subjective—that beauty
need not justify itself through political utility. But this too
was a form of encoding. To argue for aesthetic freedom in an
authoritarian context is itself political. To insist that art serves
no master is to resist the state’s demand that culture legitimize
power.
The Crystalists understood this. Their work appeared abstract,
decorative even. But abstraction, in a surveillance state, is a
form of protection. You cannot be punished for what you have
not explicitly said. This refusal is itself a form of sovereignty. It
says: we will not become content for your conscience. We will
not perform our wounds on demand. We will carry them in our
own languages, at our own volume, with our own ethics. This is
why Sudanese beauty can be so disciplined. It is beauty that has
learned not to trust the spectator. It is beauty that has learned
that visibility can be dangerous. It is beauty that has learned to
survive without applause.
Throughout this period, certain artists maintained prac-
tices outside institutional recognition altogether. Self-taught

painters like Ali Osman and Ahmed Salim developed visual
languages without formal training, working in styles that com-
bined local iconography with personal vision. Their work often
circulated in contexts far from galleries and museums, in homes,
in markets, in community spaces.
This parallel aesthetic economy mattered precisely because
it refused institutional validation. It said: we make beauty for
ourselves, not for your approval.
Women artists faced particular challenges.
Even within
progressive movements like the Khartoum School, gendered
assumptions about who could be a “serious” artist persisted.
Kamala Ibrahim Ishaq, one of the few women to gain recogni-
tion, had to ﬁght for legitimacy in ways her male colleagues
did not. Her work—often addressing women’s experiences,
domestic spaces, bodily autonomy—was sometimes dismissed
as “feminine” rather than “universal.” This gendered rupture
within the aesthetic rupture reveals how colonialism’s hierar-
chies reproduced themselves even in anticolonial movements.
The lens of rupture, then, is not a lens of despair. It is a
lens of diagnostic clarity. It teaches us to see the border not
merely as history, but as an ongoing aesthetic condition. It
teaches us to suspect the categories we inherited from empires
and institutions. It teaches us to read silence as intelligence,
abstraction as shelter, pattern as code, continuity as deﬁance.
It also teaches us to be humble: to admit that we will not always
decode what we see, and that decoding is not the highest form
of respect.
Sometimes the highest respect is to recognize the existence
of a code and not demand its keys.
Consider the archive itself as a site of rupture.
Colonial
administrators photographed, catalogued, collected Sudanese

THE LENS OF AFTERMATH: ART AFTER THE BORDER WAS DRAWN
objects and practices. These became the “Sudanese archive”
in European museums and research institutions.
But this
archive is structured by violence. It contains what was stolen,
what was purchased under duress, what was extracted without
consent. It contains photographs of scariﬁed bodies presented
as ethnographic data, with no record of the people’s names,
stories, or consent.
It contains textiles ripped from ritual contexts and displayed
as “decorative arts.” The archive appears objective, scientiﬁc,
preservationist. But it is theft organized as knowledge.
Against this colonial archive, Sudanese artists have had to
build alternative archives. Oral traditions that refuse written
codiﬁcation. Practices that live only in transmission from body
to body. Visual languages that cannot be translated into museum
labels.
These counter-archives are deliberately ephemeral,
deliberately resistant to extraction.
They survive precisely
by refusing to be captured.
And yet, the tension persists:
how to preserve without playing into preservation’s colonial
history? How to document without reproducing the violence
of documentation? How to make Sudanese aesthetic traditions
accessible to younger generations without turning them into
museum pieces?
These questions have no easy answers. They are the questions
that artists after rupture must live with.
If Chapter 1 showed that Sudan’s earliest aesthetic life was a
complete world, and Chapter 2 showed that the environment
itself trained the eye, then this chapter reveals what happens
when an external power attempts to overwrite that training
with administrative narratives. The work does not disappear. It
becomes double. It becomes guarded. It becomes haunted. It
becomes cunning. It becomes careful. It becomes, in the deepest

sense, a scar, because the scar is not the wound, but the proof
that the wound did not ﬁnish you.
And so, as we move forward, hold this as doctrine: rupture
is not an event that ended when ﬂags changed. It is a pressure
that continues whenever Sudanese art is asked to justify itself
in the language of others. It continues whenever “authenticity”
is demanded like a performance.
It continues whenever “modernity” is deﬁned as resemblance
to Europe.
It continues whenever institutions treat Sudan
as a theme rather than a living complexity. The critic who
approaches Sudanese art must therefore be more than apprecia-
tive.
They must be vigilant. They must see the border not as a line
on a map, but as a line drawn across the imagination, and they
must learn to read what survives on either side of it without
forcing it to become simple.
Let the record show: after the border was drawn, Sudanese art
did not become merely political. It became morally intelligent—
learning how to speak under pressure, how to remain beautiful
without becoming decorative, and how to survive the most
subtle violence of all: being made legible only in someone else’s
terms.

The Lens of Erasure: When Civilizing
Became a Curriculum
The most effective empire doesn’t merely take land. It takes
your capacity to believe in your own forms. It doesn’t need to
burn every archive if it can teach you to feel embarrassed by
what you inherited.
That is the true meaning of “civilizing missions”—not the
crude spectacle of conquest, but the slower, administrative
seduction of shame. In Sudan, the violence of “civilizing” was
often performed with paperwork, pedagogy, and polite language.
It arrived as improvement. It arrived as instruction. It arrived as
a promise to make the world more legible, more ordered, more
modern. And it did what all such promises do when they are
attached to power: it made the local feel secondary, the inherited
feel suspect, and the indigenous feel like a superstition that must
be outgrown.
There is a particular cruelty in the way institutions weaponize
taste. Taste, when honest, is intimate, an accumulation of
place, memory, climate, and communal rhythm. But taste,
when institutionalized, becomes a leash.
It teaches people

records.text:
is often the condition of staying alive. So I have structured this
book as a series of lenses, not categories, not movements, not a
checklist of masterpieces. A lens is an ethic. A lens is a way of
holding your gaze so it doesn’t become predatory.
Each lens asks a different kind of attention: one attends to
rupture, another to scripture, another to oral memory, another
to craft, another to exile, another to architecture, another to war,
and ﬁnally, to ghosts. Not ghosts as metaphor, but as the real
afterlife of what Sudan was made to forget: slavery, assimilation,
forced hierarchies of identity, suppressed civilizations, and the
quiet violence of being misnamed by the world.
This is not a comprehensive history. It is something harder: a
custodial approach. I will not claim a ﬁnal map of Sudanese art.
I will instead build rooms in which you can stand long enough
for the work to begin addressing you. The critic is not the one
who speaks ﬁrst. The critic is the one who stays.
If a sentence in this book ever feels too certain, too triumphant,
too quick, treat that as a failure of discipline. Sudan does not
need another authorial conquest. It needs witnesses with clean
hands.
A word about what this book will not do: it will not rescue.
The rescue narrative, where the Western writer “discovers” or
“elevates” the neglected artist is itself a rehearsal of dominance.
It assumes the work was waiting, inert, for external validation.
But Sudanese artists have never stopped working.
They have organized exhibitions in Khartoum and Omdurman
while the international art world looked elsewhere. They have
maintained studios through coups, through sanctions, through
the amputation of South Sudan, through the 2019 revolution,
through the war that began in 2023. The work did not pause for

what to admire and what to dismiss, and it does so under the
cover of “standards.” The colonial apparatus was not only a
system of extraction; it was a school of perception. It taught
which forms deserved seriousness and which belonged to the
realm of “craft,” “custom,” “folk,” “ritual,” “tribal.” These
labels were not innocent. They created a hierarchy of legitimacy.
They positioned European-derived “ﬁne art” as the endpoint
of aesthetic evolution and positioned local practices as raw
material, interesting, perhaps, but not quite art in the way the
colonizer meant it. A culture can survive war and still be undone
by classiﬁcation. Because classiﬁcation, when enforced, is an
aesthetic form of dispossession.
This is why I call it erasure as curriculum. Not erasure as
absence, but erasure as training. To be trained into erasure is
not to forget your past outright; it is to learn to mistrust it. It is
to learn to look at your own forms with a foreign eye, to judge
them by foreign standards, and to internalize the sense that
your inheritance is incomplete unless it can be translated into
the dominant aesthetic language of power.
The tragedy is not simply that certain practices were discour-
aged or banned; it is that a new generation learns to inherit with
embarrassment. It learns to treat continuity as backwardness. It
learns to treat ancestral intelligence as a museum artifact rather
than a living system. The colonizer’s deepest victory is achieved
when the colonized begins to perform the colonizer’s contempt
without needing to be asked.
Education, in this story, is never neutral. The classroom
becomes a border checkpoint for the imagination. It decides
which images are worthy of attention and which are dismissed
as decorative noise. It decides which histories count as “civ-
ilization” and which are treated as preface. It decides what

records.text:
THE LENS OF ERASURE: WHEN CIVILIZING BECAME A CURRICULUM
the student is trained to want. And wanting is not a small
matter.
If you can train a people to want what resembles
the conqueror, you don’t need to police them forever. They
will police themselves with aspiration. They will pursue the
imported as sophistication. They will treat the local as the thing
one must transcend. This is why “civilizing” is such an elegant
word for violence: it makes domination sound like mentorship.
It turns theft into pedagogy.
Consider the mechanics.
Gordon Memorial College was
founded in 1902 as part of an educational project championed
by Lord Kitchener, named after a British general killed during
the fall of Khartoum in 1885. The symbolism is instructive:
an institution designed to educate Sudanese was named for a
colonial military officer.
The message was clear before a single student entered: this
building represents not your victory, but ours. This is where you
will learn what we decide you need to know. The curriculum was
conceived to meet the colonial administration’s requirements.
Primary students learned reading, writing, arithmetic—but
always in service of creating subordinate administrators for the
colonial state. The student body grew steadily through the early
decades—hundreds of young men entering a building named
for the man colonialism had martyred.
And as it grew, the curriculum expanded: religious law, engi-
neering, teacher training, clerical administration, accounting.
Notice what is absent. Nothing that would produce independent
thought, independent vision, independent aesthetic judgment.
These were not neutral educational offerings. They were train-
ing programs designed to produce a class of intermediaries,
Sudanese who could staff the lower and middle ranks of colonial
bureaucracy, who could translate between rulers and ruled, who

could manage the mechanics of extraction and administration
without requiring British personnel at every level.
What it produced, as intended, was a class of educated Su-
danese men reshaped away from indigenous frameworks—
intermediaries ﬂuent enough in colonial logic to staff its ma-
chinery, and sufficiently alienated from local authority to re-
main reliably useful. This was not an accidental side effect. It
was the point.
Colonial education creates a particular kind of subject: some-
one who speaks the language of power, who understands the
colonizer’s categories, who has internalized the colonizer’s
hierarchies of value.
This person becomes useful precisely
because they are alienated from their own context. They can see
their own culture through foreign eyes. They can assess local
practices by imported standards. They become, in the deepest
sense, translators—but translation is never innocent. Every
translation is also a betrayal.
The mechanisms of this violence are often subtle enough that
they can be denied. The institution says, “We simply offered
education.” The administrator says, “We simply introduced
standards.” The museum says, “We simply preserved artifacts.”
But preservation can be a form of freezing, and freezing can be a
form of death. When local forms are preserved as ethnography—
ﬂattened into timeless “tradition”—they are denied their right
to evolve. They are separated from their contexts, displayed
under glass, and admired as “heritage,” while living artists
are pressured to prove their modernity by abandoning the very
continuities that made their culture coherent. This is a double
erasure: the old is fossilized, the new is assimilated. The living
bridge between them is weakened.
The result is a culture forced to choose between nostalgia

THE LENS OF ERASURE: WHEN CIVILIZING BECAME A CURRICULUM
and imitation, between being “authentically local” for the
foreign gaze or “properly modern” for institutional recognition.
Both choices are traps. Both are forms of control disguised as
opportunity.
On the eve of independence—as if anticipating the need to ﬁx,
in amber, the image of what Sudan was supposed to be—the
colonial administration institutionalized its vision of Sudanese
culture as ethnographic specimen. A museum branch, opened
in the closing hours of foreign rule, as if to say: we may leave
the land, but we leave behind our way of seeing it. The timing
was not incidental. The colonizers institutionalized a particular
way of seeing Sudanese culture—as ethnography, as specimens,
as objects to be collected and displayed rather than as living
practices embedded in ongoing social worlds.
The Museum of Antiquities, established at Gordon Memo-
rial College around 1905 by Reginald Wingate, extended this
logic: its collections were conﬁgured for scholarly investigation
rather than public encounter. Sudanese cultural objects became
data—not living inheritance, not sources of meaning for the
communities who had made them, but specimens held under
institutional custody.
This elite access reveals the colonial
attitude: Sudanese cultural objects were data for scholarly
investigation, not sources of meaning for the communities that
produced them.
The violence here is epistemological. It determines who gets
to know, and how. It determines whose interpretation matters.
When Sudanese objects are collected by British adminis-
trators, catalogued by European-trained scholars, displayed
in institutional settings designed for foreign consumption,
and interpreted through colonial frameworks, the objects are
severed from the people who made them. They become evidence

in someone else’s argument about civilization, about progress,
about the stages of human development. The craftsperson who
wove the basket, the woman who shaped the pot, the community
that used the talisman—these people have no voice in how their
work is understood. They are rendered mute. Their objects
speak, but only in languages imposed by others. What is erased,
in such a system, is not only content, it is conﬁdence. The
artist begins to doubt their own visual language. The critic
begins to treat imported frameworks as more legitimate than
local ones. The audience begins to mistrust what is familiar.
This is a psychological occupation. It does not require soldiers.
It requires curricula, funding patterns, exhibition standards,
and the quiet authority of those who decide what gets called
“serious.” Once seriousness is monopolized, the rest of culture
becomes a decorative annex. And a decorative annex is the
easiest thing in the world to disregard when the politics become
violent.
Think about what it means for a young Sudanese artist in the
1940s or 1950s to encounter this institutional apparatus. They
might grow up surrounded by textiles with geometric patterns,
by henna designs with complex symmetries, by architectural
forms that manage light and heat with elegant efficiency. But
when they enter Gordon Memorial College’s School of Design
(established 1945), what do they learn? They learn European
academic drawing. They learn perspective systems developed
in Renaissance Italy. They learn color theory as articulated by
German scientists. They learn that “art” means easel painting,
that “sculpture” means carved stone or cast bronze, that “com-
position” follows Western principles of balance and harmony.
None of this knowledge is inherently violent. Perspective can
be useful. Color theory can illuminate.

THE LENS OF ERASURE: WHEN CIVILIZING BECAME A CURRICULUM
Bronze casting is a legitimate skill. The violence lies in what
is excluded, in what is devalued, in what is never mentioned.
The violence lies in the implication that these imported tech-
niques represent advancement, while local aesthetic traditions
represent a stage you are meant to outgrow. The violence lies in
teaching you to see your grandmother’s embroidery as “craft”
but a European painting as “art,” to see your uncle’s calligraphy
as “decoration” but a Western abstract painting as “serious,”
to see a Sudanese pattern as “ethnic” but a Parisian design as
“universal.”
The phrase “civilizing mission” also hides a deeper moral
insult: it implies that the people being “civilized” were not
already in possession of ethics, beauty, and order. But Sudan,
as we have already seen, possessed sophisticated systems of
continuity long before modern bureaucracies arrived. The desert
taught restraint. The Nile taught rhythm and interconnect-
edness. The body and the home carried archives of meaning
through marks, textiles, and ritual practices that were not
random but structured. The colonial project did not introduce
order into chaos. It introduced one order by humiliating another.
It did not bring morality into amorality. It brought a new moral
hierarchy that positioned itself as universal while treating local
cosmologies as quaint.
The insult was not simply political; it was metaphysical. It
told a people that their ways of knowing the world were childish.
And here we encounter a fundamental aesthetic consequence:
when local epistemologies are demeaned, local forms are dis-
torted. If a culture’s relationship to the unseen is mocked, its
talismanic practices become “superstition” rather than care.
If its oral traditions are dismissed, its poetic rhythms become
“primitive” rather than sophisticated memory technology. If

its craft lineages are relegated, its most disciplined material
intelligence is pushed out of the category of art. Erasure as
curriculum is not only the removal of images; it is the removal
of the right to interpret one’s own images on one’s own terms.
It is the displacement of the local viewer. It tells the community:
you may live here, but you may not be the authority on your
own forms. Authority belongs to the institution, the archive,
the foreign scholar, the imported canon.
This hierarchical thinking shows up everywhere in colonial
documentation.
When British administrators collected Su-
danese objects, they classiﬁed them rigorously: this is “tribal
art,” this is “Islamic craft,” this is “weapons,” this is “domestic
utensils.” These categories appear neutral, merely descriptive.
But they are normative. They enforce distinctions that didn’t
necessarily exist in Sudanese life. A basket might be simultane-
ously functional, beautiful, and spiritually signiﬁcant. A textile
might be everyday wear, artistic expression, and social marker
all at once.
But the museum’s categories force separation.
The basket goes in the “ethnography” collection. The textile
becomes “craft.” The talisman is ﬁled under “religious objects.”
Each object is extracted from its web of meanings and reduced
to a single function legible to institutional logic.
Moreover, certain types of objects were collected while others
were ignored. Colonial interest focused on what appeared exotic,
what illustrated difference, what could be used as evidence of
“primitive” culture. Elaborate ceremonial objects were collected
because they looked dramatic in display cases. Simple, everyday
objects that demonstrated sophisticated aesthetic intelligence—
a perfectly balanced water vessel, an elegantly efficient cooking
implement, a textile with subtle pattern variations—were often
overlooked because they didn’t perform “difference” dramati-
