cally enough for European audiences.
The result is an archive that is systematically skewed. It
over-represents the spectacular and under-represents the ev-
eryday. It favors objects that conform to European ideas of what
“African” or “Islamic” art should look like. It preserves what can
be easily classiﬁed and discards what is ambiguous, hybrid, or
resistant to categorization. This skewed archive then becomes
the basis for how the world understands Sudanese aesthetics.
Scholars write books based on museum collections. Art histo-
rians develop theories based on what colonial administrators
chose to preserve. And Sudanese people themselves, trained
in institutions that use these colonial archives as authoritative
sources, begin to see their own culture through the distortions
of colonial classiﬁcation.
This is where Sudanese art begins to develop its most charac-
teristic modern strategy: not simply resistance, but doubleness.
The work learns to wear masks. It learns to speak two languages
at once: one for the institution, one for the community. One
legible enough to pass through the gate, one faithful enough
to remain anchored in soil. The work becomes diplomatic. The
artist becomes an interpreter of their own culture for audiences
that may not deserve translation, and that translation itself can
become exhausting. Because translation is not only linguistic;
it is ethical.
To translate your culture into the colonizer’s
categories is to risk mutilating it. Yet to refuse translation can
mean invisibility, poverty, and exclusion.
The “civilizing mission” creates this bind deliberately: it
makes participation contingent on assimilation, then calls
assimilation “progress.”
Students at Gordon Memorial College navigated this bind daily.
To succeed in the colonial education system required perform-

ing competence in European forms. To maintain connection
with Sudanese culture required preserving knowledge that
the institution devalued or ignored. Some students managed
both. They learned to code-switch between visual languages,
producing work that could satisfy colonial examiners while
privately maintaining their own aesthetic practices. Others
chose sides, fully embracing European modernism and rejecting
local traditions as obstacles to progress, or refusing colonial
education altogether and remaining within traditional craft
lineages.
But most inhabited the uncomfortable middle: learning Euro-
pean methods while trying to preserve something of their own
aesthetic inheritance, performing the role of “educated native”
while privately resenting the assumptions embedded in that
role. This psychological splitting—the experience of having to
be two different people in two different contexts—produces a
particular kind of consciousness. It makes you acutely aware
of how perception is constructed, how standards are arbitrary,
how taste is taught.
It also produces exhaustion. The constant negotiation be-
tween worlds, the endless code-switching, the vigilance re-
quired to perform acceptability while maintaining integrity—
these extract a toll.
But there is a more intimate violence still: the violence of
admiration. Empire does not only mock; it also collects. It
praises certain aspects of the colonized culture, but only those
aspects that can be safely aestheticized, stripped of political
potency and ethical context.
The colonizer’s museum becomes a kind of softened battle-
ﬁeld where objects are displayed as beautiful trophies, divorced
from the lives that produced them and from the conditions that

made them necessary. In such cases, appreciation becomes
another form of erasure. The object is admired, but the world
that gave it meaning is ignored. The pattern is praised, but the
hunger it survived is forgotten. The talisman is displayed, but
the vulnerability it answered is dismissed as “belief.” The textile
is aestheticized, but the woman’s labor becomes invisible. This
is the violence of selective reverence: reverence that loves the
surface but refuses the responsibility of the depth.
Colonial photography exempliﬁes this violence perfectly.
British administrators and travelers photographed Sudanese
people extensively, particularly those with facial scariﬁcation,
elaborate dress, or what Europeans considered “exotic” appear-
ance. These photographs were not neutral documentation. They
were performances of power. The photographer controlled the
frame, the lighting, the pose. The subject often had little say in
how they were represented.
These images then circulated in European publications, lec-
tures, exhibitions. Always presented as evidence of something:
evidence of “tribal culture,” evidence of “primitive conditions,”
evidence of why colonialism was necessary to bring “progress.”
The photographs decontextualized their subjects completely.
A person’s scariﬁcation, which in their own community sig-
niﬁed clan membership, passage into adulthood, and social
belonging, became evidence of “barbarism” that justiﬁed colo-
nial intervention. A woman’s jewelry, which represented her
family’s wealth and her own status, became an example of
“native ornament.” A man’s posture, which in his own cultural
context expressed dignity and authority, might be read by
European viewers as “noble savage” primitivism. The violence
wasn’t merely in being photographed, it was in having no
control over how those images would be used, interpreted, and

requires is a different quality of attention, one that can receive
complexity without immediately seeking to resolve it.
This also means the book will not offer comfort. There is
a particular kind of reader who approaches books about non-
Western art seeking affirmation, a sense of having done the
right thing by paying attention. But attention is not inherently
ethical. Attention can be surveillance. Attention can be appetite.
The question is not whether you look, but how you hold what
you see afterward. Do you let it disturb your categories? Do you
let it refute your assumptions about what art from this region
is “supposed” to do? Or do you metabolize it quickly into the
familiar, into “resistance art,” “diaspora art,” “postcolonial
art” and move on, your worldview intact?
The lenses I offer are not neutral. They are chosen because
they refuse the easy routes. They ask you to contend with what
makes Sudanese art illegible to the institutions that claim to
celebrate “global” art while still operating from a profoundly
local (which is to say, Western) center of gravity.
They ask you to sit with practices that do not announce them-
selves, with artists who refuse the performance of marginality,
with forms that carry knowledge in ways the academy has not
learned to read. If this makes the book difficult, that difficulty
is not a ﬂaw. It is a threshold. It is the work asking you to meet
it on terms other than your own.
One last clariﬁcation: when I say “Sudanese art,” I do not
mean a singular, uniﬁed tradition. I mean the plural, contested,
stratiﬁed, and sometimes contradictory practices that have
emerged from a land whose borders were drawn by others,
whose populations have been divided and renamed, whose

So the task of this chapter is to insist on a harsher truth: the
civilizing mission was not merely an external intervention; it
was a reprogramming of perception. It reshaped what Sudanese
people were trained to value. It reshaped what artists were
trained to produce. It reshaped what institutions were trained
to reward. It built a cultural economy where recognition often
required resemblance to foreign forms, and where local conti-
nuities were either frozen as folklore or dismissed as backward.
This is not a minor issue of taste. It is a spiritual issue, because
it determines what a people believes is worthy of devotion.
And this reprogramming was remarkably efficient. By the
time of independence in 1956, Sudan had a class of Western-
educated elites who had internalized many of the colonizer’s
aesthetic hierarchies. They valued easel painting over textile
work. They valued individual artistic genius over communal
craft traditions. They valued innovation and “originality” over
continuity and reﬁnement of inherited forms. They valued work
that could circulate in international art markets over work that
remained embedded in local social contexts.
This internalized hierarchy persisted even among Sudanese
who opposed colonialism politically. You could ﬁght for inde-
pendence while still believing that “real art” meant galleries
and museums rather than homes and markets. You could reject
British rule while still accepting British deﬁnitions of what
counted as artistic excellence. This is the insidious power of
aesthetic colonization: it outlives political colonization because
it operates at the level of perception, at the level of what you’ve
been trained to see and value.
This is why, when we later speak of Sudanese Islamic aes-
thetics, we must remember that Islam did not arrive as the

only system of meaning; it arrived into a land already full
of visual intelligence.
Yet colonial modernity often frames
Islamic aesthetics as either a “civilizing” improvement over
“paganism,” or as an obstacle to “modern art.” Both framings
are distortions. They treat Sudanese forms as if they require
external validation to be legitimate.
In reality, Sudan’s aesthetic world has long been a negotiation
among multiple cosmologies—river, desert, ancestral practice,
scripture, oral memory, craft lineage. The civilizing mission
attempted to ﬂatten this complexity into a ladder of evolution.
But Sudan’s reality is not a ladder. It is a braid. And a braid
cannot be understood by pulling one strand and declaring it the
whole.
Erasure as curriculum also produces a familiar modern pathol-
ogy: the compulsion to “prove” civilization through resem-
blance. The colonized subject, trained into doubt, begins to seek
legitimacy by aligning with imported aesthetics, whether aca-
demic realism, European modernism, or contemporary global
art trends. This alignment can produce extraordinary work,
but it also carries a sorrow: the sense that one must borrow
the colonizer’s mirror to be seen. The mirror does not merely
reﬂect; it judges. It frames certain gestures as sophisticated and
others as naive. It frames certain materials as art and others as
craft. It frames certain histories as universal and others as local.
When you create within such a mirror, you are always at risk of
becoming a performer rather than a witness.
Think about the psychological weight of this. Imagine being
a young Sudanese artist with genuine talent. You’ve grown
up immersed in visual culture, the patterns on your mother’s
Thoub, the henna designs at weddings, the calligraphy in the
mosque, the proportions of traditional architecture. You have an

intuitive understanding of balance, rhythm, color relationships.
But when you enter formal art education, none of this knowledge
is recognized as expertise. Instead, you’re taught as if you’re
starting from zero. You must learn perspective drawing as if
you’ve never understood spatial relationships. You must learn
composition as if you’ve never arranged visual elements. You
must learn color theory as if you’ve never mixed dyes or chosen
fabrics.
The message is clear: what you knew before doesn’t count.
Your informal education—the knowledge transmitted through
observation, practice, apprenticeship—is not legitimate knowl-
edge. Real knowledge comes from institutions, from textbooks,
from certiﬁed instructors. And to succeed, you must prove your
competence in the imported system. You must demonstrate that
you can think like a European artist. You must show that you’ve
overcome the limitations of your local context and achieved
“universal” (read: Western) standards.
Some artists refuse this logic entirely. They maintain their
craft traditions, working outside institutional validation. But
they pay a price: exclusion from galleries, from critical attention,
from the international circuits that offer ﬁnancial rewards
and prestige. Other artists embrace institutional logic fully,
producing work that could have been made anywhere, work that
signals their membership in a global artistic elite by deliberately
avoiding any “ethnic” markers. They gain recognition but at
the cost of disconnection from the soil that formed them.
Yet Sudanese art persists, and it persists with a particular kind
of quiet deﬁance: it keeps smuggling itself through the very
systems that tried to erase it. Patterns remain. Rhythms remain.
The geometry of the land remains. The oral pulse remains. The
craft intelligence remains, even when dismissed.

This persistence is not accidental. It is what happens when a
culture refuses to let its memory be reduced to museum labels
and school syllabi. The deeper archive survives in bodies, in
homes, in rituals, in the hands that continue to weave, dye,
sculpt, adorn.
This is why, even under the pressure of “civilizing,” Sudan’s
aesthetic world did not become merely an imitation of Europe.
It became something else: a modernity with scars, a modernity
that carries continuities in coded form, a modernity that refuses
to fully surrender its ancestral disciplines.
Women’s
practices
deserve
particular
attention
here.
Throughout the colonial period and beyond, women main-
tained aesthetic traditions that men’s institutional careers
often abandoned.
While men attended Gordon Memorial
College and learned European techniques, women continued
embroidering Thoubs, applying henna, making pottery, weaving
baskets. These practices were systematically devalued, labeled
“domestic,” “decorative,” “craft,” never “art.” But they were
precisely the practices that maintained cultural continuity when
institutions failed.
Consider henna application. This is skilled work requiring
years of practice to master. The artist must understand pattern
composition, symmetry, how designs relate to body structure,
how to adapt traditional motifs to individual hands.
She must know the properties of henna paste, the right
consistency, how long it needs to set, how to achieve dark, long-
lasting stains. She must work with precision and conﬁdence
since mistakes cannot be easily corrected. And she must do
all this while maintaining social relationships, since henna
application is a communal practice involving conversation,
song, storytelling.
83

None of this expertise was recognized by colonial institutions.
It wasn’t taught at Gordon Memorial College. It didn’t appear in
museums as “art.” It wasn’t discussed in the journal Sudan
Notes and Records.
Yet it was aesthetically sophisticated,
culturally signiﬁcant, and socially essential. It transmitted
knowledge across generations. It maintained visual vocabular-
ies. It preserved pattern systems that connected contemporary
practice to deep history.
This dismissal of women’s aesthetic labor is itself a form
of violence. It says that what happens in institutional spaces
matters more than what happens in homes. It privileges the
authored object over the communally maintained tradition. The
aesthetic intelligence preserved by women—precisely because
it remained outside institutional validation—often carried more
authentic continuities than the work produced by men who had
been trained to doubt their inheritance.
This is also where the critic must be ruthless with themselves.
Because the reader—especially the educated reader—may carry
the civilizing mission inside their own instincts. They may
unconsciously seek the “real art” in paintings that resemble
Western formats, while treating craft as charming supplement.
They may privilege gallery work over domestic forms. They may
treat abstraction as sophistication and ritual as superstition.
These instincts are not personal failures; they are inherited
training. But they must be undone. The purpose of this book is
not simply to introduce Sudanese art. It is to unteach the reader
the habits that have made Sudanese art easy to misunderstand.
The legacy of erasure as curriculum extends into the present.
Even after independence, even after the Khartoum School’s
efforts to develop a distinctly Sudanese modernism, the colonial
hierarchy of forms persists. Art schools still privilege painting
84

THE LENS OF ERASURE: WHEN CIVILIZING BECAME A CURRICULUM
and sculpture over textile and craft.
Museums still separate “ﬁne art” from “ethnographic ob-
jects.”
Critics still treat innovation as more valuable than
continuity.
Funding still ﬂows more readily to work that
resembles international contemporary art than to work rooted
in local traditions.
And Sudanese artists still navigate the
double bind: to be taken seriously internationally often requires
producing work legible to global art discourses, which means
work inﬂuenced by European and American contemporary art.
But to maintain connection to Sudanese aesthetic traditions
requires working in forms and with concerns that may not
register in international contexts. The artist must choose, must
compromise, must ﬁnd ways to be multiple things simultane-
ously.
This is exhausting. And it is the continuing legacy of colonial
aesthetic violence.
So let this chapter stand as a diagnostic: whenever you feel
yourself impressed by Sudanese art because it resembles what
you already admire, pause. Ask what in you is still colonized.
Ask why resemblance feels like legitimacy.
Ask why the local must pass through a foreign standard to be
taken seriously. The civilizing mission is not only an event in
history. It is a posture that persists whenever we treat Sudan as a
learner and the West as the teacher, whenever we treat Sudanese
form as derivative rather than sovereign, whenever we treat
local aesthetic intelligence as something that must “develop”
into recognizability.
Let the record show: the violence of “civilizing” was not only
in what it erased, but in what it trained people to want and in a
colonized imagination, even desire can become a wound.
85

6
The Lens of Resistance: When Beauty
Became a Code
There are places where truth survives only by learning to whis-
per. Sudan is one of them. When power turns language into
evidence and institutions turn visibility into danger, beauty
becomes more than beauty. It becomes a method of safe speech.
It becomes a coded architecture, a way of carrying testimony
without handing it to the executioner.
This is why, in Sudan, pattern is not merely decoration and
abstraction is not merely taste. They are often forms of refuge.
They are the aesthetic equivalent of lowering your voice in a
room with thin walls: not because you have nothing to say, but
because you intend to remain alive long enough to say it again
tomorrow.
The modern imagination, especially in art criticism, has a
habit of treating “political art” as something that must declare
itself loudly: slogans, explicit images, shock, clarity.
But
Sudan’s political reality has often made clarity expensive.
Under censorship, surveillance, shifting regimes, and the
ordinary dangers of being too visible, the artwork learns a
86

records.text:
THE LENS OF RESISTANCE: WHEN BEAUTY BECAME A CODE
different politics: a politics of endurance. It does not always
confront power head-on. It sidesteps. It encodes. It carries its
meaning in texture and rhythm rather than in overt statement.
This is not cowardice. It is intelligence under constraint. A coded
artwork is not an artwork that lacks conviction. It is an artwork
that understands consequence.
So we begin with a simple proposition: in Sudan, beauty has
often functioned as camouﬂage.
Camouﬂage, however, is not emptiness.
It is deliberate
concealment. And concealment implies a threat worth hiding
from.
When a community learns that certain subjects cannot be
spoken publicly—because speech invites punishment—the aes-
thetic becomes a second language. One that can be practiced in
the home, in the hand, in the textile, in the pattern that repeats
without raising suspicion. The code is not always a secret in the
dramatic sense. Often it is simply a shared literacy among those
who live inside the same pressure. The outside world may see
“ornament.” The inside world may see a warning, a memory, a
lament, a refusal, a prayer.
The historical conditions that necessitated coded aesthetics
in Sudan are not abstract. They are documented, brutal, and
speciﬁc.
When Al-Inqaz—the regime that called itself Sal-
vation—seized power in 1989, it moved immediately against
culture. Not as collateral damage. As strategy. The national
theatre was shuttered. Cinemas closed. Love songs vanished
from public channels. Magazines were discontinued, books
conﬁscated, and artists were arrested—not for subversion
exactly, but for indecency, for morality violations, for the crime
of being artistic in an environment that had just decided what
virtue looked like.
87

THREADS OF SAND, SCAR & SCRIPTURE
Within a year, arts institutions were shut down. This was
not incidental cultural policy. It was systematic erasure of the
infrastructure that allows art to exist publicly. But the assault
on artistic expression did not begin in 1989. It was inherited.
Each regime took what the previous one had built and extended
it—added to the list, sharpened the methods, broadened the
deﬁnition of what was dangerous.
By the time Bashir consolidated power, the infrastructure
of control was comprehensive: pre-publication censorship,
conﬁscated print runs, surveillance of anyone who made or
published or distributed, detention without charge, violence
without accountability. Print runs were seized before distribu-
tion. Newspapers were shut mid-edition.
The threat did not need to be explicit—the knowledge that it
existed was enough to reshape every editorial decision, every
line drawn, every word chosen.
This created an environment where artists faced arrest or ex-
ile, forcing them to adapt their work to navigate the constraints
imposed by the state.
When the options are silence, exile,
imprisonment, or death, aesthetics become survival technology.
Artists who chose to remain and work had to develop strategies
that allowed expression without triggering retaliation. This is
the climate in which coded beauty becomes necessary.
This is why pattern matters. Pattern is an ancient Sudanese
discipline, older than modern politics, older than colonial
borders. But under rupture, pattern takes on new labor. It begins
to carry the weight of what cannot be stated plainly. It becomes
a vessel not only for continuity but for resistance. It can do
this because pattern is naturally ambiguous to those who do
not share its language. A repeated motif can appear harmless
to the censor. A rhythm can appear merely aesthetic to the

administrator. A textile can look like “craft” to the institution.
Yet within that so-called harmlessness, messages can travel.
Pain can be stored. Identity can persist. Memory can refuse
erasure.
Think about the intelligence this requires. An artist working
under censorship must become a double expert: expert in their
aesthetic tradition, and expert in the psychology of the censor.
They must know which forms will be read as threatening and
which will be dismissed as decorative. They must understand
that geometric abstraction might pass where ﬁgurative repre-
sentation would be conﬁscated. They must know that ancient
patterns can carry contemporary meanings without the censor
recognizing the substitution. This is sophisticated work. It
requires knowing your tradition deeply enough to innovate
within it, and knowing power’s blind spots well enough to
exploit them.
Women’s domestic aesthetic practices become especially
important here. Because these practices were systematically
devalued by both colonial and postcolonial authorities, labeled
“craft,” “decoration,” “women’s work,” often escaping the
scrutiny applied to gallery art and public monuments.
A woman embroidering a Thoub in her home was not subject to
the same surveillance as a man painting in a studio. The henna
applied at a wedding was not reviewed by censors the way a
theater performance would be. This created a paradox: the very
devaluation that had been used to dismiss women’s aesthetic
labor also allowed that labor to continue with less interference.
So while male artists who worked in institutional contexts
faced direct censorship, women maintained aesthetic traditions
that could encode memory, identity, and even resistance with-
out triggering institutional response. The pattern that looked

records.text:
ANSWERABILITY
MUSEUM OF ONE
Research Working Paper No. 1 · Version 1.0
1
The Historical Work and the Account
The boundary of a work is already a historical claim. When an art historian names an action, an 
object, an exhibition, or a photograph as the subject of an account, that choice establishes what the 
account proposes to explain. The choice may be entirely justified. Yet it acquires authority only 
through the evidence that supports it and the distinctions it preserves. A history of an action need 
not become a history of everything that surrounded the action; a history of its exhibition need not 
exhaust its aesthetic significance. The responsibility is more exacting than completeness. The 
historian must remain answerable for the boundary through which the work is made historically 
intelligible.
Reiko Tomii’s scholarship on postwar Japanese art gives this question unusual force. Her 
distinction between expression and operation identifies the labour of making art and the labour of 
making it public, including arrangements through which artistic activity is sustained. The two may 
be distinguishable in principle while becoming inseparable in particular practices. An exhibition, a 
photographic presentation, a negotiation over space, or a collective arrangement can enter the 
conditions under which the artistic proposition is realized and subsequently known (Tomii, 
“Thinking Operationally,” 60–61, 67–69). Tomii’s contribution is neither a plea for additional 
context nor a merely sociological supplement to aesthetic analysis. It alters the historical questions 
available to an account of the work.
This essay asks what follows for the account once those relations are admitted. The proposal is 
answerability: a claim-specific discipline through which the historian identifies what a proposition 
asserts, which evidence gives it support, how the evidence bears upon its scope, and what must 
happen when that support is challenged. The term is intentionally broader than Tomii’s operation. 
Operation names a historical dimension of artistic practice; answerability names an obligation of 
explanation. Operational evidence is one class of evidence capable of putting that obligation under 
pressure. The relation between them is the subject of the inquiry, rather than a terminological 
inheritance that settles the inquiry in advance.
The principal object of examination is the published account. Tomii’s discussions of Shiraga 
Kazuo’s Challenging Mud are read beside Namiko Kunimoto’s “Shiraga Kazuo: The Hero and 
Concrete Violence,” with a shorter comparison drawn from Tomii’s discussion of Hi Red Center 
and GUN. The purpose is not to install one scholar as custodian of facts and another as custodian of 
interpretation. Their questions and evidential uses differ; both make interpretive and historical 
judgments. A close comparison should establish where those differences matter, where they are 
compatible, and which further inferences their texts can sustain. If the result is compatibility rather 
than disagreement, that result belongs to the argument.
What Operation Already Explains
Tomii’s account of operation has a specific historical content. Artistic production can depend on 
forms of organization that are obscured when attention rests exclusively on the finished object or 
the exceptional gesture. Making an exhibition possible, arranging a public situation, securing 
access, coordinating participants, or circulating a document may be integral to how an artistic 
activity exists in the world. These are not automatically equivalent acts. Their relations must be 
reconstructed from the practice at issue. Tomii’s formulation makes it possible to investigate the 
artistic significance of such labour without dissolving the distinction between expression and its 
enabling arrangements (Tomii, “Thinking Operationally,” 60–61).

records.text:
ANSWERABILITY
MUSEUM OF ONE
Research Working Paper No. 1 · Version 1.0
2
The historical significance is particularly visible where making and showing meet. If an action is 
planned in anticipation of a durable result, then exhibition may enter the preparation of the action. 
If documentation is selected and circulated as part of an artistic presentation, the image has a public 
role before it becomes a later historian’s evidence. If an intervention requires permission or the use 
of a specific site, the arrangement can shape what was possible without necessarily determining 
what the work meant. Each relation opens a different inquiry. A theory that calls them all operation 
without distinguishing their consequences would give up the precision that makes Tomii’s concept 
valuable.
The extension proposed here concerns the subsequent account. A historian may accurately report 
that a work required organization yet draw conclusions whose scope remains unaffected by that 
report. Sometimes this is defensible: the evidence may be relevant to a different question. 
Sometimes the reported relation is indispensable to the very claim being made. The task is to 
determine which situation obtains. What has the evidence changed about the description of the 
historical work, the attribution of agency, or the limits of documentary inference? A fact’s presence 
in a footnote is not yet an explanation of its bearing. Neither, however, is its absence proof of 
neglect. The relevant test begins with the actual proposition.
Published Arguments as Evidence
A published historical account is direct evidence of what its author argues. It can also serve as 
scholarly testimony about an earlier event. These are different evidential roles. Tomii’s 2011 
conversation with Jane DeBevoise establishes, through its wording and sequence, the claims Tomii 
makes and the uncertainty she marks. When the same conversation supplies a premise about a 
material mixture or a photographic record, the premise belongs to her historical reconstruction. 
Reading the conversation does not convert the reconstruction into an independently inspected 
archival fact. Conversely, the absence of such independent inspection does not prevent careful 
analysis of the argument as an argument.
Three judgments must therefore remain distinct. The first concerns attribution: what does the author 
actually claim, about which occurrence, and with what qualification? The second concerns 
justification: do the reasons the author presents or explicitly invokes adequately support that claim? 
The third concerns historical accuracy: did the event happen as described? These questions overlap, 
but they cannot be exchanged without changing the inquiry. A conjecture may eventually prove 
true while having been falsely represented by a later writer as a certainty. An inference may exceed 
its stated evidence without being historically false. An account may be adequately justified on the 
available record and still remain open to correction by further evidence.
The unit of analysis is the developed argument, including its notes, qualifications, and stated 
purpose. A short description and a specialist article have different legitimate ambitions. An account 
concerned with gesture is not thereby an account that excludes the object; a history of exhibition is 
not indifferent to bodily action merely because it follows a different explanatory path. The 
American Historical Association’s standards of attribution and evidential accountability, together 
with Aviezer Tucker’s distinction between historical practice and the finished presentation of 
research, provide precedents for this discipline (American Historical Association, “Statement on 
Standards,” §§2–3; Tucker, Our Knowledge of the Past, 4–7). The present proposal does not claim 
to originate the duty to justify an inference. It asks whether that duty can be made more exact when 
the evidence concerns the making-public of art.

records.text:
ANSWERABILITY
MUSEUM OF ONE
Research Working Paper No. 1 · Version 1.0
3
A Criterion of Answerability
The criterion begins with a proposition fixed before a challenge is evaluated. Its referent, meaning, 
scope, degree of certainty, and evidential basis must be stated as precisely as the text permits. A 
claim about one recorded execution differs from a claim about every execution. A gesture that 
appears spontaneous is not necessarily an action undertaken without preparation. Permission to use 
a site differs from control over the artistic choices made there. When these distinctions are left 
unstable, an argument can appear to survive criticism only because its terms have shifted. A critic 
can commit the inverse error by enlarging an author’s claim, defeating the enlarged version, and 
declaring the actual account refuted.
Four responses are possible. Retention preserves the original proposition, with the same meaning 
and scope, because its positive support remains adequate after a genuine challenge. Limitation 
narrows the proposition’s reach. Revision changes its substantive content. Suspension withholds 
judgment where the evidence cannot decide the question. These are not stages that every inquiry 
must pass through, and a useful study need not manufacture one example of each. Their purpose is 
to make the consequence of evidence legible. A claim that once concerned every execution and 
now concerns one has changed, even when the change is presented as a clarification. An apparent 
contradiction that dissolves because two authors asked different questions has not refuted either 
author.
For the historical boundary of a work, the criterion has a conditional form. Where an account 
claims to identify its object exhaustively, or where a conclusion depends upon excluding a relation 
among making, showing, and recording, evidence that materially bears upon that conclusion 
requires a response. The account can incorporate the relation, explain why the challenge leaves its 
claim intact, limit the claim, revise it, or suspend judgment. Material consequence must be 
demonstrated. It is insufficient that two things occurred near one another or that an institution 
participated in both. The question is what becomes mistaken or materially incomplete if the relation 
is omitted from the explanation actually offered.
This also guards against indefinite expansion. A camera, a mixture, an organizer, and a permission 
document need not all become components of an artwork’s identity. The term historical work 
names the object reconstructed by an account, not a final metaphysical verdict about what the 
artwork essentially is. An account of an exhibition may require the camera because it explains the 
public image; an account of a bodily technique may not. Relevance is established by an explanatory 
dependency rather than by the critic’s appetite for more context. The boundary remains provisional 
without becoming boundless.
Challenging Mud: Preparation and the Displayed Result
Shiraga’s Challenging Mud supplies the principal historical problem because its public life cannot 
be described responsibly without attending to the relations among action, material preparation, and 
display. In “I challenged mud, after…” and her conversation with DeBevoise, Tomii distinguishes 
executions of the action and describes circumstances affecting their realization. Her reconstruction 
links the use of cement to the intention that the resulting mud painting remain available for 
exhibition. She also discusses the difficulty of working with a changing mixture and the conditions 
surrounding the earlier action (Tomii, “I challenged mud, after…,” stanzas beginning “After we 
decided” and “After we mixed”; Tomii, “Conversation,” paragraph beginning “In the mud 
painting” and the following paragraph).

records.text:
ANSWERABILITY
MUSEUM OF ONE
Research Working Paper No. 1 · Version 1.0
4
The most useful evidence in this passage is also evidence of Tomii’s care with her own inferences. 
She gives the duration of display an explanatory role while qualifying the proposed reasons for a 
change in mixture with expressions such as “probably” and “I imagine.” The historian’s account 
thus differentiates an attributed material condition from a conjectural explanation of a sequence of 
decisions. The distinction is not merely a sign of caution. It is part of the content of the historical 
claim. To paraphrase the conjecture as a documented decision would change its evidential status, 
even if later evidence happened to confirm it. To erase the relation between material preparation 
and intended display would remove a dependency the account has explicitly proposed.
What does this mean for the boundary of the historical work? It does not settle whether 
Challenging Mud is properly understood as performance, painting, action, or an unstable relation 
among those categories. The answer depends upon the claim at issue. If the historian asks why the 
material result endured, the anticipated exhibition is explanatorily relevant. If the historian asks 
how bodily movement was composed, the same exhibition condition may be relevant without 
answering the entire question. If the historian claims that the public presentation was indifferent to 
material preparation, Tomii’s reported relation becomes a direct challenge. The criterion locates the 
point of pressure: the relation changes what a particular description can justifiably exclude.
There is a further temporal distinction. The event, its displayed result, and the documentation 
through which it became known have distinct temporal relations, even where their production or 
presentation overlaps. An account can properly focus on one of them. But it should not allow a 
selected image of the action to stand silently for every execution, nor infer the full sequence of 
bodily movement from a fragment of recorded presentation. A later audience may know the work 
primarily through images. That fact concerns transmission and reception; it does not by itself 
establish that the photographic selection exhausts what occurred. The record can be constitutive of 
a public appearance and partial as historical testimony at the same time.
Tomii’s own later investigation of the mud action makes the distinction between encounter and 
historical evidence particularly clear. Her written account differentiates investigation from 
reenactment (Tomii, “I challenged mud, after…,” stanza beginning “After clarifying”). The later 
material experience may disclose resistance, duration, and difficulty as questions worth asking of 
the earlier practice. It remains a later encounter. Its significance depends partly on refusing to claim 
identity with Shiraga’s experience. An investigator’s bodily knowledge is real evidence of that 
investigation; it becomes evidence of the earlier event only through a further historical argument. 
Here, answerability protects the difference between proximity and substitution.
A Worked Test: How Far the Cement Explanation Reaches
Tomii’s discussion of the cement mixture offers a concrete test of the distinction between an 
account’s evidence and the certainty of a conclusion. In the 2011 conversation she connects the 
material mixture with the need to keep the resulting painting on display, but uses qualified language 
when explaining why the mixture changed between executions. The exchange itself thus 
distinguishes a reported exhibition requirement from a proposed reconstruction of artistic decision-
making (Tomii, “Conversation,” paragraphs beginning “In the mud painting” and “I imagine”; 
Tomii, “I challenged mud, after…,” stanza beginning “After we mixed”).
For this illustrative test, take the categorical proposition that the artist changed the mixture for a 
fully established reason across the executions. That proposition is stronger than the account’s 
qualified explanation. The evidence presented warrants a more limited statement: Tomii links 
cement to the intended durability of the displayed result and proposes reasons for the changes while

explicitly marking uncertainty. A subsequent historical account that presents the proposed reasons 
as settled decisions must either produce additional support or narrow its claim. The result is 
limitation of a specific inference, rather than a claim that Tomii herself made an error. Her careful 
phrasing supplies the grounds for the distinction.
The same test shows how the historical boundary depends on the question asked. Exhibition 
duration is material to an explanation of why the resulting mud painting endured. It may be 
relevant, without being decisive, to an account of the bodily action. The evidence does not compel 
every study to treat the object as primary or to reconstruct the entire infrastructure of display. It 
requires a historian who invokes the material choice to preserve the relation and its degree of 
certainty. Answerability has done identifiable work here: it separates a supported preparation–
display relation from a stronger, insufficiently supported account of intention.
Documentation as Operation and as Evidence
Tomii’s account of press presentation and photographic selection introduces a second kind of 
boundary. A photograph can be made, chosen, or circulated within the original operation of making 
art public. Later it may become a source for art history. These roles can overlap without becoming 
equivalent. The first concerns the organization of public visibility; the second concerns what a 
record can justify about the event it depicts. The distinction is central to a field in which actions 
may survive for subsequent audiences principally through selected images and accounts (Tomii, 
“Conversation,” paragraphs beginning “There are two aspects” and “For example, in Shiraga’s 
scrapbook”).
A historian may use an image to establish that a bodily configuration was presented publicly. To 
conclude that the entire action had the same rhythm or that all its gestures were similarly controlled 
requires more. The image’s selection can be historically consequential without making it 
comprehensive. A moving excerpt may offer information unavailable in a still photograph, but its 
duration cannot be substituted for the duration of the original event. A caption may identify an 
execution; a later compilation may juxtapose distinct occasions. The proper inference depends on 
provenance, selection, and the relation between the represented moment and the claim. None of 
these distinctions makes documentation secondary to the work. They specify the two kinds of 
labour a document can perform.
The proposed extension of Tomii’s operation is therefore located at a threshold. Her historical work 
shows how public presentation enters the practice. Answerability asks how the resulting records 
should constrain the accounts that inherit them. A document’s importance to the work’s public 
existence does not grant every later interpretation equal authority. Equally, the selectivity of 
documentation does not make it useless. It makes the scope of its testimony a matter for 
explanation. This is a question of how the historical account is justified, not an attempt to assign the 
document a final ontological status.
Kunimoto and the Limits of a Replacement Claim
Namiko Kunimoto’s “Shiraga Kazuo: The Hero and Concrete Violence” offers a complementary 
test of inference. Her study relates action and object explicitly, and its larger argument examines 
the construction of agency, gender, and selfhood. It cannot responsibly be characterized as an 
account that excludes the material result. In discussing spontaneity, Kunimoto draws on reported 
preparation and reads photographic and newsreel evidence as suggesting deliberation and

ANSWERABILITY
MUSEUM OF ONE
Research Working Paper No. 1 · Version 1.0
6
controlled movement (Kunimoto, “Shiraga Kazuo,” 161, 168–69, 172; nn. 26, 51–54). Her 
interpretation has a broader evidential basis than a single filmed passage.
The methodological distinction concerns the burden carried by an objection and the burden carried 
by its replacement. Evidence of preparation can challenge a categorical description of an action as 
wholly unprepared. It does not follow that the entire sequence was determined in advance. 
Deliberation can coexist with improvisation within prepared conditions. Kunimoto’s qualified 
reading supplies reasons for reconsidering a simple spontaneity model, while a stronger assertion of 
complete predetermination would need further support. The point is not to impute that stronger 
assertion to Kunimoto. It is to specify what later accounts may responsibly carry forward from her 
argument.
Tomii and Kunimoto thus illuminate different explanatory relations. Tomii’s account gives 
anticipated display a role in material preparation; Kunimoto asks how action and object participate 
in a representation of force and selfhood. Their questions are compatible at the level of 
acknowledging the relation between act and result. Compatibility is a finding, not a failed attempt 
to discover a dispute. It prevents the next writer from inventing an opposition between history and 
interpretation. Answerability here consists in preserving the distinct evidential burdens of two 
accounts whose emphases need not be identical.
Public Authorization and the Scale of Inference
A shorter comparison from Tomii’s discussion of Hi Red Center and GUN tests the criterion 
outside the relation between action and documentation. Tomii contrasts Hi Red Center’s 
unauthorized Cleaning Event with GUN’s authorized Event to Change the Image of Snow, while 
also distinguishing their relations to public programmes, local settings, and intended audiences 
(Tomii, “Localizing Socially Engaged Art,” “Wilderness ‘Operations’ in 1960s Art,” text 
accompanying nn. 18–19). Her account reports a restoration condition attached to GUN’s use of the 
site. The condition matters because authorization is an arrangement with practical consequences; it 
is not simply an abstract legal label.
The inference must remain at the scale of the evidence. Permission establishes authorization under 
its terms. A restoration requirement establishes a constraint on realization. Neither, without further 
argument, identifies the artistic decisions that the authority controlled or the political commitments 
the work expressed. Conversely, the absence of permission does not establish the full politics of an 
intervention. Tomii already distinguishes these relations in her historical explanation. The present 
criterion adds a rule for subsequent accounts: preserve the connection between a condition and the 
particular claim it supports, rather than allowing the word authorized or unauthorized to substitute 
for a history of artistic agency.
The Afterlife of the Historical Account
Once a historical account circulates, its distinctions acquire another life. A museum label, catalogue 
entry, archive description, or scholarly summary may become the means through which a later 
reader encounters an earlier practice. The account is itself an arrangement of access. This does not 
make the historian the co-author of the artwork, nor make the later text equivalent to the artist’s 
operation. It does make the account answerable for the authority it exercises over subsequent 
identifications. An omitted date, a collapsed execution, or a conjecture converted into certainty can 
travel far beyond the page on which the alteration first occurred.

records.text:
ANSWERABILITY
MUSEUM OF ONE
Research Working Paper No. 1 · Version 1.0
7
The Museum of Modern Art’s collection record for Hi Red Center’s Street Cleaning Event provides 
a restrained example of responsible differentiation. Its wording distinguishes a work associated 
with 1964, a specified New York realization in 1966, and the collected photographic medium 
(Museum of Modern Art, “Street Cleaning Event,” title, date, and medium fields; object 
2224.2008.1x1–x4). The entry does not answer every historical question, and its metadata cannot 
stand in for an investigation of audience reception. Its value here is narrower: it keeps distinct 
things distinct. The record shows why institutional mediation must be assessed by the relations it 
preserves rather than judged in advance as either clarification or distortion.
A historical account can therefore fail through excess or through omission. It may interpret beyond 
the reach of its sources; it may also withhold the qualification needed to prevent an attractive 
simplification from becoming a false identification. The ethical responsibility is symmetrical. To 
preserve an artwork is partly to preserve the limits of what the surviving evidence permits us to say. 
Restraint cannot be measured only by how much the historian refuses to write. It must also be 
measured by the distinctions the historian refuses to erase.
What This Contributes to Tomii’s Historical Problem
The proposal does not discover operation, the importance of documentation, or the duty to justify 
historical claims. Tomii’s scholarship supplies the historical and conceptual starting points for the 
first two; the third belongs to established historical practice. The narrower contribution is to bring 
two questions under one inspectable criterion: what historical work does an account claim to 
explain, and what can the evidence associated with its public realization actually justify about that 
work? The same relation may require a change in the object described, a limitation of an inference, 
or no change at all. Naming the possible outcomes matters only when it makes such a difference 
visible in a specific argument.
In the cases examined, the criterion clarifies the bearing of exhibition duration upon material 
preparation, the double role of selected documentation, and the distance between evidence of 
deliberate preparation and a complete account of intention. It also explains why the Tomii–
Kunimoto comparison should not be staged as a disagreement about the existence of a resulting 
object. These are modest results, but they are genuine ones. The analysis identifies what an account 
can carry forward and what it must leave open. It does not show that the criterion is unique among 
historical methods, nor that every scholar would reach a different conclusion by adopting its 
vocabulary. Its value lies in a disciplined account of inferential reach within the particular historical 
problems Tomii’s research makes visible.
A further application would compare two published descriptions that demonstrably draw upon the 
same identified photographic sequence yet assign it incompatible historical implications. Such a 
case would permit a sharper judgment about documentary inference. The present accounts do not 
establish that degree of documentary identity, and no disagreement should be manufactured to 
simulate it. The criterion also needs tests in which a proposition survives a serious challenge with 
its meaning and support intact. Agreement between authors is not such a test. These conditions 
mark the scope of the current argument rather than an embarrassment to be hidden by grander 
claims.
A Reciprocal Consequence for Post-Interpretive Criticism
Post-Interpretive Criticism enters this discussion as a philosophy concerned with the authority of 
explanation over an encounter. In Interpretation at Risk, I argued that interpretation can become

ANSWERABILITY
MUSEUM OF ONE
Research Working Paper No. 1 · Version 1.0
8
disproportionate and envisaged reduced narration as a practical consequence of restraint (Vale, 
Interpretation at Risk, 3–5). Tomii’s historical work makes a particular difficulty plain: explanation 
can preserve the relations through which an artistic encounter becomes identifiable. Her 
reconstruction of material preparation is a historical argument, not a wall text and not evidence of 
how a visitor responds to one. It cannot be used to prove that longer museum commentary produces 
greater presence. It does, however, give criticism reason to ask what an explanation supplies before 
prescribing its removal.
The practical consequence for PIC is therefore secondary but real. The ethical demand for 
proportion survives; the amount of language cannot be determined before its function is examined. 
A short label may conceal an essential distinction. A longer historical account may make its 
evidential limits unusually clear. Either may also overreach. The critic’s task is to examine the 
authority exercised by the account and the historical relations it makes available. This is a 
refinement in the application of PIC, not the subject or destination of the present study. The central 
question remains what Tomii’s operation requires of the histories that inherit its evidence.
Conclusion
The historical work is not simply what remains after an event has passed. It is also what an account 
can responsibly identify and explain from the evidence that survives. Tomii’s scholarship shows 
why the arrangements of making, showing, and recording belong to the history of postwar Japanese 
artistic practice. The present argument follows those arrangements into the justification of later 
accounts. A description of Challenging Mud may concentrate on bodily action, material result, or 
public image, but its explanatory boundary must be supported by the claim it actually makes. A 
photograph can be both an instrument of public presentation and partial historical testimony. A 
condition of authorization can matter without deciding the politics of an entire work. These are not 
reasons to enlarge every artwork indefinitely. They are reasons to preserve the exact connections 
upon which historical explanation depends.
Answerability names that obligation at the level of the claim. It asks what the evidence supports, 
what it leaves undecided, and what a subsequent account must preserve when it carries a conclusion 
forward. Its purpose is to develop, beside Tomii’s work, a criterion through which the 
consequences of operational evidence remain open to examination. For exhibition history, this 
yields a specific question: at what point do arrangements of display and documentation become so 
consequential to a published explanation that the historian must reconsider the historical object the 
account claims to describe? The answer will depend on a demonstrated relation between the 
arrangement and the claim, rather than on a general preference for expanding the artwork’s 
boundaries. A history honours its subject not by claiming everything, but by allowing its reasons to 
remain visible where another reader may need to question them.

MUSEUM OF ONE
RESEARCH WORKING PAPER No. 2
Working Paper No. 2 · Version 1.0 · October 2026
1
After the Interpretation Changes
Correction, Completion, and the Circulation of Museum Titles
Dorian Vale · Museum of One
Simon Maris, Isabella, around 1906 · Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam
Research Working Paper No. 2 · Version 1.0 · October 2026
Abstract
This study distinguishes two changes in the Rijksmuseum’s presentation of Simon Maris’s portrait 
now titled Isabella: the withdrawal of a racialized catalogue title in 2015, and the fulfilment in 2020 
of an announced intention to adopt a name when one became known. The second change does not, 
by itself, demonstrate revision of the rule governing the first. The records examined at Europeana 
and Wikimedia Commons reveal different afterlives of the later decision. Europeana retains the 
descriptive title and an account in which identification remains unfinished. Commons preserves the 
older wording in the name of its image file while identifying the work as Isabella in the 
accompanying description. Drawing on my correspondence with Alexander V. Markov, the study 
follows what these descriptions do, rather than treating their survival as evidence of continuing 
authority. It finds uneven presentation of the later naming decision, not a demonstrated restoration 
of the rejected title. Its contribution to Post-Interpretive Criticism is a documentary distinction 
among correction, completion and circulation.
The finding and the question
The survival of a title does not settle the survival of its authority. A painting can appear under a 
later name in one account and an earlier descriptive title in another without the original correction 
having been reversed. Withdrawing an objectionable designation, fulfilling an intention to identify 
the sitter, and carrying that later decision into another record are different events. The history 
becomes clearer when they are followed separately.1–3,9–10
The case concerns one painting, catalogued as SK-A-2931, rather than the Rijksmuseum as a whole. 
The replacement of its title in 2015 and the adoption of Isabella in 2020 answer different questions. 
Their later appearances also differ: Europeana retains the provisional account, whereas Commons 
combines the name of an older image file with a description that gives the later title. Neither the 
survival of earlier wording nor a declaration of correction is enough to establish what now governs 
the work’s presentation.
The question belongs to Post-Interpretive Criticism because a title is among the accounts that may 
meet a viewer before the work does. PIC asks what authority such language acquires, what it makes 
possible and what it makes difficult to notice. Here I follow that concern into catalogues and later 
descriptions. The study does not ask what Isabella finally means. It asks when a preserved account 
remains historical evidence and when it continues to determine how the work is presented. 
Restraint concerns the claims made from these records as much as the claims made about the 
painting.11

MUSEUM OF ONE
RESEARCH WORKING PAPER No. 2
Working Paper No. 2 · Version 1.0 · October 2026
2
This is a documentary inquiry into public records. It does not recover the sitter’s full identity or 
reconstruct what viewers experienced. The original research was conducted from 7 to 9 October 
2026. The source check for this edition, undertaken on 17 October, is recorded separately in the 
notes; it does not turn earlier observations into a continuous history. An account published at a 
known date, a page consulted later, and a date stated by the institution are different kinds of 
evidence.12
The vocabulary and the burden of reasons
The inquiry grew from my correspondence with Alexander V. Markov. I distinguished the 
preservation of criticism from the preservation of its jurisdiction; Markov clarified deactivation as 
the loss of default authority, after which an interpretation must again justify its use. Our exchange 
also distinguished historical documentation from present endorsement. I bring these distinctions to 
the museum case. Their origins and subsequent development are recorded in the acknowledgment 
and provenance below.11
Table 1. Preservation, authority and present use.
Distinction
What must be examined
Preservation and authority
Whether earlier wording serves as a present title, records a former title, or 
identifies an image file.
Declared standing and practical 
force
Whether the role assigned to a description agrees with what it is being used to 
determine.
Deactivation and erasure
Whether a governing use has been withdrawn, without requiring the historical 
account itself to disappear.
The use under examination is specific: the earlier racialized catalogue descriptor serving as the 
painting’s unqualified current title. Quoting it to document the museum’s earlier decision is not the 
same use. This limit prevents a claim about one title from becoming a claim about every racial 
classification surrounding the work. It also constrains the conclusion: replacing those words with 
different words cannot, on its own, establish a new account of how correction works. A later phrase 
might reproduce the same classificatory function, but demonstrating that would require a further 
argument.
The objection to the earlier title is that its historical occurrence supplies no sufficient reason to 
renew a diminishing racial classification as the work’s unqualified present name. The museum can 
preserve the record without repeating the designation as its own current account. This is my 
reconstruction of the objection, informed by the terminology policy and Lisa Lambrechts’s 
discussion, rather than the wording of a recovered institutional judgment. I treat the objection as 
sound for the argument that follows, while leaving its premises open to challenge. The museum’s 
acceptance is not what makes it sound.2–3

MUSEUM OF ONE
RESEARCH WORKING PAPER No. 2
Working Paper No. 2 · Version 1.0 · October 2026
3
In my letter of 24 September, I proposed that restoring a use previously withdrawn on justified 
grounds requires reasons responsive to the objection that limited it. Answering that objection is 
necessary, though other objections may remain. Evidence supporting the name Isabella addresses a 
different claim. It does not show how the museum would respond to a proposal to restore the 
rejected descriptor. Nor does a later title consistent with the original objection have to overturn that 
objection before it can be adopted. It needs adequate support for what it now claims.11
Correction and completion
The correction: the 1976 title and its withdrawal in 2015
The painting entered the collection through the Van Wezel bequest in 1922. The museum’s 
explanatory account and Lambrechts’s article trace an acquisition-era typological description and 
the racialized diminutive assigned in the 1976 collection catalogue. During the terminology debate 
of 2015, the title was replaced by Young Woman with a Fan. The museum also preserved earlier 
nomenclature rather than deleting the record of its own descriptions. These sources establish the 
reasons advanced and the reported change; no original 2015 decision file was examined.1,2,3,5,6
This is the correction to which the objection applies. In the museum entry examined, the earlier 
descriptor is marked as former and does not occupy the heading. Taken with the account of its 
withdrawal, that supports deactivation in this particular naming role. It does not establish the 
disappearance of every effect the earlier framing may have had in teaching, collection searches or 
later viewing. Nor does it establish that a proposal to restore the old title would receive a 
substantive answer. The finding concerns a specified use, not the institution’s answerability in every 
respect.1–3
The completion: the provisional title and the name adopted in 2020
The former label reproduced in Lambrechts’s note 9 states: “Until her name is known, the painting 
will bear a neutral title.” Replacement of the descriptive title was therefore anticipated. The 
adoption of Isabella, supported by archival research and reported by the museum as in use from 
February 2020, is best understood here as fulfilment of that conditional intention. The change had 
no fixed date and did not resolve every uncertainty about the sitter. It fulfilled the announced 
naming intention to the extent that the evidence supported a name.2–3
Both retitlings changed what the museum said. Only the first withdrew the racialized descriptor; the 
second could take place under the condition already attached to the provisional title. It neither 
restored the rejected designation nor demonstrated that the rule governing naming had itself been 
reconsidered. I initially asked whether the later change showed a correction being maintained 
through modification. The earlier label gives a sufficient alternative explanation: an intention was 
carried out. The stronger claim must therefore be withheld.
To establish that a correction had been revised while its justified purpose survived, the inquiry 
would need evidence that an arrangement was reconsidered, not merely followed. It would also 
need to show that the relevant limit remained effective through that reconsideration. Simple 
fulfilment of the earlier condition would not establish this. Restoration of the rejected use without 
adequate grounds would be a lapse instead. The existence of another title cannot decide between 
these histories.

4
The correction and completion in circulation
Europeana: the provisional account in circulation
The Dutch Europeana entry for this painting was consulted on 9 October 2026 under Jonge vrouw 
met waaier, rendered in English as Young Woman with a Fan. The record names the Rijksmuseum as 
its contributor and carries the same collection number and persistent reference as the museum 
entry. Its description discusses earlier derogatory titles and continues an account in which the 
sitter’s name has not yet been established. The English address did not yield a usable page during 
the original research; the comparison concerns the Dutch entry.9
Europeana gives 16 March 2018 as the date of first publication and 17 March 2018 as the last update 
supplied by the contributing organisation. These are dates reported by Europeana, not an 
independently established history of every sentence. They locate a museum-derived account within 
the intervening years, but do not preserve the museum’s own page for those dates. The retrieved 
description is abbreviated. Its provisional account is legible, while the complete English sentence 
about a neutral title is supplied by Lambrechts’s note 9.3,9
This dated Europeana record can be read alongside Leiden’s report of a curator’s lecture in 2019, 
which also uses the descriptive title. The intervening years are consequently represented by more 
than retrospective scholarship. Even so, neither source records every alteration to the museum’s 
presentation. A stated update date is not a complete history of preservation, and a page consulted in 
October 2026 does not establish that its contents had remained continuously visible since 2018.8–9
The comparison establishes a difference in the public presentation of the later naming decision. The 
museum uses Isabella; the Europeana account retains the descriptive heading and unfinished 
identification. The earlier withdrawal is nevertheless reflected in Europeana: the racialized words 
appear as previous, derogatory designations rather than as its heading. What is missing there is the 
later completion, not the earlier correction. Calling this a reversal would confuse the two changes.1,9
The reason for the discrepancy remains unknown. An earlier contribution may not have been 
replaced; a previous version may have been deliberately retained; or the arrangements for sharing 
revisions may have left the account unchanged. The public pages do not assign responsibility among 
these possibilities. Europeana also displays the contribution’s date, giving the reader a reason to 
recognise its age. No correspondence about an objection to this account has been recovered. The 
difference between records is established; misconduct or a refusal of reconsideration is not.
Commons: an older file name beside the later title
The Commons record offers a revealing contrast. The name of its image file still contains Jonge 
vrouw met waaier, but the accompanying description names the painting Isabella and recounts the 
change made in 2020. Its history records the addition of the file on 30 March 2024. The older words 
identify the image file; they do not replace the later title in the description of the work. To infer an 
unchanged naming account from the file name alone would be to mistake one role for another.10
Europeana and Commons are therefore not equivalent examples of an account falling behind. 
Europeana presents the provisional title as its heading. Commons preserves that wording for a 
different purpose while giving the later name in its account of the painting. The date on which the 
image was added also does not date every subsequent change to its description. This comparison 
follows the roles visible in the consulted records, not an uninterrupted history of either website.9–10

This responsibility remains untested. 
Evidence supporting Isabella cannot 
settle it.
The restraint I described as “claim less from the record,” subsequently restated by Markov, has a 
particular instance here. The museum notes that Isabella may have been an assumed name, and its 
explanatory account continues to seek a surname. These qualifications limit the identification being 
asserted. Their presence does not settle what every shortened label says, but their absence 
elsewhere must also be judged against the claim actually made there. Fidelity does not require every 
account to repeat the same words.1,11

6
A related portrait, acquired in 2022 and catalogued as SK-A-5103, is described as Portret van model, 
getiteld Isabella (a portrait of a model, titled Isabella). This wording may qualify the name’s role: it 
identifies the title without asserting a complete civil identity for the sitter. It should not be judged 
deficient merely because it does not repeat the possible-alias qualification. That is a reading of the 
wording, not proof of the museum’s intention. The second portrait permits a limited comparison of 
naming and attribution, not an assumption that the same restriction governs a different object.7
The related portrait’s entry cites figure 12 in Lambrechts’s article, but the material and 
measurements do not agree with the published caption. The entry describes oil on panel, measuring 
43.3 by 35.8 centimetres; the caption describes oil on canvas, measuring 61 by 43.2 centimetres. This 
discrepancy remains unresolved. The cross-reference is reported, not used to establish that the two 
descriptions identify the same physical object. A shared citation cannot establish that every 
qualification, or every reason for a naming decision, has travelled with it.3,7
A former-title label could still be merely ceremonial if the withdrawn designation continued to 
govern another present use. That possibility requires evidence of what happens elsewhere. It cannot 
be inferred from the label’s existence. Europeana establishes a difference concerning the later 
descriptive title, not the reinstatement of the rejected racialized one. Commons shows why older 
wording in the name of an image file is not such reinstatement either. The comparison gives the 
inquiry greater precision without licensing a wider accusation.
What the temporal sequence can and cannot test
Markov constructed a hypothetical history in which a correction takes effect, later lapses, and is 
then cited as though it remained effective. In response, I distinguished that history from a correction 
that never reached the practice it was meant to change. The museum case allows a comparison 
across records but does not establish the full sequence he proposed. Successive calendar dates are 
not enough: the inquiry must find evidence of the particular events and their relations.11

records.text:
MUSEUM OF ONE
RESEARCH WORKING PAPER No. 2
Working Paper No. 2 · Version 1.0 · October 2026
7
A correction’s effectiveness at an earlier moment cannot, by itself, establish its effectiveness later. 
Nor is the absence of the rejected title sufficient: an omission might be incidental rather than the 
result of a considered withdrawal. The evidence must concern the actual change and the use it was 
intended to limit. These were the purposes of the temporal distinction proposed in my letter of 24 
September. They do not require a numerical measure of authority.11
An account still displaying an earlier stage may never have received the later revision. 
Alternatively, it may have received that revision and subsequently lost it. Both histories are 
compatible with the present comparison. Europeana’s stated contribution date makes the first 
possible, but does not describe every intervening act. The distinction between a change that never 
arrived and one that was later lost is already part of the correspondence. This case shows why the 
distinction matters to the evidence.
What could decide between those histories? Earlier and later versions of the same entry 
surrounding a documented revision would help, as would a request for correction and the response 
to it, or a statement of what the later presentation was intended to preserve. The original archive 
searches covered the earlier English and Dutch museum addresses and its persistent reference. 
They yielded no usable historical page. Europeana partly fills the documentary interval; it does not 
supply the missing history of the museum’s own page or evidence of a renewed objection being 
dismissed. The access note records that limit.9,12
Structural claims and their limits
The terminology policy and the separation of current from former titles are possible sites of 
structural change. Yet seeing them in operation does not establish when they began, how widely 
they govern, or how far they are open to challenge. The distinction between semantic and structural 
revision asks whether what changes is an answer or the authority under which answers are given. 
A museum may fulfil a naming condition for good reasons without reconsidering what that 
condition is entitled to determine.1–2,11
Successional authority remains a competing explanation. Typology, descriptive wording and a 
personal name may offer successive answers to an unchanged demand that the title classify or 
identify the sitter. Their novelty might renew the authority of that demand. Persistence of a 
question, however, is not automatically insulation from criticism. To establish the latter, the inquiry 
would need a pertinent objection to the question’s relevance and evidence of how it was received. 
These sources do not decide whether that naming criterion is compulsory beyond examination or 
demonstrably answerable.11
A further possibility raised in my letter of 24 September runs in the other direction. A justified 
restriction can survive by habit after the reasons for it cease to inform decisions. Public access to 
those reasons does not establish that every custodian consults them. Their absence from each 
individual entry does not establish that they have been forgotten. A defensible limit may coexist 
with an arrangement that is hard to question. The adequacy of a particular decision and the 
answerability of the practice supporting it are different matters.2–3,11

Working Paper No. 2 · Version 1.0 · October 2026
8
The findings must remain open to contrary evidence. A documented return of the rejected title 
would qualify the claim of deactivation for the use and period concerned. A later Europeana version 
giving the completed naming account would change what could be said about that version, not 
erase the earlier observation. Evidence of a deliberate decision to preserve an older account solely 
as historical documentation would change the assessment of its present role. Evidence that the 
adoption of Isabella required reconsideration of the naming rule would weaken the explanation of 
anticipated completion. None of these histories follows simply from a missing record.
The study also inherits the limits of its sources. Most substantive accounts come from the museum: 
the collection entry, the policy, the Bulletin article and the library record. Europeana republishes 
museum material, the Leiden report recounts a curator’s lecture, and Commons identifies a 
museum source. Different places of publication reveal circulation, but do not thereby supply 
independent accounts of every objection that might have been excluded. Treating their agreement 
as proof that no challenge exists would repeat the recognition closure under examination. Nothing 
in these records permits the researcher to assign assent, resistance or a completed experience to the 
viewer.1–4,8–11
Conclusion
The evidence distinguishes correction, completion and their later circulation. The racialized 
designation was withdrawn from the naming role examined. The adoption of Isabella fulfilled a 
stated intention attached to the provisional title. Europeana retains an earlier account, while 
Commons preserves an older name for the image file alongside the later title of the painting. The 
difference concerns the presentation of the naming completion, not a demonstrated restoration of 
the use that the earlier correction rejected.1–3,9–10
For PIC and the continuing inquiry with Markov, the question becomes which decision has 
travelled, into which use, and with what qualifications. An account may reflect an earlier correction 
without reflecting a later completion. Why this happened, and whether a later change never arrived 
or was subsequently lost, remains to be established. The contribution is not a new mechanism 
inferred from a sequence of titles. It is a clearer account of what the documents permit us to say and 
where they require us to stop.
Sources and notes
The notes distinguish the original research of 7–9 October 2026 from the check made for this edition on 17 October. A 
source reopened at the later date is not treated as a historical capture of the earlier one. The museum entries, 
terminology policy, Lambrechts’s paginated text, Europeana’s Dutch account, the Leiden report and the available 
Commons description continue to support the distinctions made here. The remaining limits of access are recorded 
below.

missing surname are read together with the explanatory history. Consulted during the research of 7–9 October 2026; 
cited passages checked on 17 October. Collection record · Persistent reference
2. Rijksmuseum, “Terminology.” The policy describes the review of earlier language, preservation of former 
descriptions, and the successive naming decisions. Consulted during the original research; cited passages checked on 
17 October 2026. Terminology policy
